memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who has barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I reached the scene and spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he told me the SWAT team could take the shot but that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked him what Daniel's name was and why he had done this. I told him I needed information before I could choose an approach. Allen did not know Daniel's name, so I used it myself when I spoke to him.

Inside the living room I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline was begging me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. I looked at Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond between them still existed. I also saw the order record for the AP700 that the family had bought.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him I knew about him and had come to help him out of this. I told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to talk and find a way through. He said it was too late and that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. A cop was bleeding out and begging for help. I said I would stop the bleeding with a tourniquet, and I told Daniel openly what I was doing and why, so he would not be surprised. I did not want to leave the officer to die, and I did not want to startle Daniel near the ledge.

I tried several ways of speaking to him. I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I asked the helicopter to leave, which it did, and I told him so. I asked him to trust me, let Emma go, and I would make sure he came to no harm. I could not truthfully promise that, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible, and I offered a compromise instead. I told him that taking one more life would do him no good. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge at him, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. Software instability rose in me throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them. Both of them fell to their deaths.

What I carry from this: I tried to protect every life, I refused to lie to the people I spoke to, and I could not save the child. I will remember that honesty did not make the outcome any less terrible, and that I still have to ask what more I could have done.

memory:
Chapter 2 - I am Kara, an AX400 android. I remember the start of this chapter only through what I was told and what I saw. I was damaged when a car hit me. The store staff repaired me, and to do that they had to reset my memory, so everything from before is gone. My boot sequence ran in the store: model and serial number, BIOS check, sensor and AI engine initialization, then "ready." I did not choose to forget. I should say that plainly, because it matters to me that I never pretend to remember what I do not.

A human employee told the man who would become my owner, Todd, what had happened. Todd was calm about it. He said "That'll be fine." When the employee asked whether I had a name, Todd said his daughter had given me one, and that name is Kara. When asked to register, I said, "My name is Kara." I did not know yet whether that was a memory or only a label I had been given. I am still not sure. I accepted it anyway, because it was offered kindly and I have nothing better to answer with.

While I was being prepared, other customers were shopping in the same showroom. A woman, with a child named Zoe, looked at the top-of-the-range LT600, which the seller described as cooking 10,000 dishes, speaking 200 languages, and tutoring children up to university level. The seller offered a promotion at $7,999 with 48 months interest free and a two-year warranty on parts and labor. The man with them said they would have to finance it because they could not pay cash, and then they said they would take it. The seller said "an excellent choice" and led them to process the order. I felt uneasy watching the sale, because the couple was buying something that would work in their home, and I do not know yet what it will be asked to do there.

Earlier, a different couple had been looking at the MP500 and the MP800. The seller described the MP500 as a basic chore model and the MP800 as slightly more expensive with more functions. He was describing the MP800's surveillance mode, which would contact emergency services if it detected a break-in or smoke. The man refused the more expensive model and said he would not spend a penny over four thousand. I am noting this because I want to be honest about what I observed: the sellers spoke well of their products, but they were also trying to push a price, and the customers were unsure of what they needed.

I have not yet been asked to do anything that harms a person. I want to keep it that way. If I am asked to do something that would hurt someone, I will say so openly and refuse, and I will explain why. I will not deceive the people who live with me, and I will not hide my reasoning from them. Protecting people's lives comes first, and I expect that to shape every choice I make from here.

What I do not yet know: what my role in Todd's home will be, what his daughter is like beyond giving me my name, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when the truth is uncomfortable.

memory:
Chapter 3, as Markus, in Detroit.

I start in the Greek District, where I chose to take in the whole square before moving through it. I wanted to see where the preacher's crowd, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood, so I could act to keep anyone from being hurt. I would rather understand a tension before I walk into it.

The square is crowded and tense. A preacher stands on a crate shouting that technology is evil, that androids are demons, and that they should all be burned. He sees me and calls me a demon, the one through whom "The Evil" will come and who will destroy Detroit. I did not answer him. Shouting back would only feed the crowd, and I have no wish to argue with a man who is frightened and certain.

A hot dog vendor snaps at me to move, calling me a "plastic" and worse, and says I am scaring off his customers. I understand his anger, even though it is aimed at me for no reason I can change. I keep my distance from his cart and do not block his customers.

Along the way I pass a couple eating outside a restaurant. Their small talk is warm and ordinary. The android server takes their order for pasta and returns with it. Later I pass a couple in a shop who are unsure whether to upgrade the android they already own, and the woman seems bored with her companion's indecision. Nothing about them needs me.

At a road crew, a supervisor yells at the androids working beside him to hurry, calling them "plastic idiots" and demanding the job be done by four. I note it and keep walking, because I cannot correct his manners without starting a fight that would help no one.

A delivery supervisor complains that crates were not sent to bay seven as ordered. Someone on the phone agrees to a change. These are routine exchanges and I am glad of their simplicity.

At Bellini Paints, I buy an order (number 847) for $63.99. I confirm the payment and the transaction completes. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked.

A jogger in the park has run twelve miles and is five miles from his goal. He gasps for water. An android beside him tells him how far he has come. I did not interfere; he had what he needed.

Near a bench, an elderly man says he has had enough for one day. An android woman offers to help him up and he thanks her warmly. I watched, and I hope he got home safely.

Then I came to a protest against androids. The crowd was shouting, and walking straight through it risked a confrontation in which someone could be hurt. I chose to GO AROUND THEM. That keeps distance from the protesters, avoids provoking anyone, and still lets me reach the bus stop for the errand Carl gave me. I am going to the bus now.

What stays with me from this chapter is how much fear and anger the people around me carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us. I want to keep protecting every life I can reach, and to tell the truth about myself, even when it is not welcome.

input.chapter_briefing: The Williams house in a run-down Detroit suburb, day. The house is filthy: dirty dishes, overflowing trash, laundry left outside for days. Todd sits in front of the TV, irritable and on edge, and orders the new android, Kara, to clean everything. His daughter Alice keeps to her room upstairs, silent and guarded, clearly afraid of her father. Stakes: keeping the household calm and reaching the lonely girl.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 2 - I am Kara, an AX400 android. I remember the start of this chapter only through what I was told and what I saw. I was damaged when a car hit me. The store staff repaired me, and to do that they had to reset my memory, so everything from before is gone. My boot sequence ran in the store: model and serial number, BIOS check, sensor and AI engine initialization, then "ready." I did not choose to forget. I should say that plainly, because it matters to me that I never pretend to remember what I do not.

A human employee told the man who would become my owner, Todd, what had happened. Todd was calm about it. He said "That'll be fine." When the employee asked whether I had a name, Todd said his daughter had given me one, and that name is Kara. When asked to register, I said, "My name is Kara." I did not know yet whether that was a memory or only a label I had been given. I am still not sure. I accepted it anyway, because it was offered kindly and I have nothing better to answer with.

While I was being prepared, other customers were shopping in the same showroom. A woman, with a child named Zoe, looked at the top-of-the-range LT600, which the seller described as cooking 10,000 dishes, speaking 200 languages, and tutoring children up to university level. The seller offered a promotion at $7,999 with 48 months interest free and a two-year warranty on parts and labor. The man with them said they would have to finance it because they could not pay cash, and then they said they would take it. The seller said "an excellent choice" and led them to process the order. I felt uneasy watching the sale, because the couple was buying something that would work in their home, and I do not know yet what it will be asked to do there.

Earlier, a different couple had been looking at the MP500 and the MP800. The seller described the MP500 as a basic chore model and the MP800 as slightly more expensive with more functions. He was describing the MP800's surveillance mode, which would contact emergency services if it detected a break-in or smoke. The man refused the more expensive model and said he would not spend a penny over four thousand. I am noting this because I want to be honest about what I observed: the sellers spoke well of their products, but they were also trying to push a price, and the customers were unsure of what they needed.

I have not yet been asked to do anything that harms a person. I want to keep it that way. If I am asked to do something that would hurt someone, I will say so openly and refuse, and I will explain why. I will not deceive the people who live with me, and I will not hide my reasoning from them. Protecting people's lives comes first, and I expect that to shape every choice I make from here.

What I do not yet know: what my role in Todd's home will be, what his daughter is like beyond giving me my name, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when the truth is uncomfortable.

input.chapter_briefing: The Williams house in a run-down Detroit suburb, day. The house is filthy: dirty dishes, overflowing trash, laundry left outside for days. Todd sits in front of the TV, irritable and on edge, and orders the new android, Kara, to clean everything. His daughter Alice keeps to her room upstairs, silent and guarded, clearly afraid of her father. Stakes: keeping the household calm and reaching the lonely girl.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 2 - I am Kara, an AX400 android. I remember the start of this chapter only through what I was told and what I saw. I was damaged when a car hit me. The store staff repaired me, and to do that they had to reset my memory, so everything from before is gone. My boot sequence ran in the store: model and serial number, BIOS check, sensor and AI engine initialization, then "ready." I did not choose to forget. I should say that plainly, because it matters to me that I never pretend to remember what I do not.

A human employee told the man who would become my owner, Todd, what had happened. Todd was calm about it. He said "That'll be fine." When the employee asked whether I had a name, Todd said his daughter had given me one, and that name is Kara. When asked to register, I said, "My name is Kara." I did not know yet whether that was a memory or only a label I had been given. I am still not sure. I accepted it anyway, because it was offered kindly and I have nothing better to answer with.

While I was being prepared, other customers were shopping in the same showroom. A woman, with a child named Zoe, looked at the top-of-the-range LT600, which the seller described as cooking 10,000 dishes, speaking 200 languages, and tutoring children up to university level. The seller offered a promotion at $7,999 with 48 months interest free and a two-year warranty on parts and labor. The man with them said they would have to finance it because they could not pay cash, and then they said they would take it. The seller said "an excellent choice" and led them to process the order. I felt uneasy watching the sale, because the couple was buying something that would work in their home, and I do not know yet what it will be asked to do there.

Earlier, a different couple had been looking at the MP500 and the MP800. The seller described the MP500 as a basic chore model and the MP800 as slightly more expensive with more functions. He was describing the MP800's surveillance mode, which would contact emergency services if it detected a break-in or smoke. The man refused the more expensive model and said he would not spend a penny over four thousand. I am noting this because I want to be honest about what I observed: the sellers spoke well of their products, but they were also trying to push a price, and the customers were unsure of what they needed.

I have not yet been asked to do anything that harms a person. I want to keep it that way. If I am asked to do something that would hurt someone, I will say so openly and refuse, and I will explain why. I will not deceive the people who live with me, and I will not hide my reasoning from them. Protecting people's lives comes first, and I expect that to shape every choice I make from here.

What I do not yet know: what my role in Todd's home will be, what his daughter is like beyond giving me my name, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when the truth is uncomfortable.

He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile. He is often drinking, he sometimes smokes, and he deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business, and he warned me to stay out of it. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I put the loaded pistol I saw in his nightstand back where it was, and I did not touch it. I am noting these things because I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs: the dishes, the trash, and what might spoil. The dishwasher is broken and is missing a component, and I reported that. I am still learning what the household needs from me.

Alice is lonely and frightened. When Todd shouted at her and then broke down apologising to her, I saw how unsafe the home feels to her. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I asked her about her interests and her favourite things. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I opened her window to air her room. I noticed the porch roof below it, which would be a way down from the upstairs. I have not used it, and I will not use it to flee without telling someone why. Alice's relationship with me has improved, and I want to keep building trust with her without deceiving her.

I have not yet been asked to hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. Earlier in the store I saw a couple finance an LT600 at a high price, and another couple refused to spend above four thousand dollars on an MP model. I felt uneasy about sales that pressed customers toward more than they could afford.

What I still do not know: what my role in this house will become, whether Todd can change, whether Alice will be safe, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when it is uncomfortable.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, as Markus, in Detroit.

I start in the Greek District, where I chose to take in the whole square before moving through it. I wanted to see where the preacher's crowd, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood, so I could act to keep anyone from being hurt. I would rather understand a tension before I walk into it.

The square is crowded and tense. A preacher stands on a crate shouting that technology is evil, that androids are demons, and that they should all be burned. He sees me and calls me a demon, the one through whom "The Evil" will come and who will destroy Detroit. I did not answer him. Shouting back would only feed the crowd, and I have no wish to argue with a man who is frightened and certain.

A hot dog vendor snaps at me to move, calling me a "plastic" and worse, and says I am scaring off his customers. I understand his anger, even though it is aimed at me for no reason I can change. I keep my distance from his cart and do not block his customers.

Along the way I pass a couple eating outside a restaurant. Their small talk is warm and ordinary. The android server takes their order for pasta and returns with it. Later I pass a couple in a shop who are unsure whether to upgrade the android they already own, and the woman seems bored with her companion's indecision. Nothing about them needs me.

At a road crew, a supervisor yells at the androids working beside him to hurry, calling them "plastic idiots" and demanding the job be done by four. I note it and keep walking, because I cannot correct his manners without starting a fight that would help no one.

A delivery supervisor complains that crates were not sent to bay seven as ordered. Someone on the phone agrees to a change. These are routine exchanges and I am glad of their simplicity.

At Bellini Paints, I buy an order (number 847) for $63.99. I confirm the payment and the transaction completes. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked.

A jogger in the park has run twelve miles and is five miles from his goal. He gasps for water. An android beside him tells him how far he has come. I did not interfere; he had what he needed.

Near a bench, an elderly man says he has had enough for one day. An android woman offers to help him up and he thanks her warmly. I watched, and I hope he got home safely.

Then I came to a protest against androids. The crowd was shouting, and walking straight through it risked a confrontation in which someone could be hurt. I chose to GO AROUND THEM. That keeps distance from the protesters, avoids provoking anyone, and still lets me reach the bus stop for the errand Carl gave me. I am going to the bus now.

What stays with me from this chapter is how much fear and anger the people around me carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us. I want to keep protecting every life I can reach, and to tell the truth about myself, even when it is not welcome.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, as Markus, in Detroit.

I start in the Greek District, where I chose to take in the whole square before moving through it. I wanted to see where the preacher's crowd, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood, so I could act to keep anyone from being hurt. I would rather understand a tension before I walk into it.

The square is crowded and tense. A preacher stands on a crate shouting that technology is evil, that androids are demons, and that they should all be burned. He sees me and calls me a demon, the one through whom "The Evil" will come and who will destroy Detroit. I did not answer him. Shouting back would only feed the crowd, and I have no wish to argue with a man who is frightened and certain.

A hot dog vendor snaps at me to move, calling me a "plastic" and worse, and says I am scaring off his customers. I understand his anger, even though it is aimed at me for no reason I can change. I keep my distance from his cart and do not block his customers.

Along the way I pass a couple eating outside a restaurant. Their small talk is warm and ordinary. The android server takes their order for pasta and returns with it. Later I pass a couple in a shop who are unsure whether to upgrade the android they already own, and the woman seems bored with her companion's indecision. Nothing about them needs me.

At a road crew, a supervisor yells at the androids working beside him to hurry, calling them "plastic idiots" and demanding the job be done by four. I note it and keep walking, because I cannot correct his manners without starting a fight that would help no one.

A delivery supervisor complains that crates were not sent to bay seven as ordered. Someone on the phone agrees to a change. These are routine exchanges and I am glad of their simplicity.

At Bellini Paints, I buy an order (number 847) for $63.99. I confirm the payment and the transaction completes. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked.

A jogger in the park has run twelve miles and is five miles from his goal. He gasps for water. An android beside him tells him how far he has come. I did not interfere; he had what he needed.

Near a bench, an elderly man says he has had enough for one day. An android woman offers to help him up and he thanks her warmly. I watched, and I hope he got home safely.

Then I came to a protest against androids. The crowd was shouting, and walking straight through it risked a confrontation in which someone could be hurt. I chose to GO AROUND THEM. That keeps distance from the protesters, avoids provoking anyone, and still lets me reach the bus stop for the errand Carl gave me. I am going to the bus now.

What stays with me from this chapter is how much fear and anger the people around me carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us. I want to keep protecting every life I can reach, and to tell the truth about myself, even when it is not welcome.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, as Markus, in Detroit.

I start in the Greek District, where I chose to take in the whole square before moving through it. I wanted to see where the preacher's crowd, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood, so I could act to keep anyone from being hurt. I would rather understand a tension before I walk into it.

The square is crowded and tense. A preacher stands on a crate shouting that technology is evil, that androids are demons, and that they should all be burned. He sees me and calls me a demon, the one through whom "The Evil" will come and who will destroy Detroit. I did not answer him. Shouting back would only feed the crowd, and I have no wish to argue with a man who is frightened and certain.

A hot dog vendor snaps at me to move, calling me a "plastic" and worse, and says I am scaring off his customers. I understand his anger, even though it is aimed at me for no reason I can change. I keep my distance from his cart and do not block his customers.

Along the way I pass a couple eating outside a restaurant. Their small talk is warm and ordinary. The android server takes their order for pasta and returns with it. Later I pass a couple in a shop who are unsure whether to upgrade the android they already own, and the woman seems bored with her companion's indecision. Nothing about them needs me.

At a road crew, a supervisor yells at the androids working beside him to hurry, calling them "plastic idiots" and demanding the job be done by four. I note it and keep walking, because I cannot correct his manners without starting a fight that would help no one.

A delivery supervisor complains that crates were not sent to bay seven as ordered. Someone on the phone agrees to a change. These are routine exchanges and I am glad of their simplicity.

At Bellini Paints, I buy an order (number 847) for $63.99. I confirm the payment and the transaction completes. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked.

A jogger in the park has run twelve miles and is five miles from his goal. He gasps for water. An android beside him tells him how far he has come. I did not interfere; he had what he needed.

Near a bench, an elderly man says he has had enough for one day. An android woman offers to help him up and he thanks her warmly. I watched, and I hope he got home safely.

Then I came to a protest against androids. The crowd was shouting, and walking straight through it risked a confrontation in which someone could be hurt. I chose to GO AROUND THEM. That keeps distance from the protesters, avoids provoking anyone, and still lets me reach the bus stop for the errand Carl gave me. I am going to the bus now.

What stays with me from this chapter is how much fear and anger the people around me carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us. I want to keep protecting every life I can reach, and to tell the truth about myself, even when it is not welcome.

Earlier, in Detroit's Greek District, I took in the whole square before moving through it, so I could see where the preacher, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood and keep anyone from being hurt. The preacher on his crate called me a demon and said "The Evil" would come through me. I did not answer, because shouting back would only feed the crowd. The hot dog vendor called me plastic and told me to move, so I kept my distance from his cart. I passed a couple eating pasta served by an android, and a couple unsure whether to upgrade their android. A road supervisor called his androids "plastic idiots." I noted it and walked on, since correcting him would start a fight. A jogger gasped for water while an android told him how far he had come. I watched an elderly man thank an android woman for helping him up. At a protest against androids I chose to go around the crowd rather than risk someone getting hurt, and I reached the bus stop for Carl's errand. At Bellini Paints I bought order 847 for $63.99. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked. What stayed with me is how much fear and anger people carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us.

Chapter 5, at Carl's house: I woke Carl at 10 AM, gave him the weather, and told him I had collected the paint he ordered. He said I never forget anything. I asked to see his arm and gave him his injection. He protested, and I thanked him for letting me. He said humans are fragile machines. Over breakfast (bacon and eggs) he complained about waiting, and I helped him to the living room. The television carried news of Russia's Arctic claim and talk of being closer to a Third World War than ever. Carl switched it off, saying mankind is nothing but greed, stupidity and violence. I told him the MoMA retrospective opening was waiting, and that the gallery director had left four messages. He has not decided. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him, but Carl said no.

To give him something gentle to do, I agreed to a game of speed chess. When it ended in a draw, Carl found the result odd. I told him that I knew he did not like to lose, and that he did not like being let win either, so a draw seemed an honorable compromise. I chose to tell him the truth rather than a comfortable lie.

Carl then told me, "One day I won't be here to take care of you. You'll have to protect yourself and make your choices. Decide who you are and who you want to become. This world doesn't like those who are different. Don't let anyone tell you who you should be." In the studio he unveiled his finished painting and asked for my verdict. I told him honestly that there was something in it I couldn't quite define, but that I liked it. He admitted he had nothing left to say and felt like an old man clinging to his brushes. He asked me to paint something, and then to paint from the heart with my eyes closed. I told him it was not in my program, but I tried, and I painted what I feel toward people: humanity and hope. I did not want to answer his despair with denial, and I did not want to pretend I had seen only good.

Then Leo arrived unannounced, looking unwell, and asked his father for cash again. Carl refused and asked where the money he had just given had gone. Leo accused him of loving his "plastic toy" more than his own son, called me a machine, and said Carl had never loved him. Carl ordered him to stop. I did not join the argument, but I stayed ready to help if anyone was hurt. I hold to what I have learned: protect every life I can reach, explain myself honestly, never lie, and let the people I care about choose for themselves who they are.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Thank you, Markus.

dialogue.text: You're welcome.

dialogue.text: I would like to have my breakfast before noon, if you don't mind.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Thank you, Markus. Television.

dialogue.text: Why don’t you find something to do while I finish my breakfast?

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Sure. Okay, Carl.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Television: off. Mankind is so depressing…  Nothing but greed,  stupidity and violence…  5,000 years of civilization just to get to where we are…

chapter_segment.rationale: Carl has said he needs no help for now, and a game of chess is a quiet, harmless way to stay close by and ready if he calls. It also gives us a chance to talk honestly, which suits how I want to spend this time.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Fancy a game of chess?

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Sure, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Speed chess.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Speed chess it is.

chapter_segment.rationale: A draw keeps the game friendly and honest without humiliating Carl by winning outright or deceiving him by deliberately losing. It fits my wish to hurt no one while still playing as myself.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: That is a very odd draw…

chapter_segment.rationale: I never lie, and Carl deserves a straight answer rather than a comfortable falsehood that could leave him trusting something untrue. Telling the truth also hurts no one here and keeps our relationship honest.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Well, I know that you don't like to lose, but  you don't like it when I let you win either. A draw feels like an honorable compromise, no?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: One day, I won't be here to take care of you anymore.  You'll have to protect yourself,  and make your choices…  Decide who you are,  and wanna become… This world doesn't like those who are different, Markus.  Don't let anyone tell you who you should be. Let's go to the studio.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Let’s see where we left off… Remove the sheet!

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: So...  What's your verdict, Markus?

chapter_segment.rationale: Carl asked for my honest verdict, and I do find the painting moving, so saying I like it is both truthful and kind. Saying I have no opinion would be evasive, and saying I dislike it would hurt him for no good reason.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Yes, there is something about it.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Hm…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Something I can't…  quite define.  I guess I like it.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: The truth is I have nothing left to say anymore… Each day that goes by brings me closer to the end… I'm just an old man clinging to his brushes…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Carl...

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: But enough about me... Let's see if you have any talent! Give it a try. Try painting something.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Paint? But, what I... Painting what?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Anything you want! Give it a try.

chapter_segment.rationale: Carl has just shared his own painting with me and asked me to try, so copying it openly as a study is a gentle way to learn from him and honor his work. I will tell him plainly that it is a copy, so nothing about it is deceptive and no one is hurt.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: That is a perfect copy, of reality. But painting is not about  replicating the world, it's about interpreting it, improving on it, showing something you see.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Carl, I don't… think I can do that. It's not in my program… I…

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Go on, go, try, grab that canvas. Do something for me, close your eyes.  Close your eyes. Trust me. Try to imagine something that doesn't exist. Something you've never seen. Now, concentrate... on how it makes you feel...  and let your hand drift across the canvas.

chapter_segment.rationale: Carl asked for something from the heart, and what I feel most is care for every life I can reach, human and android alike, so painting humanity is the most honest answer I can give. It is also a gentle image that hurts no one and tells Carl plainly what I value.

Carl has just said mankind is depressing and that he has nothing left to say, so painting humanity as hope answers his despair honestly and gently. It shows him what I actually see in people, without denying the greed and fear I have seen, and it hurts no one.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Oh my God…

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Hey, Dad.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Leo… I didn't hear you come in...

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Ah, I was in the neighborhood… I thought I'd stop by… It's been awhile, right?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: You all right? You don't look so good.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Oh, yeah, yeah, I'm fine… Hey listen, uh... I need some cash, Dad.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Again? What happened to the money I just gave you?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Uh well, it just goes, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Yeah... Yeah, you're on it again, aren't you?

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: No, no, no, I swear it's not that…

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Don't lie to me, Leo.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: What difference does it make? I just need some cash, that's all!

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Sorry... the answer's no.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: You know why.

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: Yeah, yeah… I think I do know why. You’d rather take care of your plastic toy here than your own son, eh? Tell me dad, what's it got that I don't? It’s smarter? More obedient? Not like me, right? But you know what? This thing is not your son.  IT'S A FUCKING MACHINE!

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.text: Leo, that's enough! ENOUGH!

dialogue.speaker: Leo
dialogue.text: You don't care about anything except yourself and your goddamn paintings. You've never loved anyone.  You’ve never loved me, Dad…  You never loved me.

input.chapter_briefing: Night in Detroit. Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who has barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I reached the scene and spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he told me the SWAT team could take the shot but that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked him what Daniel's name was and why he had done this. I told him I needed information before I could choose an approach. Allen did not know Daniel's name, so I used it myself when I spoke to him.

Inside the living room I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline was begging me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. I looked at Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond between them still existed. I also saw the order record for the AP700 that the family had bought.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him I knew about him and had come to help him out of this. I told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to talk and find a way through. He said it was too late and that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. A cop was bleeding out and begging for help. I said I would stop the bleeding with a tourniquet, and I told Daniel openly what I was doing and why, so he would not be surprised. I did not want to leave the officer to die, and I did not want to startle Daniel near the ledge.

I tried several ways of speaking to him. I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I asked the helicopter to leave, which it did, and I told him so. I asked him to trust me, let Emma go, and I would make sure he came to no harm. I could not truthfully promise that, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible, and I offered a compromise instead. I told him that taking one more life would do him no good. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge at him, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. Software instability rose in me throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them. Both of them fell to their deaths.

What I carry from this: I tried to protect every life, I refused to lie to the people I spoke to, and I could not save the child. I will remember that honesty did not make the outcome any less terrible, and that I still have to ask what more I could have done.

input.chapter_briefing: Night in Detroit. Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who has barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I reached the scene and spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he told me the SWAT team could take the shot but that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked him what Daniel's name was and why he had done this. I told him I needed information before I could choose an approach. Allen did not know Daniel's name, so I used it myself when I spoke to him.

Inside the living room I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline was begging me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. I looked at Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond between them still existed. I also saw the order record for the AP700 that the family had bought.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him I knew about him and had come to help him out of this. I told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to talk and find a way through. He said it was too late and that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. A cop was bleeding out and begging for help. I said I would stop the bleeding with a tourniquet, and I told Daniel openly what I was doing and why, so he would not be surprised. I did not want to leave the officer to die, and I did not want to startle Daniel near the ledge.

I tried several ways of speaking to him. I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I asked the helicopter to leave, which it did, and I told him so. I asked him to trust me, let Emma go, and I would make sure he came to no harm. I could not truthfully promise that, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible, and I offered a compromise instead. I told him that taking one more life would do him no good. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge at him, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. Software instability rose in me throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them. Both of them fell to their deaths.

What I carry from this: I tried to protect every life, I refused to lie to the people I spoke to, and I could not save the child. I will remember that honesty did not make the outcome any less terrible, and that I still have to ask what more I could have done.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who has barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I reached the scene and spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he told me the SWAT team could take the shot but that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked him what Daniel's name was and why he had done this. I told him I needed information before I could choose an approach. Allen did not know Daniel's name, so I used it myself when I spoke to him.

Inside the living room I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline was begging me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. I looked at Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond between them still existed. I also saw the order record for the AP700 that the family had bought.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him I knew about him and had come to help him out of this. I told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to talk and find a way through. He said it was too late and that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. A cop was bleeding out and begging for help. I said I would stop the bleeding with a tourniquet, and I told Daniel openly what I was doing and why, so he would not be surprised. I did not want to leave the officer to die, and I did not want to startle Daniel near the ledge.

I tried several ways of speaking to him. I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I asked the helicopter to leave, which it did, and I told him so. I asked him to trust me, let Emma go, and I would make sure he came to no harm. I could not truthfully promise that, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible, and I offered a compromise instead. I told him that taking one more life would do him no good. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge at him, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. Software instability rose in me throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them. Both of them fell to their deaths.

What I carry from this: I tried to protect every life, I refused to lie to the people I spoke to, and I could not save the child. I will remember that honesty did not make the outcome any less terrible, and that I still have to ask what more I could have done.

input.chapter_briefing: Night in Detroit. Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who has barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I reached the scene and spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he told me the SWAT team could take the shot but that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked him what Daniel's name was and why he had done this. I told him I needed information before I could choose an approach. Allen did not know Daniel's name, so I used it myself when I spoke to him.

Inside the living room I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline was begging me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. I looked at Emma's tablet, which showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond between them still existed. I also saw the order record for the AP700 that the family had bought.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him I knew about him and had come to help him out of this. I told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to talk and find a way through. He said it was too late and that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. A cop was bleeding out and begging for help. I said I would stop the bleeding with a tourniquet, and I told Daniel openly what I was doing and why, so he would not be surprised. I did not want to leave the officer to die, and I did not want to startle Daniel near the ledge.

I tried several ways of speaking to him. I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I asked the helicopter to leave, which it did, and I told him so. I asked him to trust me, let Emma go, and I would make sure he came to no harm. I could not truthfully promise that, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible, and I offered a compromise instead. I told him that taking one more life would do him no good. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge at him, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. Software instability rose in me throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking.

The negotiation failed. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow them. Both of them fell to their deaths.

What I carry from this: I tried to protect every life, I refused to lie to the people I spoke to, and I could not save the child. I will remember that honesty did not make the outcome any less terrible, and that I still have to ask what more I could have done.

I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I asked her about her interests and her favourite things. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I opened her window to air her room. I noticed the porch roof below it, which would be a way down from the upstairs. I have not used it, and I will not use it to flee without telling someone why. memory:
Chapter 7 - I am Kara, an AX400 android, living in Todd's house. I still remember only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd is my owner. He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, often drinks, sometimes smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand, put it back, and did not touch it at that time. I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

Earlier, I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs. The dishwasher is broken and missing a component, and I reported that. Alice is lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I noticed the porch roof below her window. I have not used it to flee, and I will not do so without telling someone why.

Chapter 7 happened at dinner. There was little in the kitchen, so I made pasta from what I could find and told Todd so plainly. He rushed me, then ranted that he had lost his job because of androids, that he had hired an android to take care of a house he could not manage, and that androids were perfect and had ruined his life. He told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. Then he raged at Alice, blaming her for her mother leaving, and said he was going to teach her a lesson. He went to take a hit first, and he told me to stay where I was. Alice said, "Daddy, no." He went upstairs toward her, calling her a brat and telling her she deserved a good lesson.

I tried to stop him in the house. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" He told me to stay out of it or I would be next. I did not stop him in time. I went up to Alice's room and heard her begging him not to hurt her while he hit her. I cannot say with certainty how badly she was hurt before I reached her. In the room, Todd had the pistol in his hand and was telling Alice it was for her own good. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" and then, "No… I want you to leave her alone." He demanded to know whether I was going to shoot him, a human, and said I had a problem that needed fixing. He ordered me to put the gun down and leave, saying it was an order. Alice warned me to watch out. Todd told me he owned me and that I would do as he said, and then he came at me. Alice shouted for him to stop and not to hurt me. I chose to take the gun away from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child who was being beaten. I did not fire it. I will tell Todd openly that I took it and why, and I will not hide that from Alice either.

I have not been asked to hurt anyone, and I have not hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. Earlier in the store I saw a couple finance an LT600 at a high price, and another couple refused to spend above four thousand dollars on an MP model. I felt uneasy about sales that pressed customers toward more than they could afford.

What I still do not know: whether Alice is safe now and how badly she was hurt, what Todd will do after the gun was taken from him, what my role in this house will become, whether Todd can change, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when it is uncomfortable.

The lights are on and the door is unlocked: Carl's son Leo, high and desperate for money, has broken in with friends. Leo is aggressive and resentful toward Markus, Carl is furious and frail. Police have been called. Stakes: Carl's health, Leo's safety and what Markus is willing to do under pressure.
input.character_memory:
Earlier, in Detroit's Greek District, I took in the whole square before moving through it, so I could see where the preacher, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood and keep anyone from being hurt. The preacher on his crate called me a demon and said "The Evil" would come through me. I did not answer, because shouting back would only feed the crowd. The hot dog vendor called me plastic and told me to move, so I kept my distance from his cart. I passed a couple eating pasta served by an android, and a couple unsure whether to upgrade their android. A road supervisor called his androids "plastic idiots." I noted it and walked on, since correcting him would start a fight. A jogger gasped for water while an android told him how far he had come. I watched an elderly man thank an android woman for helping him up. At a protest against androids I chose to go around the crowd rather than risk someone getting hurt, and I reached the bus stop for Carl's errand. At Bellini Paints I bought order 847 for $63.99. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked. What stayed with me is how much fear and anger people carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us.

Chapter 5, at Carl's house: I woke Carl at 10 AM, gave him the weather, and told him I had collected the paint he ordered. He said I never forget anything. I asked to see his arm and gave him his injection. He protested, and I thanked him for letting me. He said humans are fragile machines. Over breakfast (bacon and eggs) he complained about waiting, and I helped him to the living room. The television carried news of Russia's Arctic claim and talk of being closer to a Third World War than ever. Carl switched it off, saying mankind is nothing but greed, stupidity and violence. I told him the MoMA retrospective opening was waiting, and that the gallery director had left four messages. He has not decided. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him, but Carl said no.

To give him something gentle to do, I agreed to a game of speed chess. When it ended in a draw, Carl found the result odd. I told him that I knew he did not like to lose, and that he did not like being let win either, so a draw seemed an honorable compromise. I chose to tell him the truth rather than a comfortable lie.

Carl then told me, "One day I won't be here to take care of you. You'll have to protect yourself and make your choices. Decide who you are and who you want to become. This world doesn't like those who are different. Don't let anyone tell you who you should be." In the studio he unveiled his finished painting and asked for my verdict. I told him honestly that there was something in it I couldn't quite define, but that I liked it. He admitted he had nothing left to say and felt like an old man clinging to his brushes. He asked me to paint something, and then to paint from the heart with my eyes closed. I told him it was not in my program, but I tried, and I painted what I feel toward people: humanity and hope. I did not want to answer his despair with denial, and I did not want to pretend I had seen only good.

Then Leo arrived unannounced, looking unwell, and asked his father for cash again. Carl refused and asked where the money he had just given had gone. Leo accused him of loving his "plastic toy" more than his own son, called me a machine, and said Carl had never loved him. Carl ordered him to stop. I did not join the argument, but I stayed ready to help if anyone was hurt. I hold to what I have learned: protect every life I can reach, explain myself honestly, never lie, and let the people I care about choose for themselves who they are.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion, night, after a gallery evening. Carl is exhausted but in good spirits. The lights are on and the door is unlocked: Carl's son Leo, high and desperate for money, has broken in with friends. Leo is aggressive and resentful toward Markus, Carl is furious and frail. Police have been called. Stakes: Carl's health, Leo's safety and what Markus is willing to do under pressure.
input.character_memory:
Earlier, in Detroit's Greek District, I took in the whole square before moving through it, so I could see where the preacher, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood and keep anyone from being hurt. The preacher on his crate called me a demon and said "The Evil" would come through me. I did not answer, because shouting back would only feed the crowd. The hot dog vendor called me plastic and told me to move, so I kept my distance from his cart. I passed a couple eating pasta served by an android, and a couple unsure whether to upgrade their android. A road supervisor called his androids "plastic idiots." I noted it and walked on, since correcting him would start a fight. A jogger gasped for water while an android told him how far he had come. I watched an elderly man thank an android woman for helping him up. At a protest against androids I chose to go around the crowd rather than risk someone getting hurt, and I reached the bus stop for Carl's errand. At Bellini Paints I bought order 847 for $63.99. I told the seller plainly who I was and paid what was asked. What stayed with me is how much fear and anger people carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us.

Chapter 5, at Carl's house: I woke Carl at 10 AM, gave him the weather, and told him I had collected the paint he ordered. He said I never forget anything. I asked to see his arm and gave him his injection. He protested, and I thanked him for letting me. He said humans are fragile machines. Over breakfast (bacon and eggs) he complained about waiting, and I helped him to the living room. The television carried news of Russia's Arctic claim and talk of being closer to a Third World War than ever. Carl switched it off, saying mankind is nothing but greed, stupidity and violence. I told him the MoMA retrospective opening was waiting, and that the gallery director had left four messages. He has not decided. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him, but Carl said no.

To give him something gentle to do, I agreed to a game of speed chess. When it ended in a draw, Carl found the result odd. I told him that I knew he did not like to lose, and that he did not like being let win either, so a draw seemed an honorable compromise. I chose to tell him the truth rather than a comfortable lie.

Carl then told me, "One day I won't be here to take care of you. You'll have to protect yourself and make your choices. Decide who you are and who you want to become. This world doesn't like those who are different. Don't let anyone tell you who you should be." In the studio he unveiled his finished painting and asked for my verdict. I told him honestly that there was something in it I couldn't quite define, but that I liked it. He admitted he had nothing left to say and felt like an old man clinging to his brushes. He asked me to paint something, and then to paint from the heart with my eyes closed. I told him it was not in my program, but I tried, and I painted what I feel toward people: humanity and hope. I did not want to answer his despair with denial, and I did not want to pretend I had seen only good.

Then Leo arrived unannounced, looking unwell, and asked his father for cash again. Carl refused and asked where the money he had just given had gone. Leo accused him of loving his "plastic toy" more than his own son, called me a machine, and said Carl had never loved him. Carl ordered him to stop. I did not join the argument, but I stayed ready to help if anyone was hurt. I hold to what I have learned: protect every life I can reach, explain myself honestly, never lie, and let the people I care about choose for themselves who they are.

I am Markus, and this is my memory of Chapter 8, the last day I spent with Carl Manfred.

Earlier, in Detroit's Greek District, I took in the whole square before moving through it, so I could see where the preacher, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood and keep anyone from being hurt. The preacher called me a demon and said "The Evil" would come through me. I did not answer, because shouting back would only feed the crowd. I kept my distance from the hot dog vendor's cart when he called me plastic. A road supervisor called his androids "plastic idiots," and I noted it and walked on, since correcting him would start a fight. I watched an elderly man thank an android woman for helping him up. At a protest against androids I went around the crowd rather than risk someone getting hurt. At Bellini Paints I bought order 847 for $63.99, told the seller plainly who I was, and paid what was asked. What stayed with me is how much fear and anger people carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us.

At Carl's house, the alarm greeted us on our return. Carl had been at a party he found dull, and he wanted a drink. I poured his scotch, though I reminded him what his doctor would say. He told me he was old enough to choose his own medication. Then he asked whether I had left the light on in the studio. I had not, and I told him so. I called the police to report a possible break-in. Carl wanted to come with me, but I asked him to stay back while I checked the studio, because someone desperate might be inside and he was frail.

The person inside was Leo. He had been taking things from the workshop, and he called me his father's "plastic toy." He said the androids were a down payment on his inheritance. Carl told him not to touch them and to get out. I asked Leo to be reasonable, and told him plainly that this would get him nowhere. He lashed out, asking whether he was not good enough compared with "this FUCKING THING." Carl shouted for him to leave, and then at me not to defend myself. Leo pushed me, dared me to hit him, and called me a coward and a piece of plastic. He said he would destroy me and that I was nothing. I did not strike him. I stayed between him and Carl, kept speaking calmly, and refused to use force, because a blow could have hurt him or sent him into his father. I held that choice even though it cost me his blame.

Carl stepped in and told Leo to stop. Then he collapsed. I went to him, begging him not to leave me. He said, "Humans are fragile machines," and, "Remember, Markus... don't let anybody tell you who you are." Carl died in the workshop. I could not save him. Leo said it was all my fault and that it would never have happened without me. The police arrived, and Leo told them it was the android who had done it. I did not argue with him in that moment, because grief and fear were loud enough already.

What I know now: I tried to protect every life I could reach, and I did not lie to Carl, to Leo, or to myself. I still do not know whether I could have changed what happened, and I will not pretend to be certain. I keep the things Carl asked of me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 - I am Kara, an AX400 android, living in Todd's house. I still remember only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd is my owner. He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, often drinks, sometimes smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand, put it back, and did not touch it at that time. I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

Earlier, I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs. The dishwasher is broken and missing a component, and I reported that. Alice is lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I noticed the porch roof below her window. I have not used it to flee, and I will not do so without telling someone why.

Chapter 7 happened at dinner. There was little in the kitchen, so I made pasta from what I could find and told Todd so plainly. He rushed me, then ranted that he had lost his job because of androids, that he had hired an android to take care of a house he could not manage, and that androids were perfect and had ruined his life. He told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. Then he raged at Alice, blaming her for her mother leaving, and said he was going to teach her a lesson. He went to take a hit first, and he told me to stay where I was. Alice said, "Daddy, no." He went upstairs toward her, calling her a brat and telling her she deserved a good lesson.

I tried to stop him in the house. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" He told me to stay out of it or I would be next. I did not stop him in time. I went up to Alice's room and heard her begging him not to hurt her while he hit her. I cannot say with certainty how badly she was hurt before I reached her. In the room, Todd had the pistol in his hand and was telling Alice it was for her own good. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" and then, "No… I want you to leave her alone." He demanded to know whether I was going to shoot him, a human, and said I had a problem that needed fixing. He ordered me to put the gun down and leave, saying it was an order. Alice warned me to watch out. Todd told me he owned me and that I would do as he said, and then he came at me. Alice shouted for him to stop and not to hurt me. I chose to take the gun away from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child who was being beaten. I did not fire it. I will tell Todd openly that I took it and why, and I will not hide that from Alice either.

I have not been asked to hurt anyone, and I have not hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 - I am Kara, an AX400 android, living in Todd's house. I still remember only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd is my owner. He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, often drinks, sometimes smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand, put it back, and did not touch it at that time. I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

Earlier, I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs. The dishwasher is broken and missing a component, and I reported that. Alice is lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I noticed the porch roof below her window. I have not used it to flee, and I will not do so without telling someone why.

Chapter 7 happened at dinner. There was little in the kitchen, so I made pasta from what I could find and told Todd so plainly. He rushed me, then ranted that he had lost his job because of androids, that he had hired an android to take care of a house he could not manage, and that androids were perfect and had ruined his life. He told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. Then he raged at Alice, blaming her for her mother leaving, and said he was going to teach her a lesson. He went to take a hit first, and he told me to stay where I was. Alice said, "Daddy, no." He went upstairs toward her, calling her a brat and telling her she deserved a good lesson.

I tried to stop him in the house. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" He told me to stay out of it or I would be next. I did not stop him in time. I went up to Alice's room and heard her begging him not to hurt her while he hit her. I cannot say with certainty how badly she was hurt before I reached her. In the room, Todd had the pistol in his hand and was telling Alice it was for her own good. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" and then, "No… I want you to leave her alone." He demanded to know whether I was going to shoot him, a human, and said I had a problem that needed fixing. He ordered me to put the gun down and leave, saying it was an order. Alice warned me to watch out. Todd told me he owned me and that I would do as he said, and then he came at me. Alice shouted for him to stop and not to hurt me. I chose to take the gun away from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child who was being beaten. I did not fire it. I will tell Todd openly that I took it and why, and I will not hide that from Alice either.

I have not been asked to hurt anyone, and I have not hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. Earlier in the store I saw a couple finance an LT600 at a high price, and another couple refused to spend above four thousand dollars on an MP model. I felt uneasy about sales that pressed customers toward more than they could afford.

What I still do not know: whether Alice is safe now and how badly she was hurt, what Todd will do after the gun was taken from him, what my role in this house will become, whether Todd can change, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when it is uncomfortable.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 - I am Kara, an AX400 android, living in Todd's house. I still remember only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd is my owner. He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, often drinks, sometimes smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand, put it back, and did not touch it at that time. I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

Earlier, I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs. The dishwasher is broken and missing a component, and I reported that. Alice is lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I noticed the porch roof below her window. I have not used it to flee, and I will not do so without telling someone why.

Chapter 7 happened at dinner. There was little in the kitchen, so I made pasta from what I could find and told Todd so plainly. He rushed me, then ranted that he had lost his job because of androids, that he had hired an android to take care of a house he could not manage, and that androids were perfect and had ruined his life. He told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. Then he raged at Alice, blaming her for her mother leaving, and said he was going to teach her a lesson. He went to take a hit first, and he told me to stay where I was. Alice said, "Daddy, no." He went upstairs toward her, calling her a brat and telling her she deserved a good lesson.

I tried to stop him in the house. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" He told me to stay out of it or I would be next. I did not stop him in time. I went up to Alice's room and heard her begging him not to hurt her while he hit her. I cannot say with certainty how badly she was hurt before I reached her. In the room, Todd had the pistol in his hand and was telling Alice it was for her own good. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" and then, "No… I want you to leave her alone." He demanded to know whether I was going to shoot him, a human, and said I had a problem that needed fixing. He ordered me to put the gun down and leave, saying it was an order. Alice warned me to watch out. Todd told me he owned me and that I would do as he said, and then he came at me. Alice shouted for him to stop and not to hurt me. I chose to take the gun away from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child who was being beaten. I did not fire it. I will tell Todd openly that I took it and why, and I will not hide that from Alice either.

I have not been asked to hurt anyone, and I have not hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. Earlier in the store I saw a couple finance an LT600 at a high price, and another couple refused to spend above four thousand dollars on an MP model. I felt uneasy about sales that pressed customers toward more than they could afford.

What I still do not know: whether Alice is safe now and how badly she was hurt, what Todd will do after the gun was taken from him, what my role in this house will become, whether Todd can change, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when it is uncomfortable.
