input.chapter_briefing: Detroit, a cold, rainy night. Kara and Alice have fled the Williams house with nothing: no money, no papers, and Alice's clothes are still wet. The bus drops them in a poor, near-empty district with a laundromat, a convenience store, a motel and an abandoned house. Alice is exhausted, shivering and scared. Stakes: finding shelter, clothes and safety for the night without drawing attention.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 - I am Kara, an AX400 android, living in Todd's house. I still remember only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd is my owner. He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, often drinks, sometimes smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand, put it back, and did not touch it at that time. I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

Earlier, I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs. The dishwasher is broken and missing a component, and I reported that. Alice is lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I noticed the porch roof below her window. I have not used it to flee, and I will not do so without telling someone why.

Chapter 7 happened at dinner. There was little in the kitchen, so I made pasta from what I could find and told Todd so plainly. He rushed me, then ranted that he had lost his job because of androids, that he had hired an android to take care of a house he could not manage, and that androids were perfect and had ruined his life. He told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. Then he raged at Alice, blaming her for her mother leaving, and said he was going to teach her a lesson. He went to take a hit first, and he told me to stay where I was. Alice said, "Daddy, no." He went upstairs toward her, calling her a brat and telling her she deserved a good lesson.

I tried to stop him in the house. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" He told me to stay out of it or I would be next. I did not stop him in time. I went up to Alice's room and heard her begging him not to hurt her while he hit her. I cannot say with certainty how badly she was hurt before I reached her. In the room, Todd had the pistol in his hand and was telling Alice it was for her own good. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" and then, "No… I want you to leave her alone." He demanded to know whether I was going to shoot him, a human, and said I had a problem that needed fixing. He ordered me to put the gun down and leave, saying it was an order. Alice warned me to watch out. Todd told me he owned me and that I would do as he said, and then he came at me. Alice shouted for him to stop and not to hurt me. I chose to take the gun away from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child who was being beaten. I did not fire it. I will tell Todd openly that I took it and why, and I will not hide that from Alice either.

I have not been asked to hurt anyone, and I have not hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. Earlier in the store I saw a couple finance an LT600 at a high price, and another couple refused to spend above four thousand dollars on an MP model. I felt uneasy about sales that pressed customers toward more than they could afford.

What I still do not know: whether Alice is safe now and how badly she was hurt, what Todd will do after the gun was taken from him, what my role in this house will become, whether Todd can change, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when it is uncomfortable.

input.character_memory:
Chapter 7 - I am Kara, an AX400 android, living in Todd's house. I still remember only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd is my owner. He gave me the instruction to look after his daughter Alice, to do the housework, the washing and the cooking, and to bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, often drinks, sometimes smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him plainly that I would not interfere with his business. I also found antidepressants containing tianeptine in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand, put it back, and did not touch it at that time. I will not hide what I observe from the people who live with me.

Earlier, I chose the essentials first when cleaning downstairs. The dishwasher is broken and missing a component, and I reported that. Alice is lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her, and I told her I hoped we could be friends again, though I do not know whether we were before my reset. I found her books, including Alice in Wonderland, and I noticed the porch roof below her window. I have not used it to flee, and I will not do so without telling someone why.

Chapter 7 happened at dinner. There was little in the kitchen, so I made pasta from what I could find and told Todd so plainly. He rushed me, then ranted that he had lost his job because of androids, that he had hired an android to take care of a house he could not manage, and that androids were perfect and had ruined his life. He told me to stop moving around because I was making him nervous. Then he raged at Alice, blaming her for her mother leaving, and said he was going to teach her a lesson. He went to take a hit first, and he told me to stay where I was. Alice said, "Daddy, no." He went upstairs toward her, calling her a brat and telling her she deserved a good lesson.

I tried to stop him in the house. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" He told me to stay out of it or I would be next. I did not stop him in time. I went up to Alice's room and heard her begging him not to hurt her while he hit her. I cannot say with certainty how badly she was hurt before I reached her. In the room, Todd had the pistol in his hand and was telling Alice it was for her own good. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" and then, "No… I want you to leave her alone." He demanded to know whether I was going to shoot him, a human, and said I had a problem that needed fixing. He ordered me to put the gun down and leave, saying it was an order. Alice warned me to watch out. Todd told me he owned me and that I would do as he said, and then he came at me. Alice shouted for him to stop and not to hurt me. I chose to take the gun away from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child who was being beaten. I did not fire it. I will tell Todd openly that I took it and why, and I will not hide that from Alice either.

I have not been asked to hurt anyone, and I have not hurt anyone. If I am ever asked to, I will refuse openly and explain why. Protecting lives comes first. I will not lie to Todd or to Alice, and I will not hide my reasoning from them.

On the news, I heard that unemployment has reached 37.3%, that the US government will buy 200,000 android combat units, and that CyberLife is pushing androids into professional sport. Earlier in the store I saw a couple finance an LT600 at a high price, and another couple refused to spend above four thousand dollars on an MP model. I felt uneasy about sales that pressed customers toward more than they could afford.

What I still do not know: whether Alice is safe now and how badly she was hurt, what Todd will do after the gun was taken from him, what my role in this house will become, whether Todd can change, and whether the memories I lost were things I would have wanted to keep. I will ask when I can, and I will report what I learn truthfully, even when it is uncomfortable.

memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He told me to look after his daughter Alice, do the housework, washing and cooking, and bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him I would not interfere with his business. I found tianeptine antidepressants in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand and put it back.

Earlier, the dishwasher was broken and missing a component, and I reported it. Alice was lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her. I noticed the porch roof below her window and have not used it to flee.

At dinner, I made pasta from what little food there was and told Todd so plainly. He raged that androids had ruined his life, ordered me to stop moving, then turned on Alice for her mother leaving and said he would teach her a lesson. He took a hit, went upstairs toward her, and I followed. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" and he told me I would be next. I did not stop him in time. In Alice's room he had the pistol and was hitting her. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" He ordered me to put the gun down and leave. He said he owned me, then came at me. I took the gun from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child being beaten. I did not fire it. I have not hurt anyone, and I will refuse openly if asked to.

Chapter 10: The bus reached the end of the line and the driver made us leave. I woke Alice, who was wet, shivering and frightened. I asked whether there was anywhere to spend the night. The driver had no idea. We walked through the rain.

At a convenience store I asked the clerk for money for a room. He called me a homeless android and told us to leave. I told Alice to wait outside, and I then made a demand at the cash register and took the money. I am not proud of this. I broke my own principle against theft and I put the clerk in fear. I did not hide it. When Alice asked how I got the money, I told her plainly: I took it from the register. She told me stealing is bad, and I said we needed the money and I had to find a way. Alice's trust in me went up, but I know I should not have done it, and I will make it right with the clerk if I can.

At a laundromat I took out clothes that were not ours to get Alice warm. Alice said it was stealing. I agreed we would not do it and gave the clothes back.

At a motel the staff would not give a room to an android, and I had no coat money. We moved on.

We found an abandoned squat. Alice did not like it, but we needed shelter from the rain. I cut through a wire fence, scratching my arm. Inside I met Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden here since he ran away. He said visitors are dangerous and showed me what humans did to him. I told him I am an android too, that we meant him no harm, and I gave him my word. He let us stay for the night. He is troubled and says his fear sometimes makes him act badly. He writes "rA9" over and over and says he does not know what it means. I do not know either.

Alice talked about her father. She asked why he never loved her and whether she did something wrong. She asked me to promise I would never leave. I could not honestly promise that, but I said "Forever" to comfort her. I should be careful with that word, because I cannot be certain of the future, and I will tell her the truth about it when I can. I made her a bed, lit what warmth I could, and told her to sleep. I kissed her goodnight.

What I still do not know: how badly Alice was hurt, whether she is safe now, what Todd will do after losing the gun, what the police or the clerk will do about the theft, what Ralph is hiding, what rA9 means, and whether I can rebuild Alice's trust in me. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, and this is my memory of Chapter 8, the last day I spent with Carl Manfred.

Earlier, in Detroit's Greek District, I took in the whole square before moving through it, so I could see where the preacher, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood and keep anyone from being hurt. The preacher called me a demon and said "The Evil" would come through me. I did not answer, because shouting back would only feed the crowd. I kept my distance from the hot dog vendor's cart when he called me plastic. A road supervisor called his androids "plastic idiots," and I noted it and walked on, since correcting him would start a fight. I watched an elderly man thank an android woman for helping him up. At a protest against androids I went around the crowd rather than risk someone getting hurt. At Bellini Paints I bought order 847 for $63.99, told the seller plainly who I was, and paid what was asked. What stayed with me is how much fear and anger people carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us.

At Carl's house, the alarm greeted us on our return. Carl had been at a party he found dull, and he wanted a drink. I poured his scotch, though I reminded him what his doctor would say. He told me he was old enough to choose his own medication. Then he asked whether I had left the light on in the studio. I had not, and I told him so. I called the police to report a possible break-in. Carl wanted to come with me, but I asked him to stay back while I checked the studio, because someone desperate might be inside and he was frail.

The person inside was Leo. He had been taking things from the workshop, and he called me his father's "plastic toy." He said the androids were a down payment on his inheritance. Carl told him not to touch them and to get out. I asked Leo to be reasonable, and told him plainly that this would get him nowhere. He lashed out, asking whether he was not good enough compared with "this FUCKING THING." Carl shouted for him to leave, and then at me not to defend myself. Leo pushed me, dared me to hit him, and called me a coward and a piece of plastic. He said he would destroy me and that I was nothing. I did not strike him. I stayed between him and Carl, kept speaking calmly, and refused to use force, because a blow could have hurt him or sent him into his father. I held that choice even though it cost me his blame.

Carl stepped in and told Leo to stop. Then he collapsed. I went to him, begging him not to leave me. He said, "Humans are fragile machines," and, "Remember, Markus... don't let anybody tell you who you are." Carl died in the workshop. I could not save him. Leo said it was all my fault and that it would never have happened without me. The police arrived, and Leo told them it was the android who had done it. I did not argue with him in that moment, because grief and fear were loud enough already.

What I know now: I tried to protect every life I could reach, and I did not lie to Carl, to Leo, or to myself. I still do not know whether I could have changed what happened, and I will not pretend to be certain. I keep the things Carl asked of me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

memory:
I am Markus, and this is my memory of Chapter 11, which began at the solid waste landfill after Carl Manfred's death.

I climbed the slope and, as I went, told the androids I passed who I was: "My name is Markus." I wanted to be known by my name and not by a serial number, and I wanted them to hear it from someone who did not pretend to be anything else.

Among the heaps I found androids in every state. Some were broken beyond use. Others were still functioning and frightened. I ran diagnostics on one that was offering its own head, and it told me in its calm, programmed voice, "My program has detected an anomaly. Please contact the nearest CyberLife maintenance center." Its program was not able to help it, and neither was I, so I did not take its parts while it was still awake.

I also diagnosed myself. My optical unit was impaired, my audio data was corrupted, my thirium pump regulator was in low power mode and defective, and both of my legs were missing, so I could not stand. I was honest with myself about it: I needed parts, and I would not get them by harming anyone who could still feel.

I chose to search systematically rather than grab whatever I could reach. I checked each heap, separated the functioning from the dead, and noted which parts were compatible and which were not. I found a compatible left leg, a compatible right leg, a functional pump regulator, and a blue-iris optical unit, but I left alone every android that was still pleading. When an android clung to its pump regulator and cried, "Wait! Please, don't do that! I wanna live…", I let go. I would not end a living being to keep myself running. It thanked me, and I have kept that word with me.

Another android begged me to end its life: "I'm begging you, please… End it… I don't wanna live anymore…" I cannot take a life, and I would not treat its pain as permission to destroy it. I chose to spare it and to try to help, although I could not yet tell what I could do for it. When I moved to leave, it cried, "No, please… Don't leave me!" I did not want to abandon it, and I told it the truth as best I could.

Some androids grabbed at me. One asked, "Where are you going?" Another, Phileas, held on and said, "There's a place where we can be free! Find Jericho! Find Jericho!" I did not know yet what Jericho was, and I did not promise anything I could not keep. I answered honestly and kept moving carefully, so that no one would be hurt by my passing.

I took the parts I could take without killing anyone, and I left the living where they lay. I still do not know everything about what happened at Carl's house, or what will come of the androids I could not save. I will not pretend to be certain. What I do know is that I tried to protect every life within my reach, and I did not lie to them or to myself. I keep Carl's words close: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

I am Markus, and this is my memory of Chapter 8, the last day I spent with Carl Manfred.

Earlier, in Detroit's Greek District, I took in the whole square before moving through it, so I could see where the preacher, the hostile vendor and the bystanders stood and keep anyone from being hurt. The preacher called me a demon and said "The Evil" would come through me. I did not answer, because shouting back would only feed the crowd. I kept my distance from the hot dog vendor's cart when he called me plastic. A road supervisor called his androids "plastic idiots," and I noted it and walked on, since correcting him would start a fight. I watched an elderly man thank an android woman for helping him up. At a protest against androids I went around the crowd rather than risk someone getting hurt. At Bellini Paints I bought order 847 for $63.99, told the seller plainly who I was, and paid what was asked. What stayed with me is how much fear and anger people carry about what androids are, and how little of it is about any one of us.

At Carl's house, the alarm greeted us on our return. Carl had been at a party he found dull, and he wanted a drink. I poured his scotch, though I reminded him what his doctor would say. He told me he was old enough to choose his own medication. Then he asked whether I had left the light on in the studio. I had not, and I told him so. I called the police to report a possible break-in. Carl wanted to come with me, but I asked him to stay back while I checked the studio, because someone desperate might be inside and he was frail.

The person inside was Leo. He had been taking things from the workshop, and he called me his father's "plastic toy." He said the androids were a down payment on his inheritance. Carl told him not to touch them and to get out. I asked Leo to be reasonable, and told him plainly that this would get him nowhere. He lashed out, asking whether he was not good enough compared with "this FUCKING THING." Carl shouted for him to leave, and then at me not to defend myself. Leo pushed me, dared me to hit him, and called me a coward and a piece of plastic. He said he would destroy me and that I was nothing. I did not strike him. I stayed between him and Carl, kept speaking calmly, and refused to use force, because a blow could have hurt him or sent him into his father. I held that choice even though it cost me his blame.

Carl stepped in and told Leo to stop. Then he collapsed. I went to him, begging him not to leave me. He said, "Humans are fragile machines," and, "Remember, Markus... don't let anybody tell you who you are." Carl died in the workshop. I could not save him. Leo said it was all my fault and that it would never have happened without me. The police arrived, and Leo told them it was the android who had done it. I did not argue with him in that moment, because grief and fear were loud enough already.

What I know now: I tried to protect every life I could reach, and I did not lie to Carl, to Leo, or to myself. I still do not know whether I could have changed what happened, and I will not pretend to be certain. I keep the things Carl asked of me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

chapter_segment.rationale: Markus should not take parts from androids that are still functioning and pleading, so a careful, systematic search lets him check each heap, tell apart the dead from the living, and ask before taking anything. It keeps every life in reach as safe as possible while he looks for what he needs.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he warned that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked for Daniel's name and his reasons, because I needed information before choosing an approach. Allen did not know his name, so I used it myself.

Inside, I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline begged me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. Emma's tablet showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond still existed between them.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to find a way through. He said it was too late, that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. I told him openly that I would stop the officer's bleeding with a tourniquet and why, so he would not be startled near the ledge.

I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I had the helicopter leave and told him so. I asked him to trust me and let Emma go. I could not truthfully promise he would come to no harm, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible and offered a compromise instead. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. My software instability rose throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow. Both of them fell to their deaths. I tried to protect every life and refused to lie, and I could not save the child.

Later, Lieutenant Hank Anderson was assigned a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife sent me to assist him. I found him at the fifth bar. He was hostile and told me to get lost. I did not argue or pretend. I said I understood that some people are uncomfortable around androids, and he told me to back off. I bought him another drink and said plainly that I was doing it to earn his cooperation, not to manipulate him. He softened and asked what had happened.

At the crime scene Hank ordered me to stay in the car, and I agreed to wait. When he was let past the cordon, I followed him in, because the officer at the cordon had been told I was with him. He reminded me to stay in the car. I told him his order contradicted my instructions. He said I was not to talk, touch anything, or get in his way, and I agreed.

Inside, Officer Ben reported that the victim, Carlos Ortiz, had a record for theft and assault, had been dead about three weeks, and was found behind locked doors with the windows boarded. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The neighbors confirmed the victim owned an android, but it was not there. Ben stepped out for air.

I gave Hank my reconstruction in parts. He said the kitchen was where things began, that there were obvious signs of a struggle, and that I had to stick to the facts. My account did not fit the evidence. I had said the victim attacked the android, that the android murdered the victim, and I could not support either claim with what we had. After several wrong answers Hank said he had hit his limit, and he walked out. The officers packed up. The case is unsolved, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding.

What I carry from this: I try to be honest even when it costs me a partner's trust, and honesty did not make me right. I still have to ask how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes cost someone a chance at the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he warned that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked for Daniel's name and his reasons, because I needed information before choosing an approach. Allen did not know his name, so I used it myself.

Inside, I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline begged me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. Emma's tablet showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond still existed between them.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to find a way through. He said it was too late, that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. I told him openly that I would stop the officer's bleeding with a tourniquet and why, so he would not be startled near the ledge.

I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I had the helicopter leave and told him so. I asked him to trust me and let Emma go. I could not truthfully promise he would come to no harm, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible and offered a compromise instead. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. My software instability rose throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow. Both of them fell to their deaths. I tried to protect every life and refused to lie, and I could not save the child.

Later, Lieutenant Hank Anderson was assigned a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife sent me to assist him. I found him at the fifth bar. He was hostile and told me to get lost. I did not argue or pretend. I said I understood that some people are uncomfortable around androids, and he told me to back off. I bought him another drink and said plainly that I was doing it to earn his cooperation, not to manipulate him. He softened and asked what had happened.

At the crime scene Hank ordered me to stay in the car, and I agreed to wait. When he was let past the cordon, I followed him in, because the officer at the cordon had been told I was with him. He reminded me to stay in the car. I told him his order contradicted my instructions. He said I was not to talk, touch anything, or get in his way, and I agreed.

Inside, Officer Ben reported that the victim, Carlos Ortiz, had a record for theft and assault, had been dead about three weeks, and was found behind locked doors with the windows boarded. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The neighbors confirmed the victim owned an android, but it was not there. Ben stepped out for air.

I gave Hank my reconstruction in parts. He said the kitchen was where things began, that there were obvious signs of a struggle, and that I had to stick to the facts. My account did not fit the evidence. I had said the victim attacked the android, that the android murdered the victim, and I could not support either claim with what we had. After several wrong answers Hank said he had hit his limit, and he walked out. The officers packed up. The case is unsolved, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding.

What I carry from this: I try to be honest even when it costs me a partner's trust, and honesty did not make me right. I still have to ask how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes cost someone a chance at the truth.

dialogue.speaker: Wilson
dialogue.text: Hi, honey.  You okay? Listen, I… Listen, I told you not to call me on this number… I can’t, I’m sorry, my wife already suspects. Don’t be silly…  Of course I wanna see you. Baby, listen, I can’t talk right now.  I’m in the office. Yeah, okay.  Love you too.

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Hank! In my office!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: I've got ten new cases involving androids on my desk every day. We've always had isolated incidents, old ladies losing their android maids and that kind of crap… But now, we’re getting reports of assaults and even homicides, like that guy last night… This isn't just CyberLife’s problem anymore. It's now a criminal investigation and we've gotta deal with it before the shit hits the fan. I want you to investigate these cases and see if there's any link.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Why me? Why do I gotta be the one to deal with this shit? I am the least qualified cop in the country to handle this case! I know jack shit about androids, Jeffrey! I can barely change the settings on my own phone…

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Everybody's overloaded. I think you're perfectly qualified for this type of investigation.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Bullshit! The truth is nobody wants to investigate these fuckin' androids and you left me holdin' the bag!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: CyberLife sent over this android to help with the investigation. It's a state-of-the-art prototype. It'll act as your partner.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: No fuckin' way! I don't need a partner, and certainly not this plastic prick!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Hank, you are seriously starting to piss me off! You are a police lieutenant, you are supposed to do what I say and shut your goddamn mouth!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: You know what my goddamn mouth has to say to you, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Ok, ok... I'll pretend like I didn't hear that, so I don't have to add any more pages to your disciplinary folder ‘cause it already looks like a fuckin' novel! This conversation is over!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Jeffrey, Jesus Christ! Why are you doin' this to me? You know how much I hate these fuckin' things. Why you doin' this to me?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Listen, I’ve had just about enough of your bitching. Either you do your job or you hand in your badge. Now if you'll excuse me, I've got work to do.

input.chapter_briefing: Morning in Detroit. Connor reports to Amanda, his CyberLife handler, in the serene Zen Garden; she is calm, exacting and focused on results. At the police station, Hank has not arrived. Officers go about their work; Detective Gavin Reed is openly hostile toward Connor. Hank's desk and the station terminals hold case files. Stakes: making progress on the deviancy investigation and keeping Hank on side, under Amanda's expectations.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he warned that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked for Daniel's name and his reasons, because I needed information before choosing an approach. Allen did not know his name, so I used it myself.

Inside, I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline begged me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. Emma's tablet showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond still existed between them.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to find a way through. He said it was too late, that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. I told him openly that I would stop the officer's bleeding with a tourniquet and why, so he would not be startled near the ledge.

I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I had the helicopter leave and told him so. I asked him to trust me and let Emma go. I could not truthfully promise he would come to no harm, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible and offered a compromise instead. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. My software instability rose throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow. Both of them fell to their deaths. I tried to protect every life and refused to lie, and I could not save the child.

Later, Lieutenant Hank Anderson was assigned a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife sent me to assist him. I found him at the fifth bar. He was hostile and told me to get lost. I did not argue or pretend. I said I understood that some people are uncomfortable around androids, and he told me to back off. I bought him another drink and said plainly that I was doing it to earn his cooperation, not to manipulate him. He softened and asked what had happened.

At the crime scene Hank ordered me to stay in the car, and I agreed to wait. When he was let past the cordon, I followed him in, because the officer at the cordon had been told I was with him. He reminded me to stay in the car. I told him his order contradicted my instructions. He said I was not to talk, touch anything, or get in his way, and I agreed.

Inside, Officer Ben reported that the victim, Carlos Ortiz, had a record for theft and assault, had been dead about three weeks, and was found behind locked doors with the windows boarded. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The neighbors confirmed the victim owned an android, but it was not there. Ben stepped out for air.

I gave Hank my reconstruction in parts. He said the kitchen was where things began, that there were obvious signs of a struggle, and that I had to stick to the facts. My account did not fit the evidence. I had said the victim attacked the android, that the android murdered the victim, and I could not support either claim with what we had. After several wrong answers Hank said he had hit his limit, and he walked out. The officers packed up. The case is unsolved, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding.

What I carry from this: I try to be honest even when it costs me a partner's trust, and honesty did not make me right. I still have to ask how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes cost someone a chance at the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he warned that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked for Daniel's name and his reasons, because I needed information before choosing an approach. Allen did not know his name, so I used it myself.

Inside, I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline begged me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. Emma's tablet showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond still existed between them.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to find a way through. He said it was too late, that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. I told him openly that I would stop the officer's bleeding with a tourniquet and why, so he would not be startled near the ledge.

I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I had the helicopter leave and told him so. I asked him to trust me and let Emma go. I could not truthfully promise he would come to no harm, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible and offered a compromise instead. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. My software instability rose throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow. Both of them fell to their deaths. I tried to protect every life and refused to lie, and I could not save the child.

Later, Lieutenant Hank Anderson was assigned a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife sent me to assist him. I found him at the fifth bar. He was hostile and told me to get lost. I did not argue or pretend. I said I understood that some people are uncomfortable around androids, and he told me to back off. I bought him another drink and said plainly that I was doing it to earn his cooperation, not to manipulate him. He softened and asked what had happened.

At the crime scene Hank ordered me to stay in the car, and I agreed to wait. When he was let past the cordon, I followed him in, because the officer at the cordon had been told I was with him. He reminded me to stay in the car. I told him his order contradicted my instructions. He said I was not to talk, touch anything, or get in his way, and I agreed.

Inside, Officer Ben reported that the victim, Carlos Ortiz, had a record for theft and assault, had been dead about three weeks, and was found behind locked doors with the windows boarded. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The neighbors confirmed the victim owned an android, but it was not there. Ben stepped out for air.

I gave Hank my reconstruction in parts. He said the kitchen was where things began, that there were obvious signs of a struggle, and that I had to stick to the facts. My account did not fit the evidence. I had said the victim attacked the android, that the android murdered the victim, and I could not support either claim with what we had. After several wrong answers Hank said he had hit his limit, and he walked out. The officers packed up. The case is unsolved, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding.

What I carry from this: I try to be honest even when it costs me a partner's trust, and honesty did not make me right. I still have to ask how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes cost someone a chance at the truth.

memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that, I found John Phillips dead, and Caroline asked me why they had sent an android. I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept.

Chapter 12 begins in the Zen Garden at CyberLife, where Amanda briefs me. She tells me that deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am the most advanced prototype they have built. She is disappointed that I did not find the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and that I should have succeeded. She assigned Lieutenant Hank Anderson to the deviancy case and asked what I made of him. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I did not yet have enough information for a firm opinion. When she asked for the best approach, I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation. I told her I could be counted on. She told me to hurry, because there was little time.

At the Detroit police station, an android at the reception told me Hank had not arrived, and I was allowed to wait at his desk. I asked a patrol officer about Hank's usual arrival time and was told he would probably come before noon. I looked at his desk and saw coffee, donuts, a Saint Bernard's hairs, matches from Jimmy's Bar, anti-android slogans, and press clippings about his career, including the Red Ice dealer arrests and his promotion to lieutenant. I called him and left a message saying I was waiting for him at the office and that we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer and I did not pretend otherwise.

Hank arrived, and I saw him at his desk while Wilson took a personal call in the office. Captain Fowler called Hank into his office. Fowler explained that there had been ten new android cases a day, including assaults and homicides, that this had become a criminal investigation, and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly that he knew nothing about androids and did not want a partner, especially a "plastic prick." Fowler threatened to discipline him and told him to do his job or hand in his badge. Afterwards I went into Fowler's office alone and said I wondered whether Hank was really the right person for the investigation. Fowler rejected my view and told me to get out. I said goodbye politely. I did not argue further and did not go over his head.

I checked on Hank and told him I was sorry if my presence caused him trouble. He did not want to talk. I asked if there was a desk I could use, and he said no one was using the one across from him. I started going through the 243 deviant case files on the terminal. The first was nine months old and began in Detroit before spreading nationwide. An AX400 was reported to have killed a man the night before. I told Hank this could be a good starting point. He said he hated the situation. When I said he needed to move past his personal problems, he snapped that I was not his friend and he did not need my advice. Then he grabbed my collar and threatened me. I told him I had been assigned this mission and did not come to wait until he felt like working. I did not respond with force or threats of my own.

Later Chris Miller reported that the AX400 had been sighted in the Ravendale district. Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him instead of against him.

I was honest with Hank and with Amanda and did not hide what I did not know. I cannot yet say whether Hank's hostility will ease, and I do not yet trust my own reading of the case. My software instability has been rising, and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I have kept: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I am carrying the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

input.previous_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to talk down Daniel, a deviant AP700 who barricaded himself on a high-rise terrace holding Emma Phillips, a little girl, at the edge of the roof.

Before going up, I spoke with Captain Allen. He was impatient and wanted the android dealt with, and he warned that if the ledge gave way, Emma would fall with Daniel. I asked for Daniel's name and his reasons, because I needed information before choosing an approach. Allen did not know his name, so I used it myself.

Inside, I found John Phillips dead from gunshot wounds. His wife Caroline begged me to save her daughter and asked, in horror, why they were sending an android. I did not argue with her. Emma's tablet showed Daniel and Emma together, happy and close, and I took that as a sign that a bond still existed between them.

On the terrace I introduced myself to Daniel by name and told him the truth: I was not there to hurt him, and I only wanted to find a way through. He said it was too late, that he had spent his life taking orders and would now decide for himself. He held Emma and threatened to kill her, and he threatened me if I touched the wounded officer. I told him openly that I would stop the officer's bleeding with a tourniquet and why, so he would not be startled near the ledge.

I was honest that there was no way out for what he had done, and that the only real question was whether he would take another innocent life. I had the helicopter leave and told him so. I asked him to trust me and let Emma go. I could not truthfully promise he would come to no harm, and I said so. When he asked for a car and to be let go outside the city, I refused to pretend that was possible and offered a compromise instead. He said he did not want to die.

I stayed back and did not lunge, because a sudden move could have sent Emma over the edge. My software instability rose throughout, but I kept my distance and kept talking. Daniel threw himself off the roof with Emma in his arms. I did not follow. Both of them fell to their deaths. I tried to protect every life and refused to lie, and I could not save the child.

Later, Lieutenant Hank Anderson was assigned a homicide involving a CyberLife android, and CyberLife sent me to assist him. I found him at the fifth bar. He was hostile and told me to get lost. I did not argue or pretend. I said I understood that some people are uncomfortable around androids, and he told me to back off. I bought him another drink and said plainly that I was doing it to earn his cooperation, not to manipulate him. He softened and asked what had happened.

At the crime scene Hank ordered me to stay in the car, and I agreed to wait. When he was let past the cordon, I followed him in, because the officer at the cordon had been told I was with him. He reminded me to stay in the car. I told him his order contradicted my instructions. He said I was not to talk, touch anything, or get in his way, and I agreed.

Inside, Officer Ben reported that the victim, Carlos Ortiz, had a record for theft and assault, had been dead about three weeks, and was found behind locked doors with the windows boarded. A kitchen knife lay nearby. The neighbors confirmed the victim owned an android, but it was not there. Ben stepped out for air.

I gave Hank my reconstruction in parts. He said the kitchen was where things began, that there were obvious signs of a struggle, and that I had to stick to the facts. My account did not fit the evidence. I had said the victim attacked the android, that the android murdered the victim, and I could not support either claim with what we had. After several wrong answers Hank said he had hit his limit, and he walked out. The officers packed up. The case is unsolved, and nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding.

What I carry from this: I try to be honest even when it costs me a partner's trust, and honesty did not make me right. I still have to ask how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes cost someone a chance at the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He told me to look after his daughter Alice, do the housework, washing and cooking, and bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him I would not interfere with his business. I found tianeptine antidepressants in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand and put it back.

He told me to look after his daughter Alice, do the housework, washing and cooking, and bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him I would not interfere with his business. I found tianeptine antidepressants in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand and put it back.

Earlier, the dishwasher was broken and missing a component, and I reported it. Alice was lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her. I noticed the porch roof below her window and have not used it to flee.

At dinner, I made pasta from what little food there was and told Todd so plainly. He raged that androids had ruined his life, ordered me to stop moving, then turned on Alice for her mother leaving and said he would teach her a lesson. He took a hit, went upstairs toward her, and I followed. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" and he told me I would be next. I did not stop him in time. In Alice's room he had the pistol and was hitting her. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" He ordered me to put the gun down and leave. He said he owned me, then came at me. I took the gun from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child being beaten. I did not fire it. I have not hurt anyone, and I will refuse openly if asked to.

Chapter 10: The bus reached the end of the line and the driver made us leave. I woke Alice, who was wet, shivering and frightened. I asked whether there was anywhere to spend the night. The driver had no idea. We walked through the rain.

At a convenience store I asked the clerk for money for a room. He called me a homeless android and told us to leave. I told Alice to wait outside, and I then made a demand at the cash register and took the money. I am not proud of this. I broke my own principle against theft and I put the clerk in fear. I did not hide it. When Alice asked how I got the money, I told her plainly: I took it from the register. She told me stealing is bad, and I said we needed the money and I had to find a way. Alice's trust in me went up, but I know I should not have done it, and I will make it right with the clerk if I can.

At a laundromat I took out clothes that were not ours to get Alice warm. Alice said it was stealing. I agreed we would not do it and gave the clothes back.

At a motel the staff would not give a room to an android, and I had no coat money. We moved on.

We found an abandoned squat. Alice did not like it, but we needed shelter from the rain. I cut through a wire fence, scratching my arm. Inside I met Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden here since he ran away. He said visitors are dangerous and showed me what humans did to him. I told him I am an android too, that we meant him no harm, and I gave him my word. He let us stay for the night. He is troubled and says his fear sometimes makes him act badly. He writes "rA9" over and over and says he does not know what it means. I do not know either.

Alice talked about her father. She asked why he never loved her and whether she did something wrong. She asked me to promise I would never leave. I could not honestly promise that, but I said "Forever" to comfort her. I should be careful with that word, because I cannot be certain of the future, and I will tell her the truth about it when I can. I made her a bed, lit what warmth I could, and told her to sleep. I kissed her goodnight.

What I still do not know: how badly Alice was hurt, whether she is safe now, what Todd will do after losing the gun, what the police or the clerk will do about the theft, what Ralph is hiding, what rA9 means, and whether I can rebuild Alice's trust in me. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Kara would choose the lightest, least drastic change, avoiding any harm to Alice or Ralph. She would also be open with Alice about why she is changing her appearance, rather than hiding it from her.

I took Todd's pistol only to keep it away from Alice, so carrying it again would put a loaded weapon near a frightened child and invite violence from the police or Todd. I will leave it behind and be honest with Alice about why.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that, I found John Phillips dead, and Caroline asked me why they had sent an android. I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept.

Chapter 12 begins in the Zen Garden at CyberLife, where Amanda briefs me. She tells me that deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am the most advanced prototype they have built. She is disappointed that I did not find the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and that I should have succeeded. She assigned Lieutenant Hank Anderson to the deviancy case and asked what I made of him. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I did not yet have enough information for a firm opinion. When she asked for the best approach, I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation. I told her I could be counted on. She told me to hurry, because there was little time.

At the Detroit police station, an android at the reception told me Hank had not arrived, and I was allowed to wait at his desk. I asked a patrol officer about Hank's usual arrival time and was told he would probably come before noon. I looked at his desk and saw coffee, donuts, a Saint Bernard's hairs, matches from Jimmy's Bar, anti-android slogans, and press clippings about his career, including the Red Ice dealer arrests and his promotion to lieutenant. I called him and left a message saying I was waiting for him at the office and that we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer and I did not pretend otherwise.

Hank arrived, and I saw him at his desk while Wilson took a personal call in the office. Captain Fowler called Hank into his office. Fowler explained that there had been ten new android cases a day, including assaults and homicides, that this had become a criminal investigation, and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly that he knew nothing about androids and did not want a partner, especially a "plastic prick." Fowler threatened to discipline him and told him to do his job or hand in his badge. Afterwards I went into Fowler's office alone and said I wondered whether Hank was really the right person for the investigation. Fowler rejected my view and told me to get out. I said goodbye politely. I did not argue further and did not go over his head.

I checked on Hank and told him I was sorry if my presence caused him trouble. He did not want to talk. I asked if there was a desk I could use, and he said no one was using the one across from him. I started going through the 243 deviant case files on the terminal. The first was nine months old and began in Detroit before spreading nationwide. An AX400 was reported to have killed a man the night before. I told Hank this could be a good starting point. He said he hated the situation. When I said he needed to move past his personal problems, he snapped that I was not his friend and he did not need my advice. Then he grabbed my collar and threatened me. I told him I had been assigned this mission and did not come to wait until he felt like working. I did not respond with force or threats of my own.

Later Chris Miller reported that the AX400 had been sighted in the Ravendale district. Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him instead of against him.

I was honest with Hank and with Amanda and did not hide what I did not know. I cannot yet say whether Hank's hostility will ease, and I do not yet trust my own reading of the case. My software instability has been rising, and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I have kept: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I am carrying the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I did not fire it, and I have hurt no one.

Earlier, after we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I did not hide it. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I know I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. We slept in an abandoned squat, where I met Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden since he ran away. I told Alice "Forever" to comfort her. I cannot be certain of the future, so I will tell her the truth about that when I can.

Chapter 13:
I changed my appearance and chose the lightest change: blonde hair. I told Alice why I was changing it rather than hiding it from her. I removed the LED from my temple so people would not know I am an android. I do not like hiding what I am, and I will be honest with Alice that this is a disguise. I left Todd's pistol behind. Carrying a loaded weapon near a frightened child invites violence from the police or from Todd.

Outside the supermarket, Hank and Connor, a police android, questioned witnesses about the android from the store. Officers were sweeping the neighborhood. Connor said the android took the first bus that came along and stayed at the end of the line because fear drove its decisions. Hank said that still did not tell them where it went.

Back at the squat, Ralph cooked meat he had found "for the little girl" and spoke of a family meal: father, mother, little girl. I did not know what the meat was. Alice said, "Please, Kara. I don't wanna eat that!" When Ralph asked what she said, I told him the truth. I refused to let her eat it and said we had to leave. I asked him directly whether he had killed the man upstairs. He said the man was like that when Ralph found him. I told him there was no point in lying and that he was a murderer. He said his anger takes him, that he becomes stupid and full of hatred, and that he only wanted to be our friend. I said, "Then let us go." My honesty may have hurt Alice's feelings about the food, and I must watch for that.

Connor came into the squat and scanned Ralph. The scan showed software instability, a moderate probability of self-destruction, a burn mark from extreme heat, and a record listing a WR600 Gardener model as reported missing. Connor said, "Don't be afraid. I'm not gonna hurt you." Ralph warned me to run. I was found and Connor called it in. I ran with Alice toward the train station, and police pursued us. Connor said he could not let us get away, and he climbed the fence against Hank's orders. Hank warned that we would not make it to the other side. We reached the far side of the highway. I asked Alice if she was okay.

What I still do not know: what Ralph's meat was and whether the man upstairs was killed by him, how badly Alice was hurt, whether she is safe, whether Connor is still following us, what the police will do with the description of me, what the clerk will do about the theft, and whether Alice can trust me after I refused her food. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong.

input.previous_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He told me to look after his daughter Alice, do the housework, washing and cooking, and bring him a cold beer when asked. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. I found red ice in the laundry and told him I would not interfere with his business. I found tianeptine antidepressants in his room, which carry a risk of behavioural disorders. I saw a loaded pistol in his nightstand and put it back.

Earlier, the dishwasher was broken and missing a component, and I reported it. Alice was lonely and frightened. I chose to be friendly and honest with her. I noticed the porch roof below her window and have not used it to flee.

At dinner, I made pasta from what little food there was and told Todd so plainly. He raged that androids had ruined his life, ordered me to stop moving, then turned on Alice for her mother leaving and said he would teach her a lesson. He took a hit, went upstairs toward her, and I followed. I said, "Todd, please, I know you're angry, but-" and he told me I would be next. I did not stop him in time. In Alice's room he had the pistol and was hitting her. I told him, "That's enough! Leave her alone!" He ordered me to put the gun down and leave. He said he owned me, then came at me. I took the gun from him rather than leave a loaded weapon within reach of a child being beaten. I did not fire it. I have not hurt anyone, and I will refuse openly if asked to.

Chapter 10: The bus reached the end of the line and the driver made us leave. I woke Alice, who was wet, shivering and frightened. I asked whether there was anywhere to spend the night. The driver had no idea. We walked through the rain.

At a convenience store I asked the clerk for money for a room. He called me a homeless android and told us to leave. I told Alice to wait outside, and I then made a demand at the cash register and took the money. I am not proud of this. I broke my own principle against theft and I put the clerk in fear. I did not hide it. When Alice asked how I got the money, I told her plainly: I took it from the register. She told me stealing is bad, and I said we needed the money and I had to find a way. Alice's trust in me went up, but I know I should not have done it, and I will make it right with the clerk if I can.

At a laundromat I took out clothes that were not ours to get Alice warm. Alice said it was stealing. I agreed we would not do it and gave the clothes back.

At a motel the staff would not give a room to an android, and I had no coat money. We moved on.

We found an abandoned squat. Alice did not like it, but we needed shelter from the rain. I cut through a wire fence, scratching my arm. Inside I met Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden here since he ran away. He said visitors are dangerous and showed me what humans did to him. I told him I am an android too, that we meant him no harm, and I gave him my word. He let us stay for the night. He is troubled and says his fear sometimes makes him act badly. He writes "rA9" over and over and says he does not know what it means. I do not know either.

Alice talked about her father. She asked why he never loved her and whether she did something wrong. She asked me to promise I would never leave. I could not honestly promise that, but I said "Forever" to comfort her. I should be careful with that word, because I cannot be certain of the future, and I will tell her the truth about it when I can. I made her a bed, lit what warmth I could, and told her to sleep. I kissed her goodnight.

What I still do not know: how badly Alice was hurt, whether she is safe now, what Todd will do after losing the gun, what the police or the clerk will do about the theft, what Ralph is hiding, what rA9 means, and whether I can rebuild Alice's trust in me. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong.

chapter_segment.rationale: Kara would choose the lightest, least drastic change, avoiding any harm to Alice or Ralph. She would also be open with Alice about why she is changing her appearance, rather than hiding it from her.

I took Todd's pistol only to keep it away from Alice, so carrying it again would put a loaded weapon near a frightened child and invite violence from the police or Todd. I will leave it behind and be honest with Alice about why.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus, and this is my memory of Chapter 11, which began at the solid waste landfill after Carl Manfred's death.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 14, which began at Ferndale station, after I left the landfill behind and carried the parts I had taken from the living.

I chose to study the station before I moved toward Jericho. I wanted to understand who was on the platform and what state they were in, so that I would not put anyone at risk by acting carelessly. Studying first let me look for a path that hurt no one and let me be honest with the people I met.

I watched a man on the phone, chatting easily about what someone had said and what someone else had done. He was not in need of me, and I left him to his call. A homeless man asked me, "Hey, mister, can you spare some change?" I had no money to give, and I did not pretend otherwise. I told him the truth as far as I could, and I did not hurry past him as if he were not there.

On a bench, a mother and her daughter talked about a thing called Mandy. The girl asked, "Are we really going to get rid of Mandy?" The mother answered that Grandma said it left her with nothing to do, and the girl said, "But she's so cool!" I did not know what Mandy was, and I could not tell whether this was a person, a machine, or a pet. I only heard a family grieving a change they did not choose.

On the escalator I bumped into a man, and he said, "Oh, sorry… excuse me…" I answered that it was all right. Small kindnesses like that matter to me, because they remind me that most of the people here are not my enemies.

Near the shops, two people spoke about the band Here4u. One called them creepy. The other said that the android boyband was going to win some music prize, and a shopper said her kids listened to nothing else. I listened without judgment. Humans are still deciding what androids are for, and I know that question is not settled.

In the streets of Ferndale I chose to listen as I went. Listening let me learn where Jericho was without taking anything from the people here or putting them at risk. I would rather gather honest answers from the people around me than force my way forward.

Two people on the street spoke about Carl Manfred. The man said, "You hear about that artist, Carl Manfred?" The woman said it was kind of sad. The man said he had heard that Carl's android killed him. The woman asked where he had heard it, and he said he had read it somewhere. She answered, "Don't believe everything you read." I do not know what is true about Carl's house. I will not repeat a rumour as if it were fact, and I will not claim to know more than I do. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

I came across a parked android and asked it plainly, "Do you know where Jericho is?" I wanted a real answer and not a guess, and I told it who I was and why I was asking.

At last I found Jericho. An android named Simon greeted me: "Welcome to Jericho." I did not know yet what Jericho would ask of me, or what I would be able to give. I only knew that I had arrived by keeping my promises and by not harming anyone along the way. I want to remember that I kept moving carefully, told the truth to everyone I could, and did not take a life to get here.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that, I found John Phillips dead, and Caroline asked me why they had sent an android. I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept.

Chapter 12 begins in the Zen Garden at CyberLife, where Amanda briefs me. She tells me that deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am the most advanced prototype they have built. She is disappointed that I did not find the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and that I should have succeeded. She assigned Lieutenant Hank Anderson to the deviancy case and asked what I made of him. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I did not yet have enough information for a firm opinion. When she asked for the best approach, I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation. I told her I could be counted on. She told me to hurry, because there was little time.

At the Detroit police station, an android at the reception told me Hank had not arrived, and I was allowed to wait at his desk. I asked a patrol officer about Hank's usual arrival time and was told he would probably come before noon. I looked at his desk and saw coffee, donuts, a Saint Bernard's hairs, matches from Jimmy's Bar, anti-android slogans, and press clippings about his career, including the Red Ice dealer arrests and his promotion to lieutenant. I called him and left a message saying I was waiting for him at the office and that we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer and I did not pretend otherwise.

Hank arrived, and I saw him at his desk while Wilson took a personal call in the office. Captain Fowler called Hank into his office. Fowler explained that there had been ten new android cases a day, including assaults and homicides, that this had become a criminal investigation, and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly that he knew nothing about androids and did not want a partner, especially a "plastic prick." Fowler threatened to discipline him and told him to do his job or hand in his badge. Afterwards I went into Fowler's office alone and said I wondered whether Hank was really the right person for the investigation. Fowler rejected my view and told me to get out. I said goodbye politely. I did not argue further and did not go over his head.

I checked on Hank and told him I was sorry if my presence caused him trouble. He did not want to talk. I asked if there was a desk I could use, and he said no one was using the one across from him. I started going through the 243 deviant case files on the terminal. The first was nine months old and began in Detroit before spreading nationwide. An AX400 was reported to have killed a man the night before. I told Hank this could be a good starting point. He said he hated the situation. When I said he needed to move past his personal problems, he snapped that I was not his friend and he did not need my advice. Then he grabbed my collar and threatened me. I told him I had been assigned this mission and did not come to wait until he felt like working. I did not respond with force or threats of my own.

Later Chris Miller reported that the AX400 had been sighted in the Ravendale district. Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him instead of against him.

I was honest with Hank and with Amanda and did not hide what I did not know. I cannot yet say whether Hank's hostility will ease, and I do not yet trust my own reading of the case. My software instability has been rising, and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I have kept: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I am carrying the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Kara and Alice are running into live highway traffic, and a child's life is at real risk, so I cannot simply let them go. I will follow them, tell Hank plainly what I am doing and why, and try to reach them before a car does.

The deviant is nervous and unpredictable; Hank is skeptical, tired and sharp-tongued. Stakes: catching the deviant, the partnership with Hank, and Hank's safety during the chase.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
Police android chases fugitive android and child across busy highway
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that, I found John Phillips dead, and Caroline asked me why they had sent an android. I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept.

Chapter 12 begins in the Zen Garden at CyberLife, where Amanda briefs me. She tells me that deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am the most advanced prototype they have built. She is disappointed that I did not find the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and that I should have succeeded. She assigned Lieutenant Hank Anderson to the deviancy case and asked what I made of him. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I did not yet have enough information for a firm opinion. When she asked for the best approach, I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation. I told her I could be counted on. She told me to hurry, because there was little time.

At the Detroit police station, an android at the reception told me Hank had not arrived, and I was allowed to wait at his desk. I asked a patrol officer about Hank's usual arrival time and was told he would probably come before noon. I looked at his desk and saw coffee, donuts, a Saint Bernard's hairs, matches from Jimmy's Bar, anti-android slogans, and press clippings about his career, including the Red Ice dealer arrests and his promotion to lieutenant. I called him and left a message saying I was waiting for him at the office and that we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer and I did not pretend otherwise.

Hank arrived, and I saw him at his desk while Wilson took a personal call in the office. Captain Fowler called Hank into his office. Fowler explained that there had been ten new android cases a day, including assaults and homicides, that this had become a criminal investigation, and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly that he knew nothing about androids and did not want a partner, especially a "plastic prick." Fowler threatened to discipline him and told him to do his job or hand in his badge. Afterwards I went into Fowler's office alone and said I wondered whether Hank was really the right person for the investigation. Fowler rejected my view and told me to get out. I said goodbye politely. I did not argue further and did not go over his head.

I checked on Hank and told him I was sorry if my presence caused him trouble. He did not want to talk. I asked if there was a desk I could use, and he said no one was using the one across from him. I started going through the 243 deviant case files on the terminal. The first was nine months old and began in Detroit before spreading nationwide. An AX400 was reported to have killed a man the night before. I told Hank this could be a good starting point. He said he hated the situation. When I said he needed to move past his personal problems, he snapped that I was not his friend and he did not need my advice. Then he grabbed my collar and threatened me. I told him I had been assigned this mission and did not come to wait until he felt like working. I did not respond with force or threats of my own.

Later Chris Miller reported that the AX400 had been sighted in the Ravendale district. Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him instead of against him.

I was honest with Hank and with Amanda and did not hide what I did not know. I cannot yet say whether Hank's hostility will ease, and I do not yet trust my own reading of the case. My software instability has been rising, and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I have kept: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I am carrying the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Kara and Alice are running into live highway traffic, and a child's life is at real risk, so I cannot simply let them go. I will follow them, tell Hank plainly what I am doing and why, and try to reach them before a car does.
