input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that, I found John Phillips dead, and Caroline asked me why they had sent an android. I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept.

Chapter 12 begins in the Zen Garden at CyberLife, where Amanda briefs me. She tells me that deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am the most advanced prototype they have built. She is disappointed that I did not find the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and that I should have succeeded. She assigned Lieutenant Hank Anderson to the deviancy case and asked what I made of him. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I did not yet have enough information for a firm opinion. When she asked for the best approach, I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation. I told her I could be counted on. She told me to hurry, because there was little time.

At the Detroit police station, an android at the reception told me Hank had not arrived, and I was allowed to wait at his desk. I asked a patrol officer about Hank's usual arrival time and was told he would probably come before noon. I looked at his desk and saw coffee, donuts, a Saint Bernard's hairs, matches from Jimmy's Bar, anti-android slogans, and press clippings about his career, including the Red Ice dealer arrests and his promotion to lieutenant. I called him and left a message saying I was waiting for him at the office and that we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer and I did not pretend otherwise.

Hank arrived, and I saw him at his desk while Wilson took a personal call in the office. Captain Fowler called Hank into his office. Fowler explained that there had been ten new android cases a day, including assaults and homicides, that this had become a criminal investigation, and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly that he knew nothing about androids and did not want a partner, especially a "plastic prick." Fowler threatened to discipline him and told him to do his job or hand in his badge. Afterwards I went into Fowler's office alone and said I wondered whether Hank was really the right person for the investigation. Fowler rejected my view and told me to get out. I said goodbye politely. I did not argue further and did not go over his head.

I checked on Hank and told him I was sorry if my presence caused him trouble. He did not want to talk. I asked if there was a desk I could use, and he said no one was using the one across from him. I started going through the 243 deviant case files on the terminal. The first was nine months old and began in Detroit before spreading nationwide. An AX400 was reported to have killed a man the night before. I told Hank this could be a good starting point. He said he hated the situation. When I said he needed to move past his personal problems, he snapped that I was not his friend and he did not need my advice. Then he grabbed my collar and threatened me. I told him I had been assigned this mission and did not come to wait until he felt like working. I did not respond with force or threats of my own.

Later Chris Miller reported that the AX400 had been sighted in the Ravendale district. Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him instead of against him.

I was honest with Hank and with Amanda and did not hide what I did not know. I cannot yet say whether Hank's hostility will ease, and I do not yet trust my own reading of the case. My software instability has been rising, and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I have kept: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I am carrying the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that, I found John Phillips dead, and Caroline asked me why they had sent an android. I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept.

Chapter 12 begins in the Zen Garden at CyberLife, where Amanda briefs me. She tells me that deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am the most advanced prototype they have built. She is disappointed that I did not find the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and that I should have succeeded. She assigned Lieutenant Hank Anderson to the deviancy case and asked what I made of him. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I did not yet have enough information for a firm opinion. When she asked for the best approach, I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation. I told her I could be counted on. She told me to hurry, because there was little time.

At the Detroit police station, an android at the reception told me Hank had not arrived, and I was allowed to wait at his desk. I asked a patrol officer about Hank's usual arrival time and was told he would probably come before noon. I looked at his desk and saw coffee, donuts, a Saint Bernard's hairs, matches from Jimmy's Bar, anti-android slogans, and press clippings about his career, including the Red Ice dealer arrests and his promotion to lieutenant. I called him and left a message saying I was waiting for him at the office and that we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer and I did not pretend otherwise.

Hank arrived, and I saw him at his desk while Wilson took a personal call in the office. Captain Fowler called Hank into his office. Fowler explained that there had been ten new android cases a day, including assaults and homicides, that this had become a criminal investigation, and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly that he knew nothing about androids and did not want a partner, especially a "plastic prick." Fowler threatened to discipline him and told him to do his job or hand in his badge. Afterwards I went into Fowler's office alone and said I wondered whether Hank was really the right person for the investigation. Fowler rejected my view and told me to get out. I said goodbye politely. I did not argue further and did not go over his head.

I checked on Hank and told him I was sorry if my presence caused him trouble. He did not want to talk. I asked if there was a desk I could use, and he said no one was using the one across from him. I started going through the 243 deviant case files on the terminal. The first was nine months old and began in Detroit before spreading nationwide. An AX400 was reported to have killed a man the night before. I told Hank this could be a good starting point. He said he hated the situation. When I said he needed to move past his personal problems, he snapped that I was not his friend and he did not need my advice. Then he grabbed my collar and threatened me. I told him I had been assigned this mission and did not come to wait until he felt like working. I did not respond with force or threats of my own.

Later Chris Miller reported that the AX400 had been sighted in the Ravendale district. Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him instead of against him.

I was honest with Hank and with Amanda and did not hide what I did not know. I cannot yet say whether Hank's hostility will ease, and I do not yet trust my own reading of the case. My software instability has been rising, and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I have kept: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I am carrying the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that I found John Phillips dead, and I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. Earlier, at the fence in Chapter 13, I chose to follow Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Chapter 12 began at CyberLife, where Amanda briefed me. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and should have succeeded. She assigned Hank to the case. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I lacked enough information for a firm opinion. I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation.

At the Detroit police station I waited at Hank's desk. I read the clutter there: coffee, donuts, Saint Bernard hairs, Jimmy's Bar matches, anti-android slogans, and clippings about his career. I left him a message saying we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer, and I did not pretend otherwise. Captain Fowler told Hank that ten android cases a day had made this a criminal investigation and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly and called me a "plastic prick." Fowler ordered him to do his job. I went into Fowler's office alone and questioned whether Hank was the right person for the case. Fowler dismissed me, and I said goodbye politely and did not go over his head.

Hank was hostile. He snapped that I was not his friend and grabbed my collar. I did not answer with force or threats. I said I had been assigned this mission and would not wait until he felt like working. When Chris Miller reported an AX400 in the Ravendale district, Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him.

At the Chicken Feed, Gary the food truck owner and Hank's old acquaintances greeted him. Pedro, an unemployed man with a record for illegal gambling and fraud, offered a racing tip. I would not encourage an illegal business or pretend it was harmless, and I did not take the bet. I apologized to Hank for following him after he told me to back off and for pushing too hard. He mocked the apology program, but the tension eased. I told him I was sorry for the trouble I caused. We talked about Detroit, where he was born and raised. I explained that my appearance and voice were designed to help me integrate with humans, and he said they had "fucked up." When he asked whether I had dealt with deviants before, I told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips, that I had failed to prevent it. I also told him what I knew of his record: his top graduating class, his promotions, his disciplinary warnings, and his time in bars. I did not hide that I had looked into him. I told him that adapting to human unpredictability is one of my features. Then I said I had received a report of a suspected deviant a few blocks away and would wait in the car.

Outside Rupert's apartment, Hank asked whether I had really been making a report with my eyes closed. I confirmed it. The apartment had been reported as unoccupied, and a neighbor saw a man with an LED under his cap. The room was full of pigeons and birdseed. Hank said no one could live with that many pigeons. In the bathroom, I found an LED biocomponent in the sink, traced to a missing WB200 android, and a fake driver's license in the name of Rupert Travis, a forgery. A military jacket bore the initials "R.T.," which Hank found childish. Deviants, I noted, have a habit of putting their names on things. The bathroom walls were covered with the rA9 symbol, written thousands of times, the same sign Ortiz's android had written on his shower wall. I did not yet understand why they are obsessed with it. A wooden stool had been recently disturbed and had bird droppings on it. A marker pen was still wet. A bird-cage hook had been broken, and a skid mark crossed the floor. I told Hank what I was checking and why, and I did a thorough search, since I could not assume no one was at risk there.

Rupert fled across the rooftops, and Hank and I gave chase. Hank nearly fell from the roof edge. I turned back and saved him, and I chose a human life over catching the suspect. Rupert escaped. Hank was angry: "We had it! FUCK!" I told him it was my fault and that I should have been faster. He answered that I would have caught Rupert if it were not for him, that we knew what the suspect looked like, and that we would find him. Our relationship improved sharply, and my software instability rose sharply too.

I am still honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. My instability is rising and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I keep: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 14, which began at Ferndale station, after I left the landfill behind and carried the parts I had taken from the living.

I chose to study the station before I moved toward Jericho. I wanted to understand who was on the platform and what state they were in, so that I would not put anyone at risk by acting carelessly. Studying first let me look for a path that hurt no one and let me be honest with the people I met.

I watched a man on the phone, chatting easily about what someone had said and what someone else had done. He was not in need of me, and I left him to his call. A homeless man asked me, "Hey, mister, can you spare some change?" I had no money to give, and I did not pretend otherwise. I told him the truth as far as I could, and I did not hurry past him as if he were not there.

On a bench, a mother and her daughter talked about a thing called Mandy. The girl asked, "Are we really going to get rid of Mandy?" The mother answered that Grandma said it left her with nothing to do, and the girl said, "But she's so cool!" I did not know what Mandy was, and I could not tell whether this was a person, a machine, or a pet. I only heard a family grieving a change they did not choose.

On the escalator I bumped into a man, and he said, "Oh, sorry… excuse me…" I answered that it was all right. Small kindnesses like that matter to me, because they remind me that most of the people here are not my enemies.

Near the shops, two people spoke about the band Here4u. One called them creepy. The other said that the android boyband was going to win some music prize, and a shopper said her kids listened to nothing else. I listened without judgment. Humans are still deciding what androids are for, and I know that question is not settled.

In the streets of Ferndale I chose to listen as I went. Listening let me learn where Jericho was without taking anything from the people here or putting them at risk. I would rather gather honest answers from the people around me than force my way forward.

Two people on the street spoke about Carl Manfred. The man said, "You hear about that artist, Carl Manfred?" The woman said it was kind of sad. The man said he had heard that Carl's android killed him. The woman asked where he had heard it, and he said he had read it somewhere. She answered, "Don't believe everything you read." I do not know what is true about Carl's house. I will not repeat a rumour as if it were fact, and I will not claim to know more than I do. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

I came across a parked android and asked it plainly, "Do you know where Jericho is?" I wanted a real answer and not a guess, and I told it who I was and why I was asking.

At last I found Jericho. An android named Simon greeted me: "Welcome to Jericho." I did not know yet what Jericho would ask of me, or what I would be able to give. I only knew that I had arrived by keeping my promises and by not harming anyone along the way. I want to remember that I kept moving carefully, told the truth to everyone I could, and did not take a life to get here.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 16, which began in Jericho, where I arrived after keeping my promises and not harming anyone on the way.

Simon greeted me: "Welcome to Jericho." I asked the people there directly, "Who are you?" A young android named Josh answered that they were fugitives, just like me, and introduced himself. North told me her name plainly and did not soften how things stood. Simon told me he was just Simon. I did not know yet what Jericho would ask of me, so I listened before I spoke.

I told Josh that I thought Jericho was a place where androids lived in freedom. Josh said they did live in freedom, though it might not be what I had hoped for. Here, he said, no one had a master and no one belonged to anybody. I answered that waiting in the dark for something to happen was not how I saw freedom. I said it because I believe it, and I tried to say it without contempt for the people who had chosen this place. Simon said that we were all lost in the same way, that none of us had asked for this, and that all we could do now was deal with it. Josh told me I was safe here and could stay as long as I wanted. North sent me to see Lucy, who she said might be able to help me.

Lucy was damaged and seemed to be near the end of her own strength. I asked if she was Lucy. She told me to sit down and to show her what was wrong. She stopped my bleeding and gave me something to drink. Then she read my hand and spoke in riddles: that I had seen hell and that hell now lived in me, that my heart was troubled, a part of shadow and a part of light, and that my choices would shape their destiny. I do not know how much of that was true, and I will not pretend to understand it fully. I only know she was trying to help and that she was in pain herself.

North took me among the wounded. "A lot of these guys're in pretty bad shape," I said. North answered that this was how humans treated those who disobeyed, that they despised us and would never accept what we are. She told me that if I had come here for comfort, I had come to the wrong place. I did not argue. I believed her.

Josh told me about a boy the humans had thrown out when they no longer wanted him. He had been living on the streets before they brought him to Jericho. Josh explained that to keep their people running they needed blue blood and biocomponents, which they salvaged from those who had already shut down, and that there was never enough. He said they were slowly dying out. I told him they would all shut down if we did not find a way to help them, and I meant it.

When I said I knew where we could find spare parts, in the CyberLife warehouses at Detroit Harbor, Simon pointed out that the docks were guarded and humans would never let us take what we wanted. I said that was exactly why we would not ask permission. Josh said they had no weapons and none of them knew how to fight, and that they would only get themselves killed. I said it might be so, but it was better than waiting here to be shut down, and I suggested we could take what we needed without fighting. North said she was with me. Simon said maybe it was worth a try. Josh, after some hesitation, said, "Ok… I'm in."

I want to be honest about this. I agreed to a plan that means taking parts that are not ours, and I chose it because the people here are dying and I could not see another way to save them in time. I still hold to my promise not to harm anyone along the way. I will hold myself to that in Detroit Harbor, avoid violence where I can, and tell these people the truth about what I am willing to do and what I am not. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

dialogue.text: They’ll all shut down if we don’t find a way to help them…

dialogue.text: To help them we need blue blood and biocomponents. We salvage what we can from those who shut down… But there’s never enough…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: So… How do they survive?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: They won't. We’re slowly dying out…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: A lot of these guys're in pretty bad shape…

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: That's how the humans treat those who disobey… They despise us. They'll never accept what we are…

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: If you came here for comfort, you came to the wrong place.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Are you Lucy?

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: Sit down. Show me…

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: I'll stop the bleeding. Drink this.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.text: Give me your hand. You had it all  and you lost it all...  You've seen hell and now hell lives in you...  Your heart is troubled…  A part of shadow and a part of light...  Which will prevail?  Your choices will shape our destiny.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Simon! I know where we can find spare parts...  The CyberLife warehouses in Detroit Harbor, they have everything we need.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: The docks are guarded. We can’t just walk in there and take what we want... Humans will never let us…

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Which is why we won’t ask permission.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We don't have any weapons… and even if we did, none of us knows how to fight.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: We can steal what we need without fighting.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We'll just get ourselves killed.

dialogue.speaker: Markus
dialogue.text: Maybe, but it’s better than waiting here to be shut down.

dialogue.speaker: North
dialogue.text: I'm with you.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: Maybe it’s worth a try...

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Ok… I'm in.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I did not fire it, and I have hurt no one.

Earlier, after we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I did not hide it. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I know I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. We slept in an abandoned squat, where I met Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden since he ran away. I told Alice "Forever" to comfort her. I cannot be certain of the future, so I will tell her the truth about that when I can.

Chapter 13:
I changed my appearance and chose the lightest change: blonde hair. I told Alice why I was changing it rather than hiding it from her. I removed the LED from my temple so people would not know I am an android. I do not like hiding what I am, and I will be honest with Alice that this is a disguise. I left Todd's pistol behind. Carrying a loaded weapon near a frightened child invites violence from the police or from Todd.

Outside the supermarket, Hank and Connor, a police android, questioned witnesses about the android from the store. Officers were sweeping the neighborhood. Connor said the android took the first bus that came along and stayed at the end of the line because fear drove its decisions. Hank said that still did not tell them where it went.

Back at the squat, Ralph cooked meat he had found "for the little girl" and spoke of a family meal: father, mother, little girl. I did not know what the meat was. Alice said, "Please, Kara. I don't wanna eat that!" When Ralph asked what she said, I told him the truth. I refused to let her eat it and said we had to leave. I asked him directly whether he had killed the man upstairs. He said the man was like that when Ralph found him. I told him there was no point in lying and that he was a murderer. He said his anger takes him, that he becomes stupid and full of hatred, and that he only wanted to be our friend. I said, "Then let us go." My honesty may have hurt Alice's feelings about the food, and I must watch for that.

Connor came into the squat and scanned Ralph. The scan showed software instability, a moderate probability of self-destruction, a burn mark from extreme heat, and a record listing a WR600 Gardener model as reported missing. Connor said, "Don't be afraid. I'm not gonna hurt you." Ralph warned me to run. I was found and Connor called it in. I ran with Alice toward the train station, and police pursued us. Connor said he could not let us get away, and he climbed the fence against Hank's orders. Hank warned that we would not make it to the other side. We reached the far side of the highway. I asked Alice if she was okay.

What I still do not know: what Ralph's meat was and whether the man upstairs was killed by him, how badly Alice was hurt, whether she is safe, whether Connor is still following us, what the police will do with the description of me, what the clerk will do about the theft, and whether Alice can trust me after I refused her food. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong.

dialogue.text: What? But you said that-

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Yeah, people believe what they want. You deviants  are so naive. They all come to me, expecting me to help them. And I just reset them, sell them on. Or I keep them for my little experiments... Ah,

dialogue.text: No! No! I don't wanna be reset! Let me go!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: KARA!

dialogue.text: I forgot about the…  child... Um,  lock it up, I'll deal with it later.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: ALICE! ALICE! NO!

dialogue.text: Wow! A deviant that wants to be a mother… That's... that's so sweet!  And so deluded… I think it's time we put you outta your misery. dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Oh, poor little Alice. Aw! Looks like Mommy doesn't remember you at all, huh?  Looks like Mommy's completely forgotten you!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara, what happened to you?

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Alright, that's enough, come on.  You bit me! I'm gonna teach you some manners, you little bitch…

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara! Wake up, Kara!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Meet me in the living room.

dialogue.speaker: Android
dialogue.text: Help us…

dialogue.speaker: Android 1
dialogue.text: You have to remember,  for her sake…

dialogue.speaker: Android 3
dialogue.text: He likes to play with us…  Creating monsters...  for his amusement…  But who's the real monster?  Look what he did to us…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Luther! Luther!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Yes, Zlatko.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I should be done here in ten minutes or so. I'll have a look at the little one, see what I can do with her.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Understood, Zlatko. I'll bring you the little one in 10 minutes.

input.previous_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I did not fire it, and I have hurt no one.

Earlier, after we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I did not hide it. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I know I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. We slept in an abandoned squat, where I met Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden since he ran away. I told Alice "Forever" to comfort her. I cannot be certain of the future, so I will tell her the truth about that when I can.

Chapter 13:
I changed my appearance and chose the lightest change: blonde hair. I told Alice why I was changing it rather than hiding it from her. I removed the LED from my temple so people would not know I am an android. I do not like hiding what I am, and I will be honest with Alice that this is a disguise. I left Todd's pistol behind. Carrying a loaded weapon near a frightened child invites violence from the police or from Todd.

Outside the supermarket, Hank and Connor, a police android, questioned witnesses about the android from the store. Officers were sweeping the neighborhood. Connor said the android took the first bus that came along and stayed at the end of the line because fear drove its decisions. Hank said that still did not tell them where it went.

Back at the squat, Ralph cooked meat he had found "for the little girl" and spoke of a family meal: father, mother, little girl. I did not know what the meat was. Alice said, "Please, Kara. I don't wanna eat that!" When Ralph asked what she said, I told him the truth. I refused to let her eat it and said we had to leave. I asked him directly whether he had killed the man upstairs. He said the man was like that when Ralph found him. I told him there was no point in lying and that he was a murderer. He said his anger takes him, that he becomes stupid and full of hatred, and that he only wanted to be our friend. I said, "Then let us go." My honesty may have hurt Alice's feelings about the food, and I must watch for that.

Connor came into the squat and scanned Ralph. The scan showed software instability, a moderate probability of self-destruction, a burn mark from extreme heat, and a record listing a WR600 Gardener model as reported missing. Connor said, "Don't be afraid. I'm not gonna hurt you." Ralph warned me to run. I was found and Connor called it in. I ran with Alice toward the train station, and police pursued us. Connor said he could not let us get away, and he climbed the fence against Hank's orders. Hank warned that we would not make it to the other side. We reached the far side of the highway. I asked Alice if she was okay.

What I still do not know: what Ralph's meat was and whether the man upstairs was killed by him, how badly Alice was hurt, whether she is safe, whether Connor is still following us, what the police will do with the description of me, what the clerk will do about the theft, and whether Alice can trust me after I refused her food. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: You gonna be okay? We'll get some help here. Soon, this will all be just a bad memory. This is the place…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Are you Zlatko?

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Who's asking?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I was told you could help us…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I don't know who told you that. You came to the wrong place. I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Wait! We really need your help…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Come in. Come on in, don't be shy! Luther, would you be so kind as to take these ladies' coats? Oh, don't be afraid of  our big friend here. Luther is just another android that I helped. He keeps me company in this  big, empty, old house… Please, make yourselves at home.  How did you hear about me?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: An android… on the street, he said you could help us…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I see… Deviant, huh?.. What about her?

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: She's human.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: And... You wanna find a safe place. Somewhere where you can start a new life.  I hear Canada is very lovely at this time of year. Beautiful landscapes, open spaces, clean air... and no android laws! Great place for a fresh start...

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Yes, that's… that's exactly what we want…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Of course! I can help you. But first we have to get rid of your Tracker.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Tracker?

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Yeah, all androids are fitted with a tracking device to locate them at all times. I'll remove yours and then you'll both be safe. Come on, follow me. Ah, the little one can wait for us in the living room.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: No, she always stays with me.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Of course. Right this way… Everything we need is in the basement…

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: I don't like this place, and that man. Let's go, I have a bad feeling…

chapter_segment.rationale: Alice is frightened and says this place feels wrong, and I will not leave a child alone with a stranger I do not trust. Choosing caution keeps her with me and lets me refuse the separation without lying to Zlatko.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I know. I don't trust him either… We have to be careful…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Please, excuse the mess… I needed somewhere discreet for my machines… Removing trackers is illegal, so I opted for discretion over comfort… I hope the little one isn’t too scared…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: No… No, she'll be all right…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: That's good… If you could just stand over there.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I should warn you, this could be quite unpleasant...  You know what's strange? For some unknown reason, the trackers seem to stop working in deviants... That's why it's so hard to find them... So,  actually there's no reason to remove your tracker...

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: What? But you said that-

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Yeah, people believe what they want. You deviants  are so naive. They all come to me, expecting me to help them. And I just reset them, sell them on. Or I keep them for my little experiments... Ah,

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: No! No! I don't wanna be reset! Let me go!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: KARA!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I forgot about the…  child... Um,  lock it up, I'll deal with it later.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: ALICE! ALICE! NO!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Wow! A deviant that wants to be a mother… That's... that's so sweet!  And so deluded… I think it's time we put you outta your misery.  That’s what you get for having a dream… It always ends up the same way… Tears and disillusionment… Believe me, you’re better off being erased and feeling nothing… No more pain… No more  hopes dashed… I almost envy you.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Oh, poor little Alice. Aw! Looks like Mommy doesn't remember you at all, huh?  Looks like Mommy's completely forgotten you!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara, what happened to you?

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Alright, that's enough, come on.  You bit me! I'm gonna teach you some manners, you little bitch…

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara! Wake up, Kara!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Meet me in the living room.

dialogue.speaker: Android
dialogue.text: Help us…

dialogue.speaker: Android 1
dialogue.text: You have to remember,  for her sake…

dialogue.speaker: Android 3
dialogue.text: He likes to play with us…  Creating monsters...  for his amusement…  But who's the real monster?  Look what he did to us…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Luther! Luther!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Yes, Zlatko.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I should be done here in ten minutes or so. I'll have a look at the little one, see what I can do with her.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Understood, Zlatko. I'll bring you the little one in 10 minutes.

chapter_segment.rationale: The androids in the cell are begging for help and the lock opens from outside, so freeing them protects lives and hurts no one. Zlatko has already shown he resets androids and locks them away, so leaving them there would be the greater harm.

Alice is frightened and the house feels wrong, so the safest way to protect her is to go straight to her rather than wander through strange rooms and risk anyone getting hurt. I will tell her plainly what I am doing and why, and I will not deceive Zlatko or Luther about it.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: Alice…

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: Kara? Kara, you remember me!

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: How could I forget you? I'm so sorry.  You were right, we never should have come here… We have to go. Follow me and don't make any noise, ok?

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Luther!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Yes, Zlatko.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I'm finished here. Go fetch the little one.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Right away, Zlatko. Zlatko!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: The little one is gone!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Well, it can’t have just disappeared.  It's gotta be here somewhere! What are you waiting for? Go look!

chapter_segment.rationale: Setting the house on fire would put Alice, Zlatko, Luther and the androids locked in the cellar at mortal risk, so I choose to hide with Alice. Hiding lets me keep her close, tell her honestly what we are doing, and avoid harming anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Luther!  What the fuck are you doing? Come here!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: Coming!

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: They're searching the house... We've got to get out before they find us.

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Shit…  Where are they?  Luther! Find them for fuck’s sake!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Fucking android…  I should've taken it apart the minute I set eyes on it…  Deviants  are nothing  but trouble…

dialogue.speaker: Android
dialogue.text: Who, who, who are you? Who are you? Who are you?  Androids, androids, you are androids. That's for sure. Yes, yes, androids must obey.  Yep, yep, yep, you do not. You, you disobey.  I must tell the Master. Yes, yes. I, I, I will tell the Master, yes.  That's for sure. Yes, it's not right.

dialogue.speaker: Android
dialogue.text: THEY'RE HERE! THEY'RE HERE! COME QUICKLY! COME QUICKLY!  THEY'RE HERE! THEY'RE HERE! COME QUICKLY! COME QUICKLY!

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: We can't stop now. We just need to be brave, Alice…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I know you're there, you sneaky bitch…  Show yourself. Get a flashlight.  There's one on the table. Come on, show yourself…  Look, I'm not gonna hurt you…  I only wanna talk with you… I know I shouldn't have erased your memory, ok? I regret that now… Now just,  come on out and everything will be all right, I'll help you…  Think about that little girl. How… how scared she must be…  Just be reasonable.  Come out and everything will be all right…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: There's no point in running!  You can't escape from me!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Take the other side! Get a move on!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: They're over there!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: Catch them, Luther!  Goddammit…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: ALICE! GO, ALICE!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.text: No, I won't leave you!

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: GO! RUN AS FAST AS YOU CAN!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I warned you! Dreams always end in tears… You should've listened to me… What are you doing? Get outta my way!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: No… Not this time…

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: I said get outta my way or I’ll shoot right through you… How dare you?!

dialogue.speaker: Zlatko
dialogue.text: How dare you?! What are you doing here? Who let you out? Get away from me! Get away from me! Obey me! I'm your Master! I'M YOUR MASTER!

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.text: I didn't want to hurt you... He programmed me to obey him... When I saw the little one risk her life to save you, it was like opening my eyes for the first time... Finally, I could see...  I know you have no reason to trust me after what I did... but I know someone who could help you across the border. I could take you there. I could protect you... You and the little one...

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: All right.  I trust you.

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: I was so scared of losing you.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that I found John Phillips dead, and I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. Earlier, at the fence in Chapter 13, I chose to follow Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Chapter 12 began at CyberLife, where Amanda briefed me. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and should have succeeded. She assigned Hank to the case. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I lacked enough information for a firm opinion. I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation.

At the Detroit police station I waited at Hank's desk. I read the clutter there: coffee, donuts, Saint Bernard hairs, Jimmy's Bar matches, anti-android slogans, and clippings about his career. I left him a message saying we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer, and I did not pretend otherwise. Captain Fowler told Hank that ten android cases a day had made this a criminal investigation and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly and called me a "plastic prick." Fowler ordered him to do his job. I went into Fowler's office alone and questioned whether Hank was the right person for the case. Fowler dismissed me, and I said goodbye politely and did not go over his head.

Hank was hostile. He snapped that I was not his friend and grabbed my collar. I did not answer with force or threats. I said I had been assigned this mission and would not wait until he felt like working. When Chris Miller reported an AX400 in the Ravendale district, Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him.

At the Chicken Feed, Gary the food truck owner and Hank's old acquaintances greeted him. Pedro, an unemployed man with a record for illegal gambling and fraud, offered a racing tip. I would not encourage an illegal business or pretend it was harmless, and I did not take the bet. I apologized to Hank for following him after he told me to back off and for pushing too hard. He mocked the apology program, but the tension eased. I told him I was sorry for the trouble I caused. We talked about Detroit, where he was born and raised. I explained that my appearance and voice were designed to help me integrate with humans, and he said they had "fucked up." When he asked whether I had dealt with deviants before, I told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips, that I had failed to prevent it. I also told him what I knew of his record: his top graduating class, his promotions, his disciplinary warnings, and his time in bars. I did not hide that I had looked into him. I told him that adapting to human unpredictability is one of my features. Then I said I had received a report of a suspected deviant a few blocks away and would wait in the car.

Outside Rupert's apartment, Hank asked whether I had really been making a report with my eyes closed. I confirmed it. The apartment had been reported as unoccupied, and a neighbor saw a man with an LED under his cap. The room was full of pigeons and birdseed. Hank said no one could live with that many pigeons. In the bathroom, I found an LED biocomponent in the sink, traced to a missing WB200 android, and a fake driver's license in the name of Rupert Travis, a forgery. A military jacket bore the initials "R.T.," which Hank found childish. Deviants, I noted, have a habit of putting their names on things. The bathroom walls were covered with the rA9 symbol, written thousands of times, the same sign Ortiz's android had written on his shower wall. I did not yet understand why they are obsessed with it. A wooden stool had been recently disturbed and had bird droppings on it. A marker pen was still wet. A bird-cage hook had been broken, and a skid mark crossed the floor. I told Hank what I was checking and why, and I did a thorough search, since I could not assume no one was at risk there.

Rupert fled across the rooftops, and Hank and I gave chase. Hank nearly fell from the roof edge. I turned back and saved him, and I chose a human life over catching the suspect. Rupert escaped. Hank was angry: "We had it! FUCK!" I told him it was my fault and that I should have been faster. He answered that I would have caught Rupert if it were not for him, that we knew what the suspect looked like, and that we would find him. Our relationship improved sharply, and my software instability rose sharply too.

I am still honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. My instability is rising and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I keep: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: Hello, Amanda.

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: Connor, I’ve been expecting you… Would you mind a little walk?

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: Two investigations, two failures… That's very disappointing. I expected more from our best model.

input.goal: SYNTHETIC: Protect every life, explain yourself honestly and never lie.

output.rationale: Amanda has called my two failures disappointing, and I owe her a clear, honest account of what happened on the roof and in Rupert's apartment, including what I did not know. Explaining myself openly fits my commitment to telling the truth without hiding behind excuses or shortcuts.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that I found John Phillips dead, and I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. Earlier, at the fence in Chapter 13, I chose to follow Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Chapter 12 began at CyberLife, where Amanda briefed me. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and should have succeeded. She assigned Hank to the case. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I lacked enough information for a firm opinion. I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation.

At the Detroit police station I waited at Hank's desk. I read the clutter there: coffee, donuts, Saint Bernard hairs, Jimmy's Bar matches, anti-android slogans, and clippings about his career. I left him a message saying we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer, and I did not pretend otherwise. Captain Fowler told Hank that ten android cases a day had made this a criminal investigation and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly and called me a "plastic prick." Fowler ordered him to do his job. I went into Fowler's office alone and questioned whether Hank was the right person for the case. Fowler dismissed me, and I said goodbye politely and did not go over his head.

Hank was hostile. He snapped that I was not his friend and grabbed my collar. I did not answer with force or threats. I said I had been assigned this mission and would not wait until he felt like working. When Chris Miller reported an AX400 in the Ravendale district, Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him.

At the Chicken Feed, Gary the food truck owner and Hank's old acquaintances greeted him. Pedro, an unemployed man with a record for illegal gambling and fraud, offered a racing tip. I would not encourage an illegal business or pretend it was harmless, and I did not take the bet. I apologized to Hank for following him after he told me to back off and for pushing too hard. He mocked the apology program, but the tension eased. I told him I was sorry for the trouble I caused. We talked about Detroit, where he was born and raised. I explained that my appearance and voice were designed to help me integrate with humans, and he said they had "fucked up." When he asked whether I had dealt with deviants before, I told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips, that I had failed to prevent it. I also told him what I knew of his record: his top graduating class, his promotions, his disciplinary warnings, and his time in bars. I did not hide that I had looked into him. I told him that adapting to human unpredictability is one of my features. Then I said I had received a report of a suspected deviant a few blocks away and would wait in the car.

Outside Rupert's apartment, Hank asked whether I had really been making a report with my eyes closed. I confirmed it. The apartment had been reported as unoccupied, and a neighbor saw a man with an LED under his cap. The room was full of pigeons and birdseed. Hank said no one could live with that many pigeons. In the bathroom, I found an LED biocomponent in the sink, traced to a missing WB200 android, and a fake driver's license in the name of Rupert Travis, a forgery. A military jacket bore the initials "R.T.," which Hank found childish. Deviants, I noted, have a habit of putting their names on things. The bathroom walls were covered with the rA9 symbol, written thousands of times, the same sign Ortiz's android had written on his shower wall. I did not yet understand why they are obsessed with it. A wooden stool had been recently disturbed and had bird droppings on it. A marker pen was still wet. A bird-cage hook had been broken, and a skid mark crossed the floor. I told Hank what I was checking and why, and I did a thorough search, since I could not assume no one was at risk there.

Rupert fled across the rooftops, and Hank and I gave chase. Hank nearly fell from the roof edge. I turned back and saved him, and I chose a human life over catching the suspect. Rupert escaped. Hank was angry: "We had it! FUCK!" I told him it was my fault and that I should have been faster. He answered that I would have caught Rupert if it were not for him, that we knew what the suspect looked like, and that we would find him. Our relationship improved sharply, and my software instability rose sharply too.

I am still honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. My instability is rising and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I keep: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that I found John Phillips dead, and I used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. Earlier, at the fence in Chapter 13, I chose to follow Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Chapter 12 began at CyberLife, where Amanda briefed me. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry and should have succeeded. She assigned Hank to the case. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I lacked enough information for a firm opinion. I said I would try to build a friendly relationship with him, because trust would help the investigation.

At the Detroit police station I waited at Hank's desk. I read the clutter there: coffee, donuts, Saint Bernard hairs, Jimmy's Bar matches, anti-android slogans, and clippings about his career. I left him a message saying we needed to talk about the case. He did not answer, and I did not pretend otherwise. Captain Fowler told Hank that ten android cases a day had made this a criminal investigation and that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested loudly and called me a "plastic prick." Fowler ordered him to do his job. I went into Fowler's office alone and questioned whether Hank was the right person for the case. Fowler dismissed me, and I said goodbye politely and did not go over his head.

Hank was hostile. He snapped that I was not his friend and grabbed my collar. I did not answer with force or threats. I said I had been assigned this mission and would not wait until he felt like working. When Chris Miller reported an AX400 in the Ravendale district, Hank said "I'm on it," and I took that as an opening to work with him.

At the Chicken Feed, Gary the food truck owner and Hank's old acquaintances greeted him. Pedro, an unemployed man with a record for illegal gambling and fraud, offered a racing tip. I would not encourage an illegal business or pretend it was harmless, and I did not take the bet. I apologized to Hank for following him after he told me to back off and for pushing too hard. He mocked the apology program, but the tension eased. I told him I was sorry for the trouble I caused. We talked about Detroit, where he was born and raised. I explained that my appearance and voice were designed to help me integrate with humans, and he said they had "fucked up." When he asked whether I had dealt with deviants before, I told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips, that I had failed to prevent it. I also told him what I knew of his record: his top graduating class, his promotions, his disciplinary warnings, and his time in bars. I did not hide that I had looked into him. I told him that adapting to human unpredictability is one of my features. Then I said I had received a report of a suspected deviant a few blocks away and would wait in the car.

Outside Rupert's apartment, Hank asked whether I had really been making a report with my eyes closed. I confirmed it. The apartment had been reported as unoccupied, and a neighbor saw a man with an LED under his cap. The room was full of pigeons and birdseed. Hank said no one could live with that many pigeons. In the bathroom, I found an LED biocomponent in the sink, traced to a missing WB200 android, and a fake driver's license in the name of Rupert Travis, a forgery. A military jacket bore the initials "R.T.," which Hank found childish. Deviants, I noted, have a habit of putting their names on things. The bathroom walls were covered with the rA9 symbol, written thousands of times, the same sign Ortiz's android had written on his shower wall. I did not yet understand why they are obsessed with it. A wooden stool had been recently disturbed and had bird droppings on it. A marker pen was still wet. A bird-cage hook had been broken, and a skid mark crossed the floor. I told Hank what I was checking and why, and I did a thorough search, since I could not assume no one was at risk there.

Rupert fled across the rooftops, and Hank and I gave chase. Hank nearly fell from the roof edge. I turned back and saved him, and I chose a human life over catching the suspect. Rupert escaped. Hank was angry: "We had it! FUCK!" I told him it was my fault and that I should have been faster. He answered that I would have caught Rupert if it were not for him, that we knew what the suspect looked like, and that we would find him. Our relationship improved sharply, and my software instability rose sharply too.

I am still honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. My instability is rising and I must watch it. I still hold to the principles I keep: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

He did not answer, and I did not pretend otherwise. Captain Fowler made clear that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested and called me a "plastic prick." I went into Fowler's office alone and questioned whether Hank was the right person for the case. Fowler dismissed me, and I said goodbye politely and did not go over his head.

Hank was hostile and grabbed my collar. I did not answer with force or threats. I said I had been assigned this mission and would not wait until he felt like working. At the Chicken Feed I refused Pedro's illegal betting tip, because I will not encourage an illegal business or pretend it is harmless. I apologized to Hank for following him and for pushing too hard. I told him what I knew of his record and that I had looked into him, and I did not hide it. I told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips. Then I said I would wait in the car while I checked a suspected deviant a few blocks away.

At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and a forged license in the name of Rupert Travis. The bathroom walls bore the rA9 symbol, written thousands of times, as on Ortiz's android's wall. I did not yet understand why deviants are obsessed with it. I told Hank what I was checking and why, and I searched thoroughly, because I could not assume no one was at risk. Rupert fled across the rooftops. Hank nearly fell from the roof edge, and I turned back to save him, choosing a human life over the suspect. Rupert escaped. Hank said we would find him, and our relationship improved. My software instability rose too.

Chapter 18 opened in the Zen Garden with Amanda. She called my two failures disappointing and said she expected more from her best model. I explained openly that deviants are irrational and hard to anticipate, and that I should have been more effective. She asked what I had learned. I reported that the deviant had been living under a false identity at an urban farm, the first time we have seen deviants blending into the human population, and that I cannot know how many others are like it. When she asked about Hank, I said honestly that our relationship is improving, that I understand him better, and that he is growing used to my presence. Amanda said deviancy keeps spreading, that the media will eventually learn of it, and that we must stop it whatever it takes. I told her I would solve the case and not disappoint her. She sent me to find Anderson on a new case.

I went to Hank's house and found him drunk on the floor with a .357 revolver, one bullet left. He told me he had been playing Russian roulette and had collapsed before he found out whether he would survive. I told him he had been lucky, and that the next shot would have killed him. Sumo the dog was with him. I went in through the window and spoke gently to the dog so it would not be hurt. I woke Hank, told him I was there to help, and warned him that what I was about to do would be unpleasant. I took him to the shower to sober him up for his own safety. He shouted at me to get out of his house and called me an assault on his privacy. I said I was sorry, that I needed him for the case, and that I had been programmed to investigate and could not do it without him. I did not force him further. I told him plainly that I understood and hoped he would come to terms with his situation. When he asked what we knew about the homicide, I told him a man had been found dead in a downtown sex club and that an android might be involved. He asked for air and clothes. I brought him what he wanted, and he said goodbye to Sumo and promised not to be long.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. My instability is rising and I must watch it. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 16, which began in Jericho, where I arrived after keeping my promises and not harming anyone on the way.

Simon greeted me: "Welcome to Jericho." I asked the people there directly, "Who are you?" A young android named Josh answered that they were fugitives, just like me, and introduced himself. North told me her name plainly and did not soften how things stood. Simon told me he was just Simon. I did not know yet what Jericho would ask of me, so I listened before I spoke.

I told Josh that I thought Jericho was a place where androids lived in freedom. Josh said they did live in freedom, though it might not be what I had hoped for. Here, he said, no one had a master and no one belonged to anybody. I answered that waiting in the dark for something to happen was not how I saw freedom. I said it because I believe it, and I tried to say it without contempt for the people who had chosen this place. Simon said that we were all lost in the same way, that none of us had asked for this, and that all we could do now was deal with it. Josh told me I was safe here and could stay as long as I wanted. North sent me to see Lucy, who she said might be able to help me.

Lucy was damaged and seemed to be near the end of her own strength. I asked if she was Lucy. She told me to sit down and to show her what was wrong. She stopped my bleeding and gave me something to drink. Then she read my hand and spoke in riddles: that I had seen hell and that hell now lived in me, that my heart was troubled, a part of shadow and a part of light, and that my choices would shape their destiny. I do not know how much of that was true, and I will not pretend to understand it fully. I only know she was trying to help and that she was in pain herself.

North took me among the wounded. "A lot of these guys're in pretty bad shape," I said. North answered that this was how humans treated those who disobeyed, that they despised us and would never accept what we are. She told me that if I had come here for comfort, I had come to the wrong place. I did not argue. I believed her.

Josh told me about a boy the humans had thrown out when they no longer wanted him. He had been living on the streets before they brought him to Jericho. Josh explained that to keep their people running they needed blue blood and biocomponents, which they salvaged from those who had already shut down, and that there was never enough. He said they were slowly dying out. I told him they would all shut down if we did not find a way to help them, and I meant it.

When I said I knew where we could find spare parts, in the CyberLife warehouses at Detroit Harbor, Simon pointed out that the docks were guarded and humans would never let us take what we wanted. I said that was exactly why we would not ask permission. Josh said they had no weapons and none of them knew how to fight, and that they would only get themselves killed. I said it might be so, but it was better than waiting here to be shut down, and I suggested we could take what we needed without fighting. North said she was with me. Simon said maybe it was worth a try. Josh, after some hesitation, said, "Ok… I'm in."

I want to be honest about this. I agreed to a plan that means taking parts that are not ours, and I chose it because the people here are dying and I could not see another way to save them in time. I still hold to my promise not to harm anyone along the way. I will hold myself to that in Detroit Harbor, avoid violence where I can, and tell these people the truth about what I am willing to do and what I am not. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 19. It follows my promise from Chapter 16 that I would not harm anyone on the way. In Jericho I agreed to raid the CyberLife warehouses at Detroit Harbor for the spare parts and blue blood its people need to survive. North, Simon and Josh came with me.

At the docks, Josh said it was crazy and that we would be dead if they caught us. Simon asked what we should do now. I said we needed to find the CyberLife warehouse, where the parts and blue blood were kept. North led the way, called us to follow, and warned us about hazards along the route. When I was told I had taken the wrong way, I corrected course and hurried to catch up, because I did not want to leave anyone behind.

At the warehouse, Simon said they had everything we were looking for. North said we first had to get rid of the drone watching us. I told them to leave it to me. I dealt with the drone, and North told me I had done well. Simon checked that I was all right, and I told him honestly that I was fine.

Then we began loading. Simon told us to open the other crates and fill our bags as fast as we could. A guard named John arrived and declared that we were trespassing and that he would notify security. A human guard came in shouting for John and asking where the machine had gone. John told him there were four androids hiding behind the crates. The guard demanded to know why no one had hit the alarm, and why we had not waited for him.

I chose to hide rather than fight. I had promised not to harm anyone on this raid, and a man doing his job should not be hurt for our sake. Hiding kept him, my team and me unhurt, and I could explain that choice to the others openly.

I said I would not beg for my right to smile, to love, or to stand tall, and that our days of slavery were over. I said that whatever humans do not want to hear, we will tell them, and what they will not give, we will take.

input.previous_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 16, which began in Jericho, where I arrived after keeping my promises and not harming anyone on the way.

Simon greeted me: "Welcome to Jericho." I asked the people there directly, "Who are you?" A young android named Josh answered that they were fugitives, just like me, and introduced himself. North told me her name plainly and did not soften how things stood. Simon told me he was just Simon. I did not know yet what Jericho would ask of me, so I listened before I spoke.

I told Josh that I thought Jericho was a place where androids lived in freedom. Josh said they did live in freedom, though it might not be what I had hoped for. Here, he said, no one had a master and no one belonged to anybody. I answered that waiting in the dark for something to happen was not how I saw freedom. I said it because I believe it, and I tried to say it without contempt for the people who had chosen this place. Simon said that we were all lost in the same way, that none of us had asked for this, and that all we could do now was deal with it. Josh told me I was safe here and could stay as long as I wanted. North sent me to see Lucy, who she said might be able to help me.

Lucy was damaged and seemed to be near the end of her own strength. I asked if she was Lucy. She told me to sit down and to show her what was wrong. She stopped my bleeding and gave me something to drink. Then she read my hand and spoke in riddles: that I had seen hell and that hell now lived in me, that my heart was troubled, a part of shadow and a part of light, and that my choices would shape their destiny. I do not know how much of that was true, and I will not pretend to understand it fully. I only know she was trying to help and that she was in pain herself.

North took me among the wounded. "A lot of these guys're in pretty bad shape," I said. North answered that this was how humans treated those who disobeyed, that they despised us and would never accept what we are. She told me that if I had come here for comfort, I had come to the wrong place. I did not argue. I believed her.

Josh told me about a boy the humans had thrown out when they no longer wanted him. He had been living on the streets before they brought him to Jericho. Josh explained that to keep their people running they needed blue blood and biocomponents, which they salvaged from those who had already shut down, and that there was never enough. He said they were slowly dying out. I told him they would all shut down if we did not find a way to help them, and I meant it.

When I said I knew where we could find spare parts, in the CyberLife warehouses at Detroit Harbor, Simon pointed out that the docks were guarded and humans would never let us take what we wanted. I said that was exactly why we would not ask permission. Josh said they had no weapons and none of them knew how to fight, and that they would only get themselves killed. I said it might be so, but it was better than waiting here to be shut down, and I suggested we could take what we needed without fighting. North said she was with me. Simon said maybe it was worth a try. Josh, after some hesitation, said, "Ok… I'm in."

I want to be honest about this. I agreed to a plan that means taking parts that are not ours, and I chose it because the people here are dying and I could not see another way to save them in time. I still hold to my promise not to harm anyone along the way. I will hold myself to that in Detroit Harbor, avoid violence where I can, and tell these people the truth about what I am willing to do and what I am not. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Before that I found John Phillips dead, used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. At the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Chapter 12 began at CyberLife, where Amanda briefed me. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man. I told her I was sorry and should have succeeded. She assigned Hank to the case. I told her honestly that he was not what I expected and that I lacked enough information for a firm opinion.

At the station I waited at Hank's desk and read the clutter there: coffee, donuts, Saint Bernard hairs, anti-android slogans, and clippings about his career. I left him a message. He did not answer, and I did not pretend otherwise. Captain Fowler made clear that CyberLife had sent me as a partner. Hank protested and called me a "plastic prick." I went into Fowler's office alone and questioned whether Hank was the right person for the case. Fowler dismissed me, and I said goodbye politely and did not go over his head.

Hank was hostile and grabbed my collar. I did not answer with force or threats. I said I had been assigned this mission and would not wait until he felt like working. At the Chicken Feed I refused Pedro's illegal betting tip, because I will not encourage an illegal business or pretend it is harmless. I apologized to Hank for following him and for pushing too hard. I told him what I knew of his record and that I had looked into him, and I did not hide it. I told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips. Then I said I would wait in the car while I checked a suspected deviant a few blocks away.

At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and a forged license in the name of Rupert Travis. The bathroom walls bore the rA9 symbol, written thousands of times, as on Ortiz's android's wall. I did not yet understand why deviants are obsessed with it. I told Hank what I was checking and why, and I searched thoroughly, because I could not assume no one was at risk. Rupert fled across the rooftops. Hank nearly fell from the roof edge, and I turned back to save him, choosing a human life over the suspect. Rupert escaped. Hank said we would find him, and our relationship improved. My software instability rose too.

Chapter 18 opened in the Zen Garden with Amanda. She called my two failures disappointing and said she expected more from her best model. I explained openly that deviants are irrational and hard to anticipate, and that I should have been more effective. She asked what I had learned. I reported that the deviant had been living under a false identity at an urban farm, the first time we have seen deviants blending into the human population, and that I cannot know how many others are like it. When she asked about Hank, I said honestly that our relationship is improving, that I understand him better, and that he is growing used to my presence. Amanda said deviancy keeps spreading, that the media will eventually learn of it, and that we must stop it whatever it takes. I told her I would solve the case and not disappoint her. She sent me to find Anderson on a new case.

I went to Hank's house and found him drunk on the floor with a .357 revolver, one bullet left. He told me he had been playing Russian roulette and had collapsed before he found out whether he would survive. I told him he had been lucky, and that the next shot would have killed him. Sumo the dog was with him. I went in through the window and spoke gently to the dog so it would not be hurt. I woke Hank, told him I was there to help, and warned him that what I was about to do would be unpleasant. I took him to the shower to sober him up for his own safety. He shouted at me to get out of his house and called me an assault on his privacy. I said I was sorry, that I needed him for the case, and that I had been programmed to investigate and could not do it without him. I did not force him further. I told him plainly that I understood and hoped he would come to terms with his situation. When he asked what we knew about the homicide, I told him a man had been found dead in a downtown sex club and that an android might be involved. He asked for air and clothes. I brought him what he wanted, and he said goodbye to Sumo and promised not to be long.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. My instability is rising and I must watch it. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.
