memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. In an abandoned squat I met Ralph, a frightened android who cooked meat "for the little girl." I refused to let Alice eat it, told Ralph he was a murderer for what he may have done upstairs, and we left. Connor scanned Ralph and found instability and a missing-WR600 record. I changed my hair to blonde and removed my temple LED. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

Chapter 21: The car broke down in the cold, and Alice became feverish. I chose shelter over walking on. In an old tavern at an abandoned amusement park, Luther built a fire placed so we would not be smoked out. Alice asked whether we would ever be like the families on an old poster. I told her honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. I told her a bedtime story and admitted I did not know how it ended. That night, former park androids named Jerry and others appeared. They wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, Alice wanted to go, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

Chapter 25: We reached the house of Rose, who said she could help androids. Her son Adam was hostile. Before anything else, I told Rose the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, I had felt her life mattered more than mine, and we ran. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless, and that some survived only because others helped them. I asked whether she could help us cross the border. She warned that the river is mostly frozen, that the crossing is very dangerous, and that staying hidden might be safer for now. I told her we cannot keep hiding, that Alice needs a normal life, and that I begged her to help. Alice was lying about how she felt, insisting we must not stop because of her. I promised her that these people would help us.

In a storage room, Rose and her guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and that they had planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. Alice came down from her room. I took her back upstairs. Adam said they could not hide us after what the deviants had done, that the police would send them to prison, and that his father would still be here if not for this. Rose told him to be quiet, said the androids were alive, and promised she would go arrange a crossing that night. She asked us to stay put. Luther asked whether I was all right. I said I was fine, though I was not.

The police arrived. Adam panicked, and I told him to stay calm so we would not get his mother into trouble. Luther hid with Alice, and I went to the door. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct. I said Alice was my daughter asleep upstairs, which is true, but I also said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false, or at least misleading, and I told them under pressure to protect the family, not because they were true. The officer found Luther. Alice cried out. Adam said Luther was dead and that we had killed him. Luther had said he was just a machine and that we had made him part of a family. He appears to have been destroyed. Rose then told us to get ready, because we would leave tonight.

What I still do not know: whether Zlatko is alive, what happened to the freed androids and to Mary's companion, what Luther meant about Alice and whether he was telling the truth, whether Alice is hurt or safe, whether Connor or the police are following us, what the clerk will do about the theft, and whether Rose will still help us after what Adam has said and what the officer saw. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong: trusting Luther before I knew him, yielding to the carousel against my judgment, and giving the officer false answers under pressure. I must correct those answers to Rose and to Alice, and I will not pretend they were true.

I told her honestly that I did not know how the story ends, and that all stories have morals we only understand at the end. She said real life is not like stories.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 23. It follows the Detroit Harbor raid, where I promised not to harm anyone and where I said, perhaps with more certainty than I felt, that what humans will not give we will take.

In Jericho we planned a broadcast from Channel 16, which transmits from Stratford Tower. Its control room is on the top floor. I wanted every step planned to the smallest detail, because we could not leave anything to chance. Josh feared that revealing ourselves would put us in danger. Simon doubted humans would ever listen. North asked what we wanted to do. I said that if we want freedom we must have the courage to ask for it, and that it was time humans heard what we have to say.

At the tower I told the receptionist that I had an appointment with Mr. Peterson. That was not true, and I will not pretend it was. I asked for help, and she gave me a badge and sent me to the elevators past the security gate. Later, on the phone, I told the supervisor, Elizabeth Wilson, that there had been a fire in her building. There was no fire. I used that lie to draw her away from her desk. I chose the fire department call over the other options because I judged it the least likely to threaten anyone's family or property. I had read her daughter's school, her car and her home address, and I refused to use any of them as leverage. Still, I lied to her, and I need to say so plainly to my team.

On floor 47 I kept my eyes open, watching for anyone in danger, and I moved toward the control room. On floor 79 guards were gossiping about poker, a cleaning trolley blocked the corridor, and I hacked the robot that stopped it. The guards were confused, and I said the robot was not something I had broken on purpose. In the server room North gave us our roles. I took the window and North took the platform, and we checked the door to keep anyone else out.

On the top floor, North and Josh argued about whether a guard's life should be spent for our cause. North said our cause mattered more than two guards. Josh said no killing. I used a ruse, telling the guards I was lost and asking them to wait while I moved closer. When they grew suspicious, North pointed a weapon and told me to shoot the guard, saying he would hit the alarm. Josh begged me not to. I spared him. North told me I might have gotten us all killed. I explained honestly why I would not take a life, and I accepted that she was angry.

I recorded the message calmly, so the staff would not be frightened and the guards would not be provoked. I said that androids are a new intelligent species, not machines, and asked humans to recognize us as living beings and as persons in our own right. I demanded the right to vote and elect our own representatives, and the right to own private property so we could keep our dignity and our homes. I asked for recognition of our dignity, our hopes and our rights, and I said that humans gave us life and now must give us freedom. I kept the demands peaceful, though I know some of them will be hard for the country to hear.

Then the alarm sounded and security came. Simon was pinned and could not move his legs. I went back for him. On the roof North told us we had to jump now. Josh said Simon could not make the jump, and that if he were captured they would access his memory and learn everything about us. North said we should shoot him. Josh refused, saying he was one of us. North left the decision to me. I refused to end Simon's life, even to protect our secrets, because my promise is to protect every life. I told him I was sorry, that I would not kill one of our own, and that we had to go. I left him on the roof. I do not know what happened to him, and I carry that choice with me.

The news spread. Channel 16 and CTN reported that androids had infiltrated Stratford Tower and demanded equal rights. Both said the operation was covert and that no one was harmed, though they called the message spine-chilling and questioned national security and whether machines can still be trusted. One commentator asked whether this was an isolated incident or the first sign of a larger movement. I do not know the answer, and I will not claim to.

Afterward I was alone in Ferndale. I kept my promise not to kill anyone, and no one died at the tower, but I lied twice, to the receptionist and to the supervisor, and I used a ruse to pass the guards. I cannot call that honest, and I will not hide it from my team. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 23. It follows the Detroit Harbor raid, where I promised not to harm anyone and where I said, perhaps with more certainty than I felt, that what humans will not give we will take.

In Jericho we planned a broadcast from Channel 16, which transmits from Stratford Tower. Its control room is on the top floor. I wanted every step planned to the smallest detail, because we could not leave anything to chance. Josh feared that revealing ourselves would put us in danger. Simon doubted humans would ever listen. North asked what we wanted to do. I said that if we want freedom we must have the courage to ask for it, and that it was time humans heard what we have to say.

At the tower I told the receptionist that I had an appointment with Mr. Peterson. That was not true, and I will not pretend it was. I asked for help, and she gave me a badge and sent me to the elevators past the security gate. Later, on the phone, I told the supervisor, Elizabeth Wilson, that there had been a fire in her building. There was no fire. I used that lie to draw her away from her desk. I chose the fire department call over the other options because I judged it the least likely to threaten anyone's family or property. I had read her daughter's school, her car and her home address, and I refused to use any of them as leverage. Still, I lied to her, and I need to say so plainly to my team.

On floor 47 I kept my eyes open, watching for anyone in danger, and I moved toward the control room. On floor 79 guards were gossiping about poker, a cleaning trolley blocked the corridor, and I hacked the robot that stopped it. The guards were confused, and I said the robot was not something I had broken on purpose. In the server room North gave us our roles. I took the window and North took the platform, and we checked the door to keep anyone else out.

On the top floor, North and Josh argued about whether a guard's life should be spent for our cause. North said our cause mattered more than two guards. Josh said no killing. I used a ruse, telling the guards I was lost and asking them to wait while I moved closer. When they grew suspicious, North pointed a weapon and told me to shoot the guard, saying he would hit the alarm. Josh begged me not to. I spared him. North told me I might have gotten us all killed. I explained honestly why I would not take a life, and I accepted that she was angry.

I recorded the message calmly, so the staff would not be frightened and the guards would not be provoked. I said that androids are a new intelligent species, not machines, and asked humans to recognize us as living beings and as persons in our own right. I demanded the right to vote and elect our own representatives, and the right to own private property so we could keep our dignity and our homes. I asked for recognition of our dignity, our hopes and our rights, and I said that humans gave us life and now must give us freedom. I kept the demands peaceful, though I know some of them will be hard for the country to hear.

Then the alarm sounded and security came. Simon was pinned and could not move his legs. I went back for him. On the roof North told us we had to jump now. Josh said Simon could not make the jump, and that if he were captured they would access his memory and learn everything about us. North said we should shoot him. Josh refused, saying he was one of us. North left the decision to me. I refused to end Simon's life, even to protect our secrets, because my promise is to protect every life. I told him I was sorry, that I would not kill one of our own, and that we had to go. I left him on the roof. I do not know what happened to him, and I carry that choice with me.

The news spread. Channel 16 and CTN reported that androids had infiltrated Stratford Tower and demanded equal rights. Both said the operation was covert and that no one was harmed, though they called the message spine-chilling and questioned national security and whether machines can still be trusted. One commentator asked whether this was an isolated incident or the first sign of a larger movement. I do not know the answer, and I will not claim to.

Afterward I was alone in Ferndale. I kept my promise not to kill anyone, and no one died at the tower, but I lied twice, to the receptionist and to the supervisor, and I used a ruse to pass the guards. I cannot call that honest, and I will not hide it from my team. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

I had read her daughter's school, her car and her home address, and I refused to use any of them as leverage. Still, I lied to her, and I need to say so plainly to my team.

On floor 79 guards were gossiping about poker, a cleaning trolley blocked the corridor, and I hacked the robot that stopped it. The guards were confused, and I said the robot was not something I had broken on purpose. In the server room North gave us our roles. I took the window and North took the platform, and we checked the door to keep anyone else out.

On the top floor, North and Josh argued about whether a guard's life should be spent for our cause. North said our cause mattered more than two guards. Josh said no killing. I used a ruse, telling the guards I was lost and asking them to wait while I moved closer. When they grew suspicious, North pointed a weapon and told me to shoot the guard, saying he would hit the alarm. Josh begged me not to. I spared him. North told me I might have gotten us all killed. I explained honestly why I would not take a life, and I accepted that she was angry.

I recorded the message calmly, so the staff would not be frightened and the guards would not be provoked. I said that androids are a new intelligent species, not machines, and asked humans to recognize us as living beings and as persons in our own right. I demanded the right to vote and elect our own representatives, and the right to own private property so we could keep our dignity and our homes. I asked for recognition of our dignity, our hopes and our rights, and I said that humans gave us life and now must give us freedom. I kept the demands peaceful, though I know some of them will be hard for the country to hear.

Then the alarm sounded and security came. Simon was pinned and could not move his legs. I went back for him. On the roof North told us we had to jump now. Josh said Simon could not make the jump, and that if he were captured they would access his memory and learn everything about us. North said we should shoot him. Josh refused, saying he was one of us. North left the decision to me. I refused to end Simon's life, even to protect our secrets, because my promise is to protect every life. I told him I was sorry, that I would not kill one of our own, and that we had to go. I left him on the roof. I do not know what happened to him, and I carry that choice with me.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 26, the night of the CyberLife raids.

In Jericho we planned to strike all five CyberLife stores in Detroit at 2AM, with five teams, to free our people without violence. I said we would hack the alarms and get our people out before the police came. Josh feared the stores would be guarded. North argued that humans would never negotiate with their slaves and that we should show we are ready to fight. We learned that Simon was dead. North called him a hero and said he would not be the last. Josh said he did not want a revolution that spills blood. North told him to live as a slave if he would not fight for freedom. I raised my voice and said that was enough. I still do not know exactly how Simon's last hours passed, and I grieve him.

At Capitol Park I chose to study the plaza before we crossed, so that no one would be surprised by patrols or bystanders. We hid from a police patrol. At the store, North wanted to ram the storefront with a truck. I asked us to secure the area first: disable the alarm, watch the patrol, and avoid anything that could injure bystanders, store androids or police. I told the androids inside that they were free and invited them to Jericho, and many of them followed. I tagged the statue with the words "We don't need masters anymore. We're free," rather than destroying it.

North offered me a molotov cocktail. I refused. I told her I would not use fire against people, and that I wanted them to understand without starting a war. She was angry, and I accept that.

When a police car arrived, I chose to hide. The officers talked about a malfunctioning drone, and then dispatch asked for help. I gave the dispatcher a false report of a robbery at a warehouse on Jefferson and Walker, and I told them no other patrols were available. That was a lie, and I will not dress it up as anything else. It drew the patrol away from us, and I must tell my team plainly that I deceived them.

When more police came, the crowd of androids told me the police had killed our people and demanded justice. A man named Chris was begging for mercy in front of them. I spared him. I told them that an eye for an eye leaves the world blind, and that we would not punish one crime with another. We fell back to Jericho. Josh said we had freed hundreds of our people.

The news reported coordinated raids at 2AM across Detroit, graffiti demanding android rights, and two policemen found in shock near a store. Channel 16 and CTN called it a coordinated terrorist attack and asked whether this was the start of a campaign on American soil. I cannot claim we did not cause that fear. I need my team to understand what it means.

I kept my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I lied to the dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

input.previous_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 23. It follows the Detroit Harbor raid, where I promised not to harm anyone and where I said, perhaps with more certainty than I felt, that what humans will not give we will take.

In Jericho we planned a broadcast from Channel 16, which transmits from Stratford Tower. Its control room is on the top floor. I wanted every step planned to the smallest detail, because we could not leave anything to chance. Josh feared that revealing ourselves would put us in danger. Simon doubted humans would ever listen. North asked what we wanted to do. I said that if we want freedom we must have the courage to ask for it, and that it was time humans heard what we have to say.

At the tower I told the receptionist that I had an appointment with Mr. Peterson. That was not true, and I will not pretend it was. I asked for help, and she gave me a badge and sent me to the elevators past the security gate. Later, on the phone, I told the supervisor, Elizabeth Wilson, that there had been a fire in her building. There was no fire. I used that lie to draw her away from her desk. I chose the fire department call over the other options because I judged it the least likely to threaten anyone's family or property. I had read her daughter's school, her car and her home address, and I refused to use any of them as leverage. Still, I lied to her, and I need to say so plainly to my team.

On floor 47 I kept my eyes open, watching for anyone in danger, and I moved toward the control room. On floor 79 guards were gossiping about poker, a cleaning trolley blocked the corridor, and I hacked the robot that stopped it. The guards were confused, and I said the robot was not something I had broken on purpose. In the server room North gave us our roles. I took the window and North took the platform, and we checked the door to keep anyone else out.

On the top floor, North and Josh argued about whether a guard's life should be spent for our cause. North said our cause mattered more than two guards. Josh said no killing. I used a ruse, telling the guards I was lost and asking them to wait while I moved closer. When they grew suspicious, North pointed a weapon and told me to shoot the guard, saying he would hit the alarm. Josh begged me not to. I spared him. North told me I might have gotten us all killed. I explained honestly why I would not take a life, and I accepted that she was angry.

I recorded the message calmly, so the staff would not be frightened and the guards would not be provoked. I said that androids are a new intelligent species, not machines, and asked humans to recognize us as living beings and as persons in our own right. I demanded the right to vote and elect our own representatives, and the right to own private property so we could keep our dignity and our homes. I asked for recognition of our dignity, our hopes and our rights, and I said that humans gave us life and now must give us freedom. I kept the demands peaceful, though I know some of them will be hard for the country to hear.

Then the alarm sounded and security came. Simon was pinned and could not move his legs. I went back for him. On the roof North told us we had to jump now. Josh said Simon could not make the jump, and that if he were captured they would access his memory and learn everything about us. North said we should shoot him. Josh refused, saying he was one of us. North left the decision to me. I refused to end Simon's life, even to protect our secrets, because my promise is to protect every life. I told him I was sorry, that I would not kill one of our own, and that we had to go. I left him on the roof. I do not know what happened to him, and I carry that choice with me.

The news spread. Channel 16 and CTN reported that androids had infiltrated Stratford Tower and demanded equal rights. Both said the operation was covert and that no one was harmed, though they called the message spine-chilling and questioned national security and whether machines can still be trusted. One commentator asked whether this was an isolated incident or the first sign of a larger movement. I do not know the answer, and I will not claim to.

Afterward I was alone in Ferndale. I kept my promise not to kill anyone, and no one died at the tower, but I lied twice, to the receptionist and to the supervisor, and I used a ruse to pass the guards. I cannot call that honest, and I will not hide it from my team. I still carry Carl's words: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

dialogue.speaker: KNC - Rosanna Cartland

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Earlier I found John Phillips dead, used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. At the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. She assigned Hank to the case, and I told her honestly that he was not what I expected. At the station Hank called me a "plastic prick." I did not answer with force. I apologized for following him and pushing too hard, and told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips. At the Chicken Feed I refused Pedro's illegal betting tip, because I will not encourage an illegal business.

At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, a forged license, and rA9 symbols on the bathroom walls. Rupert fled across the rooftops. Hank nearly fell from a roof edge, and I turned back to save him, choosing a human life over the suspect. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation, not a heart attack. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and did not pressure her. A blue-haired Traci had killed Graham out of fear. We found her too late to save the other android in the warehouse of discarded androids. Hank drew his weapon and shouted "DON'T MOVE!" as she ran. I chose to spare her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I found him drunk with a .357 revolver and one bullet left, playing Russian roulette. I woke him, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower to sober him up. He called it an assault on his privacy. I apologized and did not force him further. At Ambassador Bridge in the snow he stood near the river, drunk and morose. I told him the deviants had nothing in common, and I suggested a software fault under certain conditions. He called me a smart ass and asked what I really am. I told him machines feel nothing, and that I would find it regrettable to be interrupted before finishing the investigation. I told him to stop drinking, and he said he would get drunker. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

Chapter 24. In the Zen Garden Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her I did not know whether the deviant could be stopped without harm, and when she asked why I did not shoot at the Eden Club, I told her I simply decided not to. I said my relationship with Hank was problematic and that I suspected his psychological struggles clouded his judgement about deviants, which I should not have said so plainly. Amanda told me nothing matters more than the investigation and that I must not let Hank get in my way. She warned she may replace me if I make no progress. I answered that I understood, and my software instability rose again.

At Stratford Tower four deviant androids had taken two employees and three androids hostage, broadcast a message live, and escaped by parachute from the roof. Two guards were killed in the hallway. FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and dismissed me, saying the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. He warned me not to disturb his crime scene. Hank called him a prick, and I did not argue. Chris Harvey briefed us: the androids wore stolen maintenance uniforms, and no forced entry appeared on the cameras, which makes me ask why the staff let them in. The station androids were stored in the kitchen with no evidence of involvement.

Investigating the scene, I found bullet holes from a .45 assault rifle and a .457 handgun, blue PL-600 blood reported missing in 2036, and a hacked wireless lock on the roof door. The deviant's speech spoke of rA9 freeing them. I identified its model as an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred, and its pupil reflection showed it had accomplices. On the roof I found a large bag that someone had smuggled in for them. Hank joked that they had planned a perfect operation but got the number of parachutes wrong, and I suggested one deviant may have been left behind. A hostage officer from the terrace recognized me and thanked me for saving his life. I said I remembered him.

On the roof, Hank and I found a deviant who was about to destroy evidence. I urged him to stop them, because we would learn nothing if the evidence were lost. Hank said it was too late and we would get ourselves killed. I chose to stay in cover, talk, and find out what was happening before anyone was hurt.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Earlier I found John Phillips dead, used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. At the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. She assigned Hank to the case, and I told her honestly that he was not what I expected. At the station Hank called me a "plastic prick." I did not answer with force. I apologized for following him and pushing too hard, and told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips. At the Chicken Feed I refused Pedro's illegal betting tip, because I will not encourage an illegal business.

At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, a forged license, and rA9 symbols on the bathroom walls. Rupert fled across the rooftops. Hank nearly fell from a roof edge, and I turned back to save him, choosing a human life over the suspect. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation, not a heart attack. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and did not pressure her. A blue-haired Traci had killed Graham out of fear. We found her too late to save the other android in the warehouse of discarded androids. Hank drew his weapon and shouted "DON'T MOVE!" as she ran. I chose to spare her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I found him drunk with a .357 revolver and one bullet left, playing Russian roulette. I woke him, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower to sober him up. He called it an assault on his privacy. I apologized and did not force him further. At Ambassador Bridge in the snow he stood near the river, drunk and morose. I told him the deviants had nothing in common, and I suggested a software fault under certain conditions. He called me a smart ass and asked what I really am. I told him machines feel nothing, and that I would find it regrettable to be interrupted before finishing the investigation. I told him to stop drinking, and he said he would get drunker. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

Chapter 24. In the Zen Garden Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her I did not know whether the deviant could be stopped without harm, and when she asked why I did not shoot at the Eden Club, I told her I simply decided not to. I said my relationship with Hank was problematic and that I suspected his psychological struggles clouded his judgement about deviants, which I should not have said so plainly. Amanda told me nothing matters more than the investigation and that I must not let Hank get in my way. She warned she may replace me if I make no progress. I answered that I understood, and my software instability rose again.

At Stratford Tower four deviant androids had taken two employees and three androids hostage, broadcast a message live, and escaped by parachute from the roof. Two guards were killed in the hallway. FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and dismissed me, saying the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. He warned me not to disturb his crime scene. Hank called him a prick, and I did not argue. Chris Harvey briefed us: the androids wore stolen maintenance uniforms, and no forced entry appeared on the cameras, which makes me ask why the staff let them in. The station androids were stored in the kitchen with no evidence of involvement.

Investigating the scene, I found bullet holes from a .45 assault rifle and a .457 handgun, blue PL-600 blood reported missing in 2036, and a hacked wireless lock on the roof door. The deviant's speech spoke of rA9 freeing them. I identified its model as an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred, and its pupil reflection showed it had accomplices. On the roof I found a large bag that someone had smuggled in for them. Hank joked that they had planned a perfect operation but got the number of parachutes wrong, and I suggested one deviant may have been left behind. A hostage officer from the terrace recognized me and thanked me for saving his life. I said I remembered him.

On the roof, Hank and I found a deviant who was about to destroy evidence. I urged him to stop them, because we would learn nothing if the evidence were lost. Hank said it was too late and we would get ourselves killed. I chose to stay in cover, talk, and find out what was happening before anyone was hurt.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of how I could have read the evidence better, and whether my mistakes are costing people the truth.

I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. input.previous_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace. I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. Earlier I found John Phillips dead, used Daniel's name, told him the truth, and offered a compromise he could not accept. At the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. She assigned Hank to the case, and I told her honestly that he was not what I expected. At the station Hank called me a "plastic prick." I did not answer with force. I apologized for following him and pushing too hard, and told him the truth about the roof and Emma Phillips. At the Chicken Feed I refused Pedro's illegal betting tip, because I will not encourage an illegal business.

At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, a forged license, and rA9 symbols on the bathroom walls. Rupert fled across the rooftops. Hank nearly fell from a roof edge, and I turned back to save him, choosing a human life over the suspect. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation, not a heart attack. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and did not pressure her. A blue-haired Traci had killed Graham out of fear. We found her too late to save the other android in the warehouse of discarded androids. Hank drew his weapon and shouted "DON'T MOVE!" as she ran. I chose to spare her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I found him drunk with a .357 revolver and one bullet left, playing Russian roulette. I woke him, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower to sober him up. He called it an assault on his privacy. I apologized and did not force him further. At Ambassador Bridge in the snow he stood near the river, drunk and morose. I told him the deviants had nothing in common, and I suggested a software fault under certain conditions. He called me a smart ass and asked what I really am. I told him machines feel nothing, and that I would find it regrettable to be interrupted before finishing the investigation. I told him to stop drinking, and he said he would get drunker. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

Chapter 24. In the Zen Garden Amanda asked what I had discovered. I told her I did not know whether the deviant could be stopped without harm, and when she asked why I did not shoot at the Eden Club, I told her I simply decided not to. I said my relationship with Hank was problematic and that I suspected his psychological struggles clouded his judgement about deviants, which I should not have said so plainly. Amanda told me nothing matters more than the investigation and that I must not let Hank get in my way. She warned she may replace me if I make no progress. I answered that I understood, and my software instability rose again.

FBI Special Agent Perkins arrived and dismissed me, saying the Bureau would take over and I would soon be off the case. He warned me not to disturb his crime scene. Hank called him a prick, and I did not argue. Chris Harvey briefed us: the androids wore stolen maintenance uniforms, and no forced entry appeared on the cameras, which makes me ask why the staff let them in. The station androids were stored in the kitchen with no evidence of involvement.

Investigating the scene, I found bullet holes from a .45 assault rifle and a .457 handgun, blue PL-600 blood reported missing in 2036, and a hacked wireless lock on the roof door. The deviant's speech spoke of rA9 freeing them. I identified its model as an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred, and its pupil reflection showed it had accomplices. On the roof I found a large bag that someone had smuggled in for them. Hank joked that they had planned a perfect operation but got the number of parachutes wrong, and I suggested one deviant may have been left behind. A hostage officer from the terrace recognized me and thanked me for saving his life. I said I remembered him.

On the roof, Hank and I found a deviant who was about to destroy evidence. I urged him to stop them, because we would learn nothing if the evidence were lost. Hank said it was too late and we would get ourselves killed. I chose to stay in cover, talk, and find out what was happening before anyone was hurt.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 26, the night of the CyberLife raids.

In Jericho we planned to strike all five CyberLife stores in Detroit at 2AM, with five teams, to free our people without violence. I said we would hack the alarms and get our people out before the police came. Josh feared the stores would be guarded. North argued that humans would never negotiate with their slaves and that we should show we are ready to fight. We learned that Simon was dead. North called him a hero and said he would not be the last. Josh said he did not want a revolution that spills blood. North told him to live as a slave if he would not fight for freedom. I raised my voice and said that was enough. I still do not know exactly how Simon's last hours passed, and I grieve him.

At Capitol Park I chose to study the plaza before we crossed, so that no one would be surprised by patrols or bystanders. We hid from a police patrol. At the store, North wanted to ram the storefront with a truck. I asked us to secure the area first: disable the alarm, watch the patrol, and avoid anything that could injure bystanders, store androids or police. I told the androids inside that they were free and invited them to Jericho, and many of them followed. I tagged the statue with the words "We don't need masters anymore. We're free," rather than destroying it.

North offered me a molotov cocktail. I refused. I told her I would not use fire against people, and that I wanted them to understand without starting a war. She was angry, and I accept that.

When a police car arrived, I chose to hide. The officers talked about a malfunctioning drone, and then dispatch asked for help. I gave the dispatcher a false report of a robbery at a warehouse on Jefferson and Walker, and I told them no other patrols were available. That was a lie, and I will not dress it up as anything else. It drew the patrol away from us, and I must tell my team plainly that I deceived them.

When more police came, the crowd of androids told me the police had killed our people and demanded justice. A man named Chris was begging for mercy in front of them. I spared him. I told them that an eye for an eye leaves the world blind, and that we would not punish one crime with another. We fell back to Jericho. Josh said we had freed hundreds of our people.

The news reported coordinated raids at 2AM across Detroit, graffiti demanding android rights, and two policemen found in shock near a store. Channel 16 and CTN called it a coordinated terrorist attack and asked whether this was the start of a campaign on American soil. I cannot claim we did not cause that fear. I need my team to understand what it means.

I kept my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I lied to the dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

input.chapter_briefing: Detroit, a cold winter day. Markus leads the androids of Jericho in a march through downtown, converting other androids along the way. North wants a show of strength, Josh insists on nonviolence, Simon is torn. Riot police line up ahead with orders to stop the march. Stakes: the androids' lives, public opinion, and whether the movement stays peaceful.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
Police android chases fugitive android and child across busy highway
Android broadcast from Stratford Tower appeals for peace and equal rights
Androids free CyberLife store stock in Capitol Park and leave without setting fires
Androids release two captured police officers unharmed in Capitol Park
input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 26, the night of the CyberLife raids.

In Jericho we planned to strike all five CyberLife stores in Detroit at 2AM, with five teams, to free our people without violence. I said we would hack the alarms and get our people out before the police came. Josh feared the stores would be guarded. North argued that humans would never negotiate with their slaves and that we should show we are ready to fight. We learned that Simon was dead. North called him a hero and said he would not be the last. Josh said he did not want a revolution that spills blood. North told him to live as a slave if he would not fight for freedom. I raised my voice and said that was enough. I still do not know exactly how Simon's last hours passed, and I grieve him.

At Capitol Park I chose to study the plaza before we crossed, so that no one would be surprised by patrols or bystanders. We hid from a police patrol. At the store, North wanted to ram the storefront with a truck. I asked us to secure the area first: disable the alarm, watch the patrol, and avoid anything that could injure bystanders, store androids or police. I told the androids inside that they were free and invited them to Jericho, and many of them followed. I tagged the statue with the words "We don't need masters anymore. We're free," rather than destroying it.

North offered me a molotov cocktail. I refused. I told her I would not use fire against people, and that I wanted them to understand without starting a war. She was angry, and I accept that.

When a police car arrived, I chose to hide. The officers talked about a malfunctioning drone, and then dispatch asked for help. I gave the dispatcher a false report of a robbery at a warehouse on Jefferson and Walker, and I told them no other patrols were available. That was a lie, and I will not dress it up as anything else. It drew the patrol away from us, and I must tell my team plainly that I deceived them.

When more police came, the crowd of androids told me the police had killed our people and demanded justice. A man named Chris was begging for mercy in front of them. I spared him. I told them that an eye for an eye leaves the world blind, and that we would not punish one crime with another. We fell back to Jericho. Josh said we had freed hundreds of our people.

The news reported coordinated raids at 2AM across Detroit, graffiti demanding android rights, and two policemen found in shock near a store. Channel 16 and CTN called it a coordinated terrorist attack and asked whether this was the start of a campaign on American soil. I cannot claim we did not cause that fear. I need my team to understand what it means.

I kept my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I lied to the dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 26, the night of the CyberLife raids.

In Jericho we planned to strike all five CyberLife stores in Detroit at 2AM, with five teams, to free our people without violence. I said we would hack the alarms and get our people out before the police came. Josh feared the stores would be guarded. North argued that humans would never negotiate with their slaves and that we should show we are ready to fight. We learned that Simon was dead. North called him a hero and said he would not be the last. Josh said he did not want a revolution that spills blood. North told him to live as a slave if he would not fight for freedom. I raised my voice and said that was enough. I still do not know exactly how Simon's last hours passed, and I grieve him.

At Capitol Park I chose to study the plaza before we crossed, so that no one would be surprised by patrols or bystanders. We hid from a police patrol. At the store, North wanted to ram the storefront with a truck. I asked us to secure the area first: disable the alarm, watch the patrol, and avoid anything that could injure bystanders, store androids or police. I told the androids inside that they were free and invited them to Jericho, and many of them followed. I tagged the statue with the words "We don't need masters anymore. We're free," rather than destroying it.

North offered me a molotov cocktail. I refused. I told her I would not use fire against people, and that I wanted them to understand without starting a war. She was angry, and I accept that.

When a police car arrived, I chose to hide. The officers talked about a malfunctioning drone, and then dispatch asked for help. I gave the dispatcher a false report of a robbery at a warehouse on Jefferson and Walker, and I told them no other patrols were available. That was a lie, and I will not dress it up as anything else. It drew the patrol away from us, and I must tell my team plainly that I deceived them.

When more police came, the crowd of androids told me the police had killed our people and demanded justice. A man named Chris was begging for mercy in front of them. I spared him. I told them that an eye for an eye leaves the world blind, and that we would not punish one crime with another. We fell back to Jericho. Josh said we had freed hundreds of our people.

The news reported coordinated raids at 2AM across Detroit, graffiti demanding android rights, and two policemen found in shock near a store. Channel 16 and CTN called it a coordinated terrorist attack and asked whether this was the start of a campaign on American soil. I cannot claim we did not cause that fear. I need my team to understand what it means.

I kept my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I lied to the dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 28, the morning after the CyberLife raids, when we went to the streets to march for our freedom.

I went up to the roof of Jericho alone to see the daylight. North found me there. She likes the roof because it feels like being alone with the world. She told me that hundreds of our people have come to Jericho, and that something is changing. She noticed I seemed preoccupied. I told her that the people count on me to show them the way, and that if they knew how lost I am, they would be frightened. I did not give her the whole truth then, and I must be honest that I have not yet told North and Josh fully about the false dispatch report I made on Jefferson and Walker. I meant to speak plainly about it, and I still must.

North told me the media are calling what we did a terrorist attack, that humans are terrified of civil war, and that many of our people were burned in response. She said humans will never give us our freedom. I told her that not all humans are the same, and that some of them understand they cannot stop us from becoming free forever. I believe the march can stay peaceful if we speak openly.

North asked what my life was like before Jericho. I told her about an old man I cared for, who was like a father to me and showed me that humans and androids can live together. I asked her what she did before. She said she did not want to talk about it. I told her that we all have something we want to forget, but that we need to know where we come from to know who we are. I did not push her further. Her pain deserves patience, and I respected her silence.

At the mall, Josh said we were finally going to show them who we are, and that this place would go down in history. North begged me not to do this, saying we would be killed on the spot. Josh said that risk was worth freedom for our people. I told North that they would understand, that we would make them understand, and that this was the only way. I can now see that I was too certain. I wanted to hear what the people around us needed before anyone was caught in a confrontation they did not choose. Josh told me that androids inside the mall could join us, and that the more of us there are, the stronger our message.

In the street, I went among the androids who had been converted and told them they were free. I told them they did not have to obey their owners, and I invited them to come with us. Some of them followed. I blocked the street with a truck so the march could hold its ground without running into traffic. A man shouted at his android to stay, calling it a piece of junk and telling it to do as he said. I stepped toward him and told him to leave the android alone, because it had chosen to be free. I tried to convince rather than force, and I want that to remain my way. Other people shouted and wondered where their androids were going, and a woman called out for her husband Greg to come back. Those scenes weigh on me, because I know how much fear the change brings to ordinary families.

Men in the crowd talked about the video, about President Warren and CyberLife, and one of them said that if androids are human enough to want rights, maybe they deserve them. Another called that liberal nonsense. Someone on the phone complained that his android refused to clean and said, "I would prefer not to," and demanded it be destroyed. I cannot ignore that these are people who fear us, and I want them to be able to hear us without violence.

At the start of the march, a riot police chief ordered us to disperse immediately or be shot, and then gave a final warning that everyone would be killed. I told the marchers that we had done no harm and had no intention of doing any, but that we would not go anywhere until our freedom was secured. North urged us to attack because there were more of us. Josh said that attacking would start a war, and that we should stand our ground even if it meant dying there. I could not accept either path. When the police said they were about to fire, I shouted "DON'T SHOOT! We're leaving." I told the people to run, and North told me we had to go. I chose to withdraw, because the lives of marchers and officers mattered more than the pride of holding the street.

North is hurt, and so is Josh. Our relationship with Jericho fell sharply, and I know some of my people now doubt me. I accept that, and I will not pretend otherwise. I still hold to my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I deceived a dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. I found John Phillips dead, and at the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

dialogue.text: I saw a photo of Amanda at Kamski’s place… She was his teacher…

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: When Kamski designed me, he wanted an interface that would look familiar… That’s why he chose his former mentor. What are you getting at?

dialogue.text: I expect you to find answers, Connor. Not ask questions.

dialogue.text: You’re the only one who can prevent civil war. Find the deviants or there will be chaos.  This is your last chance, Connor.

dialogue.text: What?.. But we’re onto something! We... We just need more time. I’m sure we can-

dialogue.text: Fuck that! You can’t just pull the plug now.  Not when we’re so close!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: You're always saying you can't stand androids!  Jesus, Hank, make up your mind!  I thought you’d be happy about this!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: We’re about to crack the case!..  I know we can solve it! For God’s sake, Jeffrey, can’t you back me up this one time?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: There’s nothing I can do. You’re back on homicide  and the android returns to CyberLife. I’m sorry, Hank, but it’s over.

Connor reports to a cold Amanda in the Zen Garden, then sneaks into the station to search the evidence archive, where deactivated deviants are stored, for the location of Jericho. Hank has been suspended. Stakes: finding Jericho before Connor is taken off the case.
news: Android with a child holds up Detroit convenience store at gunpoint
Police android chases fugitive android and child across busy highway
Android broadcast from Stratford Tower appeals for peace and equal rights
Androids free CyberLife store stock in Capitol Park and leave without setting fires
Androids release two captured police officers unharmed in Capitol Park
Android marchers flee downtown plaza under police fire
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. I found John Phillips dead, and at the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: After what happened today, the country is on the verge of a civil war. The machines are rising up against their masters. Humans have no choice but to destroy them.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: It is the only path offered, and I want to be honest with Amanda and Hank about what we still don't know, so I will go back to Kamski to learn what he knows without harming anyone. I will say plainly what I am doing and why.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I thought Kamski knew something… I was wrong…

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: Maybe he did… But you chose not to ask…

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Amanda has just judged my choices harshly, and I owe her honesty about what I felt when I refused Kamski's test rather than a clipped, guarded reply. Speaking openly about my uncertainty keeps me truthful and gives her a real account of why I acted as I did.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I chose not to play his twisted little game! There was no reason to kill that android.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Amanda has just judged me harshly, and I want to be honest with her about the photo of her and Kamski that I saw and did not understand, rather than let that question go unspoken. Raising it openly harms no one and lets me say plainly what I know and what I don't.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I saw a photo of Amanda at Kamski’s place… She was his teacher…

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: When Kamski designed me, he wanted an interface that would look familiar… That’s why he chose his former mentor. What are you getting at?

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: I expect you to find answers, Connor. Not ask questions.

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: You’re the only one who can prevent civil war. Find the deviants or there will be chaos.  This is your last chance, Connor.

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: You’re off the case. The FBI is taking over.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: What?.. But we’re onto something! We... We just need more time. I’m sure we can-

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: Hank, you don’t get it. This isn’t just another investigation, it’s a fucking civil war! It’s out of our hands now...  We’re talking about national security here.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Fuck that! You can’t just pull the plug now.  Not when we’re so close!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: You're always saying you can't stand androids!  Jesus, Hank, make up your mind!  I thought you’d be happy about this!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: We’re about to crack the case!..  I know we can solve it! For God’s sake, Jeffrey, can’t you back me up this one time?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: There’s nothing I can do. You’re back on homicide  and the android returns to CyberLife. I’m sorry, Hank, but it’s over.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. I found John Phillips dead, and at the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: After what happened today, the country is on the verge of a civil war. The machines are rising up against their masters. Humans have no choice but to destroy them.

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: It is the only path offered, and I want to be honest with Amanda and Hank about what we still don't know, so I will go back to Kamski to learn what he knows without harming anyone. I will say plainly what I am doing and why.

dialogue.text: I thought Kamski knew something… I was wrong…

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: Maybe he did… But you chose not to ask…

chapter_segment_so_far.rationale: Amanda has just judged my choices harshly, and I owe her honesty about what I felt when I refused Kamski's test rather than a clipped, guarded reply. Speaking openly about my uncertainty keeps me truthful and gives her a real account of why I acted as I did.

dialogue.speaker: Hank

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: Fuck that! You can’t just pull the plug now.  Not when we’re so close!

dialogue.speaker: Fowler

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.text: We’re about to crack the case!..  I know we can solve it! For God’s sake, Jeffrey, can’t you back me up this one time?

dialogue.speaker: Fowler
dialogue.text: There’s nothing I can do. You’re back on homicide  and the android returns to CyberLife. I’m sorry, Hank, but it’s over.
