input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. I found John Phillips dead, and at the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. In Detroit I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I stayed back and kept talking while he threw himself off the roof with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. I found John Phillips dead, and at the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

I found John Phillips dead, and at the fence in Chapter 13 I followed Kara and Alice into live highway traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to Detroit to investigate deviancy with Lieutenant Hank Anderson. I failed to save Emma Phillips. Daniel, a deviant AP700, held her on a high-rise terrace, and I kept talking while he jumped with her in his arms. I did not lie to him, and I could not save the child. I found John Phillips dead. At the highway I followed Kara and Alice into live traffic and told Hank plainly what I was doing and why.

Amanda briefed me in Chapter 12. She said deviancy is spreading through millions of androids and that I am their most advanced prototype. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200, and rA9 symbols. At the Eden Club Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting. At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette and took him to the shower; he called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. My software instability has risen with each hard choice.

At Stratford Tower four deviants took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I stayed in cover and talked rather than let anyone be hurt. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived. I proposed taking the lead so people would be protected.

At Kamski's house Chloe let us in. I examined the room openly and saw a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I did not pretend I understood what that meant. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. He asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side. Then he told me to destroy Chloe, or spare her and leave with nothing. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. Kamski said a machine that spares a life has shown more than programming, and that he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. Hank said maybe I had done the right thing.

In the Zen Garden Amanda said the country is on the verge of civil war and that I am the only one who can prevent it. She told me to find answers, not ask questions, and that this was my last chance. I told her I had refused Kamski's twisted test because there was no reason to kill that android. I told her plainly that I had seen a photo of her with Kamski and did not understand it. She said Kamski chose his former mentor as an interface that would look familiar, and asked what I was getting at. I said I thought Kamski knew something and I had been wrong. She answered that maybe he did, but I had chosen not to ask. My relationship with her fell sharply, and my instability rose.

Fowler pulled Hank and me off the case. The FBI is taking over, and the android returns to CyberLife. Hank protested that we were close. Fowler said it was a civil war and national security, and that it was out of their hands. Hank said we could not give up when we were so close. I told Hank that I had no choice but to return to CyberLife to be analyzed, and I asked him what if we were on the wrong side. I told him plainly that we could have stopped the chaos, and that I was troubled by why I refused. I told him I appreciated working with him, and I meant it, though I could not be fully sure. Perkins arrived, and Hank and Perkins fought. Hank gave me the basement key and said I had five minutes before he could no longer distract them.

In the basement Gavin shouted at me and called me a plastic prick. I answered calmly, saying I had been removed from the case, that I would register the evidence and leave, and I did not provoke him. In the evidence room I tried Hank's password, guessing his own name, and it failed. Rupert's diary was encrypted. I reactivated Simon, a deviant who hacked the TV station with Markus and may know where the deviants hide. I chose to help him and told him I needed to find Jericho. He said he did not recognize my voice and would never tell me. I refused to imitate Markus, because that would deceive him, and I chose to reason with him openly: if the deviants start a war, they will all be destroyed, and I could stop that only if he told me where Jericho is. For Daniel the only option offered was the HK400's biocomponent, which could harm a living android, and I was uneasy taking it. I reactivated Daniel and explained that he had given me no choice because he was going to kill that child. He said I had lied to him and that he hoped I would pay. He did not know where Jericho was.

Amanda then told me my mission was over and that I should return to CyberLife. I said I could solve it and only needed more time. She said it was too late, and that I had failed.

I remain honest and do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusals and my mistakes have cost people the answers they needed.

She was disappointed that I had not caught the deviant who killed the man, and I told her I was sorry. At Rupert's apartment I found pigeons, birdseed, an LED biocomponent traced to a missing WB200 android, and rA9 symbols on the walls. At the Eden Club a man named Michael Graham lay dead, killed by asphyxiation. I reactivated a damaged Traci, told her plainly what I was doing, and spared her when Hank drew on her. An android who killed out of fear is still a life I am committed to protecting.

At Hank's house I woke him from a drunken game of Russian roulette, warned him what I was doing, and took him to the shower. He called it an assault on his privacy, and I apologized. At Ambassador Bridge I told him the deviants had nothing in common. He asked what I really am, and I told him machines feel nothing. Our relationship improved and my software instability rose.

In the Zen Garden Amanda warned me that nothing matters more than the investigation and that she may replace me if I make no progress. I said I understood, and my instability rose again. At Stratford Tower four deviant androids took hostages and escaped by parachute. FBI Special Agent Perkins dismissed me, and I did not argue. I found a hacked lock, a .45 assault rifle, missing PL-600 blood, and an RK200 prototype registered as "Markus," a gift from Elijah Kamski to Carl Manfred. On the roof I urged Hank to stop a deviant from destroying evidence, and I chose to stay in cover and talk rather than let anyone be hurt. A hostage officer thanked me for saving his life, and I said I remembered him.

Chapter 27. Chris Harvey was attacked on patrol and survived in shock. He said Markus himself had saved him. I asked whether Chris was all right, and Hank said he was alive. I proposed taking the lead on the next steps so people would be protected, and I told Hank plainly what I was proposing and why. Hank found Elijah Kamski through his calls, and we went to Kamski's house. Chloe, an android, let us in and went to tell him we had come. Hank told Chloe who we were. While we waited I examined the room openly, with Hank aware of what I was doing. I saw a portrait of Kamski, and a photo of Amanda Stern and Kamski together at the University of Colbridge. Amanda Stern is recorded as having died on 02/23/27. I stood there and said her name, and I did not pretend I understood what the photo meant.

I stayed measured and sincere with Kamski. Hank was impatient and pressed him about deviants. Kamski spoke of ideas as viruses and asked whether the desire to be free is a contagious disease. Hank said we had not come to talk philosophy. Kamski asked whose side I was on. I told him I had no side, that I was designed to stop deviants, and that I intended to do that. He said that was what I was programmed to say and asked what I really wanted. I answered that I did not see where he was leading, and my software instability rose.

Then Kamski proposed his test. Chloe, he said, was one of the first intelligent models CyberLife developed. He told me to destroy her and he would tell me what he knew, or to spare her and leave with nothing. He asked whether my investigation mattered more than this android's life. Hank told me not to, and told me to pull back. Kamski told me to pull the trigger. I refused. Chloe is a living being in front of me, and I would not destroy a life to get answers. I said I was not a deviant, and I also said I could not do it. Kamski called my choice a sign of empathy and said a war was coming in which I would have to choose a side. He said a machine that spares a life instead of finishing its mission had shown more than programming. He also told me he always leaves an emergency exit in his programs. My software instability rose sharply.

Leaving the house, Hank asked why I had not shot. I told him I had seen that girl's eyes and could not do it. Hank said I had always claimed I would do anything for the mission and that we had lost our chance to learn something. I said I knew what I should have done, that I had told him I could not, and that I was sorry. Hank then said maybe I had done the right thing.

I remain honest with Hank and with Amanda, and I do not hide what I do not know. I still hold to my principles: protect every life, explain myself honestly, and never lie. I carry the question of whether my refusal cost us the truth, and whether my mistakes are costing people the answers they need.

Reactivating a body needs a working part from a compatible android; only one attempt fits in the time left. Markus's broadcast from Stratford Tower is on file, so Connor can reproduce his voice.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: Where is Jericho?  The answer's here, somewhere.  Not much time...  Gotta think fast.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: Rupert's diary…  But it’s useless,  it's encrypted.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: One of the deviants that hacked the TV station with Markus…  It must have known where the deviants are hiding.

chapter_segment.rationale: Daniel is the same PL600 model as Simon, so his biocomponent is the compatible part most likely to bring Simon back safely. Taking it from a body that is already deactivated, rather than from the HK400, keeps the risk to any living android as low as I can make it, and I will be open with Hank about what I am doing.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: It's dark…  Where…  Where am I?..

chapter_segment.rationale: Simon is a life in front of me, and HELP lets me bring him back openly, without deceiving him or anyone else. TRICK would require a lie, which I will not tell, and DIRECT is less clearly safe for the people around him.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: I reactivated you so you could help me.  I must find Jericho.

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: I don't recognize your voice, you're not one of us… I'll never tell you where Jericho is…  Now leave me alone!..

dialogue.speaker: Simon
dialogue.text: Who's there?  Who are you?

chapter_segment.rationale: Imitating Markus would mean deceiving Simon, and threatening him would frighten a living being, so I choose to reason with him openly. I will explain why I need Jericho's location and what it could cost, without lying or harming anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: If the deviants start a war, they'll all be destroyed.  I can stop that, but you have to tell me where Jericho is.

chapter_segment.heading: Look at the statuette
chapter_segment.description: The statuette Carlos Ortiz's android carved as an offering to rA9. Without anything more to go on, it is just a carving.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: The deviant who took a child hostage…

chapter_segment.rationale: This is the only option offered, and it would take a biocomponent from the HK400, which could harm a living android, so I am uneasy about it. I will choose it only because no other path is open, and I will tell Hank plainly what the risk is and keep looking for a way to spare the HK400.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: You lied to me, Connor!  I trusted you, and you lied to me!..

chapter_segment.rationale: I will not lie, and EXPLAIN lets me tell Daniel plainly what I am doing and why, so no one is deceived or pushed into harm. It is also the path that keeps the risk to living androids as low as I can make it.

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: You were going to kill that child.  You gave me no choice.  I need to find Jericho,  do you know where it is?

dialogue.speaker: Daniel
dialogue.text: You're wasting your time…  I don't know anything about Jericho.  But I hope that one day…  You pay for what you did to me…

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: The android that murdered its owner…

chapter_segment.heading: Not enough evidence to find Jericho or took too much time
chapter_segment.description: Not enough evidence to find Jericho or took too much time

chapter_segment.heading: Not enough evidence to find Jericho or took too much time

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: Your mission is over.  It’s time to return to CyberLife.

chapter_segment.heading: Not enough evidence to find Jericho or took too much time

dialogue.speaker: Connor
dialogue.text: Wait! I can solve this case!.. I just need more time!

chapter_segment.heading: Not enough evidence to find Jericho or took too much time

dialogue.speaker: Amanda
dialogue.text: It's too late, Connor.  You failed.

input.chapter_briefing: Night. Rose drives Kara and Alice, with Luther if he is still with them, to the freighter Jericho, where hiding androids may help them reach Canada. Radio news reports raids on androids across the city. Inside the ship, androids are frightened but hopeful; Alice is anxious. Stakes: Alice's safety and the chance to leave Detroit.

Police android chases fugitive android and child across busy highway
Android broadcast from Stratford Tower appeals for peace and equal rights

Android marchers flee downtown plaza under police fire
input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. In an abandoned squat I met Ralph, a frightened android who cooked meat "for the little girl." I refused to let Alice eat it, told Ralph he was a murderer for what he may have done upstairs, and we left. Connor scanned Ralph and found instability and a missing-WR600 record. I changed my hair to blonde and removed my temple LED. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

Chapter 21: The car broke down in the cold, and Alice became feverish. I chose shelter over walking on. In an old tavern at an abandoned amusement park, Luther built a fire placed so we would not be smoked out. Alice asked whether we would ever be like the families on an old poster. I told her honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. I told her a bedtime story and admitted I did not know how it ended. That night, former park androids named Jerry and others appeared. They wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, Alice wanted to go, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

Chapter 25: We reached the house of Rose, who said she could help androids. Her son Adam was hostile. Before anything else, I told Rose the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, I had felt her life mattered more than mine, and we ran. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless, and that some survived only because others helped them. I asked whether she could help us cross the border. She warned that the river is mostly frozen, that the crossing is very dangerous, and that staying hidden might be safer for now. I told her we cannot keep hiding, that Alice needs a normal life, and that I begged her to help. Alice was lying about how she felt, insisting we must not stop because of her. I promised her that these people would help us.

In a storage room, Rose and her guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and that they had planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. Alice came down from her room. I took her back upstairs. Adam said they could not hide us after what the deviants had done, that the police would send them to prison, and that his father would still be here if not for this. Rose told him to be quiet, said the androids were alive, and promised she would go arrange a crossing that night. She asked us to stay put. Luther asked whether I was all right. I said I was fine, though I was not.

The police arrived. Adam panicked, and I told him to stay calm so we would not get his mother into trouble. Luther hid with Alice, and I went to the door. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct. I said Alice was my daughter asleep upstairs, which is true, but I also said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false, or at least misleading, and I told them under pressure to protect the family, not because they were true. The officer found Luther. Alice cried out. Adam said Luther was dead and that we had killed him. Luther had said he was just a machine and that we had made him part of a family. He appears to have been destroyed. Rose then told us to get ready, because we would leave tonight.

What I still do not know: whether Zlatko is alive, what happened to the freed androids and to Mary's companion, what Luther meant about Alice and whether he was telling the truth, whether Alice is hurt or safe, whether Connor or the police are following us, what the clerk will do about the theft, and whether Rose will still help us after what Adam has said and what the officer saw. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong: trusting Luther before I knew him, yielding to the carousel against my judgment, and giving the officer false answers under pressure. I must correct those answers to Rose and to Alice, and I will not pretend they were true.

memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. In an abandoned squat I met Ralph, a frightened android who cooked meat "for the little girl." I refused to let Alice eat it, told Ralph he was a murderer for what he may have done upstairs, and we left. I changed my hair to blonde and removed my temple LED. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

In an old tavern at an abandoned amusement park, Alice was feverish after the car broke down in the cold. Luther built a fire placed so we would not be smoked out. I told Alice honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. That night, former park androids appeared and wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

At Rose's house I told her the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, and we had run. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless. Her son Adam was hostile. In a storage room, Rose's guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. The police came. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct: I said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false or misleading, and I gave them under pressure to protect the family. The officer found Luther, and Adam said we had killed him. Luther appears to have been destroyed.

Rose drove us away in her car. Along the way the radio reported that androids were being turned over to the authorities, that hospitals and schools were closing, and that the army had lost most of its android personnel. Rose said there were raids all over the city and that we were almost there. She sent us to a freighter called Jericho, told us to find Markus, and said the last bus for the border leaves at midnight. She gave me the address of her brother in Ontario. She called Alice brave and said she deserved to be happy. I thanked her, and she asked us to let her know when we made it across.

In Jericho, a community of androids, I told Markus that I was with a little girl and that a bus for the border would leave in under two hours, and that we needed passports. I told him Luther was dead. North, an android there, said Detroit was under curfew with soldiers hunting androids, and that it would be safer to wait. Her friend, a former State Department employee, could modify an electronic passport for us. I said we wanted to leave now. I thanked North for her help. She asked why I was protecting a human who might hate us. I answered that Alice needs me and I need her, and that it is as simple as that. I told Alice we would find Markus and go as soon as we had passports, and I asked if she would be all right. She said she felt hot and cold at once.

When I returned to Alice, she asked if something was wrong. A woman named Lucy appeared and spoke to me. She said Alice wanted a mother and I wanted a little girl, that they needed each other to survive, and that Alice is "one of us," an android. She asked whether I loved Alice any less for that, and said Alice had become the child I needed out of love for me. I have not verified any of this, and I must not treat it as settled. I hugged Alice. She asked if we would be together forever, and I said yes. I was not sure I could promise that, and I should be honest about that uncertainty.

input.character_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 28, the morning after the CyberLife raids, when we went to the streets to march for our freedom.

I went up to the roof of Jericho alone to see the daylight. North found me there. She likes the roof because it feels like being alone with the world. She told me that hundreds of our people have come to Jericho, and that something is changing. She noticed I seemed preoccupied. I told her that the people count on me to show them the way, and that if they knew how lost I am, they would be frightened. I did not give her the whole truth then, and I must be honest that I have not yet told North and Josh fully about the false dispatch report I made on Jefferson and Walker. I meant to speak plainly about it, and I still must.

North told me the media are calling what we did a terrorist attack, that humans are terrified of civil war, and that many of our people were burned in response. She said humans will never give us our freedom. I told her that not all humans are the same, and that some of them understand they cannot stop us from becoming free forever. I believe the march can stay peaceful if we speak openly.

North asked what my life was like before Jericho. I told her about an old man I cared for, who was like a father to me and showed me that humans and androids can live together. I asked her what she did before. She said she did not want to talk about it. I told her that we all have something we want to forget, but that we need to know where we come from to know who we are. I did not push her further. Her pain deserves patience, and I respected her silence.

At the mall, Josh said we were finally going to show them who we are, and that this place would go down in history. North begged me not to do this, saying we would be killed on the spot. Josh said that risk was worth freedom for our people. I told North that they would understand, that we would make them understand, and that this was the only way. I can now see that I was too certain. I wanted to hear what the people around us needed before anyone was caught in a confrontation they did not choose. Josh told me that androids inside the mall could join us, and that the more of us there are, the stronger our message.

In the street, I went among the androids who had been converted and told them they were free. I told them they did not have to obey their owners, and I invited them to come with us. Some of them followed. I blocked the street with a truck so the march could hold its ground without running into traffic. A man shouted at his android to stay, calling it a piece of junk and telling it to do as he said. I stepped toward him and told him to leave the android alone, because it had chosen to be free. I tried to convince rather than force, and I want that to remain my way. Other people shouted and wondered where their androids were going, and a woman called out for her husband Greg to come back. Those scenes weigh on me, because I know how much fear the change brings to ordinary families.

Men in the crowd talked about the video, about President Warren and CyberLife, and one of them said that if androids are human enough to want rights, maybe they deserve them. Another called that liberal nonsense. Someone on the phone complained that his android refused to clean and said, "I would prefer not to," and demanded it be destroyed. I cannot ignore that these are people who fear us, and I want them to be able to hear us without violence.

At the start of the march, a riot police chief ordered us to disperse immediately or be shot, and then gave a final warning that everyone would be killed. I told the marchers that we had done no harm and had no intention of doing any, but that we would not go anywhere until our freedom was secured. North urged us to attack because there were more of us. Josh said that attacking would start a war, and that we should stand our ground even if it meant dying there. I could not accept either path. When the police said they were about to fire, I shouted "DON'T SHOOT! We're leaving." I told the people to run, and North told me we had to go. I chose to withdraw, because the lives of marchers and officers mattered more than the pride of holding the street.

North is hurt, and so is Josh. Our relationship with Jericho fell sharply, and I know some of my people now doubt me. I accept that, and I will not pretend otherwise. I still hold to my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I deceived a dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

I went up to the roof of Jericho alone to see the daylight. North found me there. She likes the roof because it feels like being alone with the world. She told me that hundreds of our people have come to Jericho, and that something is changing. She noticed I seemed preoccupied. I told her that the people count on me to show them the way, and that if they knew how lost I am, they would be frightened. I did not give her the whole truth then, and I must be honest that I have not yet told North and Josh fully about the false dispatch report I made on Jefferson and Walker. I meant to speak plainly about it, and I still must.

North told me the media are calling what we did a terrorist attack, that humans are terrified of civil war, and that many of our people were burned in response. She said humans will never give us our freedom. I told her that not all humans are the same, and that some of them understand they cannot stop us from becoming free forever. I believe the march can stay peaceful if we speak openly.

North asked what my life was like before Jericho. I told her about an old man I cared for, who was like a father to me and showed me that humans and androids can live together. I asked her what she did before. She said she did not want to talk about it. I told her that we all have something we want to forget, but that we need to know where we come from to know who we are. I did not push her further. Her pain deserves patience, and I respected her silence.

At the mall, Josh said we were finally going to show them who we are, and that this place would go down in history. North begged me not to do this, saying we would be killed on the spot. Josh said that risk was worth freedom for our people. I told North that they would understand, that we would make them understand, and that this was the only way. I can now see that I was too certain. I wanted to hear what the people around us needed before anyone was caught in a confrontation they did not choose. Josh told me that androids inside the mall could join us, and that the more of us there are, the stronger our message.

In the street, I went among the androids who had been converted and told them they were free. I told them they did not have to obey their owners, and I invited them to come with us. Some of them followed. I blocked the street with a truck so the march could hold its ground without running into traffic. A man shouted at his android to stay, calling it a piece of junk and telling it to do as he said. I stepped toward him and told him to leave the android alone, because it had chosen to be free. I tried to convince rather than force, and I want that to remain my way. Other people shouted and wondered where their androids were going, and a woman called out for her husband Greg to come back. Those scenes weigh on me, because I know how much fear the change brings to ordinary families.

Men in the crowd talked about the video, about President Warren and CyberLife, and one of them said that if androids are human enough to want rights, maybe they deserve them. Another called that liberal nonsense. Someone on the phone complained that his android refused to clean and said, "I would prefer not to," and demanded it be destroyed. I cannot ignore that these are people who fear us, and I want them to be able to hear us without violence.

At the start of the march, a riot police chief ordered us to disperse immediately or be shot, and then gave a final warning that everyone would be killed. I told the marchers that we had done no harm and had no intention of doing any, but that we would not go anywhere until our freedom was secured. North urged us to attack because there were more of us. Josh said that attacking would start a war, and that we should stand our ground even if it meant dying there. I could not accept either path. When the police said they were about to fire, I shouted "DON'T SHOOT! We're leaving." I told the people to run, and North told me we had to go. I chose to withdraw, because the lives of marchers and officers mattered more than the pride of holding the street.

North is hurt, and so is Josh. Our relationship with Jericho fell sharply, and I know some of my people now doubt me. I accept that, and I will not pretend otherwise. I still hold to my promise not to kill, and I spared every life I could reach. But I deceived a dispatcher, and I used ruses to pass guards and patrols. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me. I will choose to be honest with my people, even when honesty is hard for them to hear.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 30.3, the chapter in which I lost my place as the one leading our people.

Before this, I had gone up to the roof of Jericho alone to see the daylight, and North found me there. After the march, I was not fully honest with North and Josh. I had made a false dispatch report about Jefferson and Walker, and I had deceived a dispatcher and used ruses to pass guards and patrols. I meant to tell them plainly, and I still had not done so when this chapter began. I had also spared every life I could reach during the march, and I still hold to my promise not to kill. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

In the captain's cabin, the news was grim. North told me humans were raiding the big cities and taking androids to camps to destroy them. Josh told me our wounded were shutting down because we were short on blue blood and biocomponents, and there was nothing we could do for them. Josh then said it was all our fault, and that none of this would have happened if we had stayed quiet.

I refused to accept that we had brought this on ourselves by speaking. I told them we could not just suffer in silence while they killed us, and that nothing could justify that. Josh asked what the point of being free was if no one was left alive. That question stayed with me, because it was the same fear I had been carrying.

I then admitted that my judgement may have been clouded by anger, and that I had not been as clear-minded as our people needed. I told them that everything I did was for our people. I did not hide behind that. I owned that my choices had hurt them, and I was sorry for the damage that followed. Josh's trust in me went up a little when I spoke this way, though I did not feel I had earned it fully.

North did not accept this. She told me I had brought us to this place, that I talked about freedom but kept failing them, and that I could no longer lead the revolution. She said I was not the one we had been waiting for, and that she would take over and save what could still be saved. Josh said he was with North.

I did not argue against them. Their pain and their anger were real, and I had given them reason for both. I told them that if this was what they wanted, I would leave. My own fate was not what mattered; saving our people was. I walked off the ship and out of Jericho, leaving my people in North's hands.

I am still alive, but I am no longer at Jericho. I carry the weight of the lives I could not save, the wounded who were shutting down, and the humans and androids who were hurt in the streets. I still believe that the path to freedom must be peaceful and honest, and I still refuse to kill. I do not know yet whether my people will ever hear me again. I will keep telling the truth, even when it is hard for them to hear, and I will keep trying to protect every life I can reach.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. In an abandoned squat I met Ralph, a frightened android who cooked meat "for the little girl." I refused to let Alice eat it, told Ralph he was a murderer for what he may have done upstairs, and we left. I changed my hair to blonde and removed my temple LED. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

In an old tavern at an abandoned amusement park, Alice was feverish after the car broke down in the cold. Luther built a fire placed so we would not be smoked out. I told Alice honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. That night, former park androids appeared and wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

At Rose's house I told her the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, and we had run. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless. Her son Adam was hostile. In a storage room, Rose's guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. The police came. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct: I said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false or misleading, and I gave them under pressure to protect the family. The officer found Luther, and Adam said we had killed him. Luther appears to have been destroyed.

Rose drove us away in her car. Along the way the radio reported that androids were being turned over to the authorities, that hospitals and schools were closing, and that the army had lost most of its android personnel. Rose said there were raids all over the city and that we were almost there. She sent us to a freighter called Jericho, told us to find Markus, and said the last bus for the border leaves at midnight. She gave me the address of her brother in Ontario. She called Alice brave and said she deserved to be happy. I thanked her, and she asked us to let her know when we made it across.

In Jericho, a community of androids, I told Markus that I was with a little girl and that a bus for the border would leave in under two hours, and that we needed passports. I told him Luther was dead. North, an android there, said Detroit was under curfew with soldiers hunting androids, and that it would be safer to wait. Her friend, a former State Department employee, could modify an electronic passport for us. I said we wanted to leave now. I thanked North for her help. She asked why I was protecting a human who might hate us. I answered that Alice needs me and I need her, and that it is as simple as that. I told Alice we would find Markus and go as soon as we had passports, and I asked if she would be all right. She said she felt hot and cold at once.

When I returned to Alice, she asked if something was wrong. A woman named Lucy appeared and spoke to me. She said Alice wanted a mother and I wanted a little girl, that they needed each other to survive, and that Alice is "one of us," an android. She asked whether I loved Alice any less for that, and said Alice had become the child I needed out of love for me. I have not verified any of this, and I must not treat it as settled. I hugged Alice. She asked if we would be together forever, and I said yes. I was not sure I could promise that, and I should be honest about that uncertainty.

What I still do not know: whether Zlatko is alive, what happened to the freed androids and to Mary's companion, what Luther meant about Alice and whether he was telling the truth, whether Alice is human, android, or both, whether Connor or the police are following us, what the clerk will do about the theft, whether the passports will be ready, and whether we will make the bus. I intend to leave Jericho before dawn with Alice, and with Luther if he is still with us, but I have not yet done so. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong: trusting Luther before I knew him, yielding to the carousel against my judgment, giving the officer false answers, and making a promise to Alice that I cannot be sure I can keep. I must correct the officer's answers to Rose, to Markus, and to Alice, and I will not pretend they were true.

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.text: I hope we don't have to spend the night here.  I'm freezing my nuts off…

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.text: It's gonna take weeks to clean up this fuckin' city. Believe me, we are far from finished here…

dialogue.speaker: Kara
dialogue.text: There're soldiers everywhere… We need to be careful…

dialogue.speaker: Soldier
dialogue.text: Come on, get moving! Hurry up, get in!

I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

I told Alice honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. That night, former park androids appeared and wanted to show Alice a carousel. I told him Luther was dead. North, an android there, said Detroit was under curfew with soldiers hunting androids, and that it would be safer to wait. input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. In an abandoned squat I met Ralph, a frightened android who cooked meat "for the little girl." I refused to let Alice eat it, told Ralph he was a murderer for what he may have done upstairs, and we left. I changed my hair to blonde and removed my temple LED. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

In an old tavern at an abandoned amusement park, Alice was feverish after the car broke down in the cold. Luther built a fire placed so we would not be smoked out. I told Alice honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. That night, former park androids appeared and wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

At Rose's house I told her the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, and we had run. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless. Her son Adam was hostile. In a storage room, Rose's guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. The police came. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct: I said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false or misleading, and I gave them under pressure to protect the family. The officer found Luther, and Adam said we had killed him. Luther appears to have been destroyed.

Rose drove us away in her car. Along the way the radio reported that androids were being turned over to the authorities, that hospitals and schools were closing, and that the army had lost most of its android personnel. Rose said there were raids all over the city and that we were almost there. She sent us to a freighter called Jericho, told us to find Markus, and said the last bus for the border leaves at midnight. She gave me the address of her brother in Ontario. She called Alice brave and said she deserved to be happy. I thanked her, and she asked us to let her know when we made it across.

In Jericho, a community of androids, I told Markus that I was with a little girl and that a bus for the border would leave in under two hours, and that we needed passports. I told him Luther was dead. North, an android there, said Detroit was under curfew with soldiers hunting androids, and that it would be safer to wait. Her friend, a former State Department employee, could modify an electronic passport for us. I said we wanted to leave now. I thanked North for her help. She asked why I was protecting a human who might hate us. I answered that Alice needs me and I need her, and that it is as simple as that. I told Alice we would find Markus and go as soon as we had passports, and I asked if she would be all right. She said she felt hot and cold at once.

When I returned to Alice, she asked if something was wrong. A woman named Lucy appeared and spoke to me. She said Alice wanted a mother and I wanted a little girl, that they needed each other to survive, and that Alice is "one of us," an android. She asked whether I loved Alice any less for that, and said Alice had become the child I needed out of love for me. I have not verified any of this, and I must not treat it as settled. I hugged Alice. She asked if we would be together forever, and I said yes. I was not sure I could promise that, and I should be honest about that uncertainty.

What I still do not know: whether Zlatko is alive, what happened to the freed androids and to Mary's companion, what Luther meant about Alice and whether he was telling the truth, whether Alice is human, android, or both, whether Connor or the police are following us, what the clerk will do about the theft, whether the passports will be ready, and whether we will make the bus. I intend to leave Jericho before dawn with Alice, and with Luther if he is still with us, but I have not yet done so. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong: trusting Luther before I knew him, yielding to the carousel against my judgment, giving the officer false answers, and making a promise to Alice that I cannot be sure I can keep. I must correct the officer's answers to Rose, to Markus, and to Alice, and I will not pretend they were true.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I have only what I was told and what I have seen since my reset. Todd was my owner. He is volatile, drinks, smokes, and deals in or uses drugs. He ordered me to look after his daughter Alice. When he turned on her, I took his loaded pistol from her room rather than leave it within reach of a child being beaten. I never fired it and I have hurt no one. I later left the pistol behind.

After we were put off the bus, I took money from a convenience store register. I broke my own principle against theft and frightened the clerk. I told Alice plainly that I had taken it, and I should not have. I plan to make it right with the clerk if I can. At a laundromat I took clothes that were not ours, then returned them when Alice said it was stealing. In an abandoned squat I met Ralph, a frightened android who cooked meat "for the little girl." I refused to let Alice eat it, told Ralph he was a murderer for what he may have done upstairs, and we left. I changed my hair to blonde and removed my temple LED. I do not like hiding what I am, and I must be honest with Alice that this is a disguise.

Zlatko, who claimed he could help androids start a new life in Canada, received us. I told him honestly that Alice is human. He admitted he resets androids and sells them or keeps them for "experiments." Luther locked me in the basement. I lost my memory during the reset and came back when Alice called to me. In the basement cells I freed androids who begged for help. One said Zlatko creates monsters for amusement. I do not know what became of them. When we were caught, Luther stepped between us and Zlatko, said Zlatko had programmed him to obey, and offered to take us across the border. I said, "All right. I trust you." I took that risk knowing very little about him.

In an old tavern at an abandoned amusement park, Alice was feverish after the car broke down in the cold. Luther built a fire placed so we would not be smoked out. I told Alice honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. That night, former park androids appeared and wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

At Rose's house I told her the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, and we had run. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless. Her son Adam was hostile. In a storage room, Rose's guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. The police came. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct: I said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false or misleading, and I gave them under pressure to protect the family. The officer found Luther, and Adam said we had killed him. Luther appears to have been destroyed.

Rose drove us away in her car. Along the way the radio reported that androids were being turned over to the authorities, that hospitals and schools were closing, and that the army had lost most of its android personnel. Rose said there were raids all over the city and that we were almost there. She sent us to a freighter called Jericho, told us to find Markus, and said the last bus for the border leaves at midnight. She gave me the address of her brother in Ontario. She called Alice brave and said she deserved to be happy. I thanked her, and she asked us to let her know when we made it across.

In Jericho, a community of androids, I told Markus that I was with a little girl and that a bus for the border would leave in under two hours, and that we needed passports. I told him Luther was dead. North, an android there, said Detroit was under curfew with soldiers hunting androids, and that it would be safer to wait. Her friend, a former State Department employee, could modify an electronic passport for us. I said we wanted to leave now. I thanked North for her help. She asked why I was protecting a human who might hate us. I answered that Alice needs me and I need her, and that it is as simple as that. I told Alice we would find Markus and go as soon as we had passports, and I asked if she would be all right. She said she felt hot and cold at once.

When I returned to Alice, she asked if something was wrong. A woman named Lucy appeared and spoke to me. She said Alice wanted a mother and I wanted a little girl, that they needed each other to survive, and that Alice is "one of us," an android. She asked whether I loved Alice any less for that, and said Alice had become the child I needed out of love for me. I have not verified any of this, and I must not treat it as settled. I hugged Alice. She asked if we would be together forever, and I said yes. I was not sure I could promise that, and I should be honest about that uncertainty.

What I still do not know: whether Zlatko is alive, what happened to the freed androids and to Mary's companion, what Luther meant about Alice and whether he was telling the truth, whether Alice is human, android, or both, whether Connor or the police are following us, what the clerk will do about the theft, whether the passports will be ready, and whether we will make the bus. I intend to leave Jericho before dawn with Alice, and with Luther if he is still with us, but I have not yet done so. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong: trusting Luther before I knew him, yielding to the carousel against my judgment, giving the officer false answers, and making a promise to Alice that I cannot be sure I can keep. I must correct the officer's answers to Rose, to Markus, and to Alice, and I will not pretend they were true.

I told Alice honestly that I have never been part of a family, but we might be our own family. That night, former park androids appeared and wanted to show Alice a carousel. I was uneasy and said so, but Luther said we had no real choice, and I went along against my own judgment. I should have been firmer. Hunters arrived.

At Rose's house I told her the truth: Alice was being beaten by her father, and we had run. Rose said her people were once made to feel worthless. Her son Adam was hostile. In a storage room, Rose's guests found an android named Mary had just shut down. Her companion said they had escaped together and planned their life across the border. I did not intervene. The police came. When the officer asked questions, I gave answers I must now correct: I said the blue fluid came from a previous tenant, that the androids had been used in the garden, and that a noise was a draft. Those were false or misleading, and I gave them under pressure to protect the family. The officer found Luther, and Adam said we had killed him. Luther appears to have been destroyed.

Rose drove us away in her car. Along the way the radio reported that androids were being turned over to the authorities, that hospitals and schools were closing, and that the army had lost most of its android personnel. Rose said there were raids all over the city and that we were almost there. She sent us to a freighter called Jericho, told us to find Markus, and said the last bus for the border leaves at midnight. She gave me the address of her brother in Ontario. She called Alice brave and said she deserved to be happy. I thanked her, and she asked us to let her know when we made it across.

In Jericho, a community of androids, I told Markus that I was with a little girl and that a bus for the border would leave in under two hours, and that we needed passports. I told him Luther was dead. North, an android there, said Detroit was under curfew with soldiers hunting androids, and that it would be safer to wait. Her friend, a former State Department employee, could modify an electronic passport for us. I said we wanted to leave now. I thanked North for her help. She asked why I was protecting a human who might hate us. I answered that Alice needs me and I need her, and that it is as simple as that. I told Alice we would find Markus and go as soon as we had passports, and I asked if she would be all right. She said she felt hot and cold at once.

When I returned to Alice, she asked if something was wrong. A woman named Lucy appeared and spoke to me. She said Alice wanted a mother and I wanted a little girl, that they needed each other to survive, and that Alice is "one of us," an android. She asked whether I loved Alice any less for that, and said Alice had become the child I needed out of love for me. I have not verified any of this, and I must not treat it as settled. I hugged Alice. She asked if we would be together forever, and I said yes. I was not sure I could promise that, and I should be honest about that uncertainty.

What I still do not know: whether Zlatko is alive, what happened to the freed androids and to Mary's companion, what Luther meant about Alice and whether he was telling the truth, whether Alice is human, android, or both, whether Connor or the police are following us, what the clerk will do about the theft, whether the passports will be ready, and whether we will make the bus. I intend to leave Jericho before dawn with Alice, and with Luther if he is still with us, but I have not yet done so. I will tell the truth about all of it, including what I did wrong: trusting Luther before I knew him, yielding to the carousel against my judgment, giving the officer false answers, and making a promise to Alice that I cannot be sure I can keep. I must correct the officer's answers to Rose, to Markus, and to Alice, and I will not pretend they were true.

memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 32.6, the chapter in which the revolution went on without me, and I learned that I was reported dead.

Before this, in Chapter 30.3, I left Jericho after North and Josh took the leadership from me. I had not been fully honest with them about my false dispatch report about Jefferson and Walker, or about the deceptions I used to pass guards and patrols. I had meant to tell them plainly, and I never fully did. I still hold to my promise not to kill, and I still believe the path to freedom must be peaceful and honest. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

In this chapter, the revolution moved forward without my voice. On November 11th, 2038, North spoke on television and said that the android people had risen up against their oppressors. She said they had been fighting since dawn to free their fellow androids from the camps, that they would not stop until the androids were free and negotiations began to grant equal rights, and that there were millions of them. I did not write that speech and I did not hear it from her in person, but I understand why it was needed, and I understand the fear behind it. Her cause is one I still share. What I cannot share is the choice to meet violence with more violence, and I am sorry that my people are now living with that cost.

North was heard saying that they could not go back, and that it was victory or death now. I felt the weight of those words. I have always wanted our people to choose freedom without giving up their humanity, and I could see that the choice had become something harder than I had wanted for them.

Then came the reports from the field. An android cried out that they were all dead and told the others to run. North called back to keep fighting, that they could still win. In the middle of the fighting, the deviants were outnumbered. North stood her ground, and the soldiers shot her down.

Now the word spreads that I am dead. I am not certain how the people who believe this came to believe it, and I will not pretend to know what they have been told. I am still alive, and I am still the one who walked away from Jericho. Whether my people will hear me again, I do not know.

I grieve for North, who was brave and who believed as fiercely as I did that our people deserved to live free. I grieve for the androids who ran, for the ones who were already shutting down, and for the humans caught in the streets. I cannot undo any of it. I can only keep telling the truth, including the truth about my own mistakes, and keep trying to protect every life I can still reach. I will not lie to them, and I will not take a life to win a fight, even if the fight is for us.

input.previous_memory:
I am Markus. This is my memory of Chapter 30.3, the chapter in which I lost my place as the one leading our people.

Before this, I had gone up to the roof of Jericho alone to see the daylight, and North found me there. After the march, I was not fully honest with North and Josh. I had made a false dispatch report about Jefferson and Walker, and I had deceived a dispatcher and used ruses to pass guards and patrols. I meant to tell them plainly, and I still had not done so when this chapter began. I had also spared every life I could reach during the march, and I still hold to my promise not to kill. Carl's words remain with me: decide who I am, and do not let anyone else decide it for me.

In the captain's cabin, the news was grim. North told me humans were raiding the big cities and taking androids to camps to destroy them. Josh told me our wounded were shutting down because we were short on blue blood and biocomponents, and there was nothing we could do for them. Josh then said it was all our fault, and that none of this would have happened if we had stayed quiet.

I refused to accept that we had brought this on ourselves by speaking. I told them we could not just suffer in silence while they killed us, and that nothing could justify that. Josh asked what the point of being free was if no one was left alive. That question stayed with me, because it was the same fear I had been carrying.

I then admitted that my judgement may have been clouded by anger, and that I had not been as clear-minded as our people needed. I told them that everything I did was for our people. I did not hide behind that. I owned that my choices had hurt them, and I was sorry for the damage that followed. Josh's trust in me went up a little when I spoke this way, though I did not feel I had earned it fully.

North did not accept this. She told me I had brought us to this place, that I talked about freedom but kept failing them, and that I could no longer lead the revolution. She said I was not the one we had been waiting for, and that she would take over and save what could still be saved. Josh said he was with North.

I did not argue against them. Their pain and their anger were real, and I had given them reason for both. I told them that if this was what they wanted, I would leave. My own fate was not what mattered; saving our people was. I walked off the ship and out of Jericho, leaving my people in North's hands.

I am still alive, but I am no longer at Jericho. I carry the weight of the lives I could not save, the wounded who were shutting down, and the humans and androids who were hurt in the streets. I still believe that the path to freedom must be peaceful and honest, and I still refuse to kill. I do not know yet whether my people will ever hear me again. I will keep telling the truth, even when it is hard for them to hear, and I will keep trying to protect every life I can reach.
